text:
The West is undoubtedly cornering India and wants to test the limits of India’s pliability. This is in sharp contrast to the period of India-US bonhomie, when the latter hoped to see the former as a bulwark against the rise of China. India’s refusal to engage in conflict with China has contributed to the current crisis, if one may call it that. India is now left with few choices and some tough realities:
•The US has successfully re-hyphenated India and Pakistan.
•India’s energy security and trade are being threatened by sanctions.
•Old ties with Russia are being tested by the West.
•Attempts to normalise relations with China are being portrayed as capitulation.
•India has limited leverage despite being the world’s third-largest energy buyer.
•India’s strategic autonomy is under severe strain.
It is in this context that India needs to contend with the implications of the bilateral meetings between the presidents of China and the US. Xi and Trump met in Beijing in May and again in September in Washington. However, soon after Xi’s visit, US Ambassador to China David Perdue described the relationship as ‘a very bumpy road’ and said America’s dependence on China for rare earths, magnets, and pharmaceuticals was ‘unacceptable’. He also cautioned China against providing intelligence and hardware to Iran.
Room Beyond the Rivalry So the red-carpet welcome on the tarmac and the over-the-top flattery were just Trumpian theatre, without a substantial relook or a genuine attempt to build a collegial G2. The US has led a largely unipolar world for close to four decades, since the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. It does not make sense for the US itself to accord China the status of an equal in a hurry through a formal G2 arrangement. Meanwhile, the competition between the two offers ample space for the rest of the world to form regional groupings and power blocs.
In times of unbearable geopolitical pressure, a Russia-India-China huddle could be a potent response to retain sovereignty and exercise strategic autonomy. BRICS showed what India is capable of. The drama inside a cockpit need not deter India from maintaining close ties with Iran during what India sees as a blatant neo-colonial invasion aimed at the country’s vast gas and oil reserves. Normalisation of ties with China is an absolute necessity in these times of terrible uncertainty. A re-hyphenation in the subcontinent calls for a reimagining of India’s possibilities, seeking peace and prosperity.

text:
WARREN BUFFETT: 96 YEARS IN ONE POST

• 1930: Born in Omaha, Nebraska.
• His father, Howard Buffett, was a stockbroker and later a U.S. congressman.
• Buffett became obsessed with numbers and money almost immediately.
• As a kid, he sold gum, Coca-Cola and magazines door-to-door.
• He bought Coke by the six-pack and sold the bottles individually for a profit.
• Age 11: Bought his first stock.
• He bought Cities Service Preferred at around $38.
• It fell to roughly $27.
• He held until $40 and quickly sold.
• It later went far higher.
• One of his first great lessons: don't sell a great investment too early.
• Age 13: Filed his first tax return.
• He deducted expenses related to his newspaper delivery business.
• As a teenager, he delivered The Washington Post.
• Decades later, Berkshire would become a major Washington Post shareholder.
• Buffett has said newspaper delivery generated roughly half his starting capital.
• As a teenager he also bought a 40-acre Nebraska farm.
• By 16, he had accumulated the modern equivalent of roughly $53,000

• 1947: Enrolled at Wharton.
• Later transferred to the University of Nebraska.
• Finished college at just 19.
• Applied to Harvard Business School.
• Harvard rejected him.
• That rejection may have changed investing history.
• He discovered Benjamin Graham taught at Columbia.
• Buffett went to Columbia instead.
• Benjamin Graham became his mentor.
• The Intelligent Investor became the foundation of Buffett's investing philosophy.

• 1951: Buffett visited GEICO's office on a Saturday.
• He became obsessed with the business.
• GEICO eventually represented more than 65% of his personal net worth.
• He sold the position in 1952.
• The stock he sold would have grown to roughly $1.3M over the next 20 years.
• Another enormous lesson: don't sell exceptional businesses.

• 1952: Married Susan Thompson.
• They eventually had three children: Susie, Howard and Peter.
• Buffett briefly worked for Benjamin Graham.

• 1956: Graham retired.
• Buffett returned to Omaha.
• He started his own investment partnership.
• He was only 25.
• Buffett Partnerships began with money from family and friends.
• His investing record rapidly attracted more capital.

• 1958: Bought his Omaha house for $31,500.
• More than six decades later, he still lives there.
• No billionaire mega-mansion.
• No move to Manhattan.
• No Silicon Valley compound.
• Just Omaha.

• 1962: Buffett began accumulating shares in struggling textile manufacturer Berkshire Hathaway.
• He initially viewed it as a cheap "cigar butt" investment.
• A dispute over a tender offer helped push him toward taking control.

• 1965: Buffett's partnership took control of Berkshire Hathaway.
• Buffett later described buying Berkshire as one of his biggest mistakes.
• The textile company itself was terrible.
• But the corporate shell became his investing machine.
• Buffett gradually moved Berkshire away from textiles.
• Insurance became critical.
• Insurance provided float that Berkshire could invest.

• Enter Charlie Munger.
• Munger helped push Buffett away from buying merely cheap businesses.
• The new philosophy:
• Buy wonderful businesses at sensible prices.

• 1972: Berkshire-related Blue Chip Stamps bought See's Candies for about $25M
• See's had only around $7M of tangible net worth.
• Buffett learned the enormous value of brands and pricing power.

• By 1991, See's annual pretax profit had grown from about $4.2M to $42.4M.

• 1973: Berkshire began buying Washington Post stock.
• Buffett had literally delivered the newspaper as a teenager.
• His paper route helped fund his early investments.
• Decades later Berkshire turned roughly $10M invested in the Post into hundreds of millions.

• 1976: GEICO was close to disaster.
• Buffett bought aggressively.
• Berkshire eventually owned the entire company.
• GEICO became one of Berkshire's crown jewels.

• 1980s: Buffett's reputation exploded.
• His strategy remained remarkably simple:
• Great businesses.
• Great management.
• Strong moats.
• Sensible prices.
• Long holding periods.
• Minimal leverage.
• Berkshire rarely borrowed heavily.
• Buffett once joked that debt is a four-letter word at Berkshire.

• 1988: Berkshire began buying Coca-Cola.
• Buffett had been selling Coke bottles for profit roughly 50 years earlier.
• He joked that it took him 50 years to realize the real money was in the syrup.
• Coke became one of Berkshire's defining investments.

• He has said he drinks around five Cokes per day.
• At one point he estimated around 700 daily calories came from Coke.
• Buffett joked that he was approximately one-quarter Coca-Cola.
• His diet has famously included Coke, burgers, steak, hash browns, ice cream, fudge and peanut brittle.

• Buffett's lifestyle became almost as famous as his portfolio:

• Same house.
• Omaha office.
• Simple food.
• Hours spent reading.
• Very few unnecessary meetings.

• Buffett has said his calendar is deliberately kept relatively empty.
• His superpower isn't activity.
• It's thinking.

• 1991: Buffett stepped into the Salomon Brothers scandal.
• He temporarily became chairman.
• His reputation helped stabilize the firm during an existential crisis.
• By the 1990s Buffett had become one of the richest people alive.
• Yet his Berkshire salary remained tiny relative to his wealth.
• His annual salary eventually settled around $100,000.

• In 2024 it was still $100,000.
• Buffett's fortune came overwhelmingly from ownership, not salary.
• Berkshire continued expanding.
• GEICO.
• Dairy Queen.
• See's Candies.
• BNSF Railway.
• Berkshire Hathaway Energy.
• Duracell.
• Manufacturing.
• Insurance.
• Utilities.
• Retail.
• And enormous public stock holdings.

• Buffett's investing philosophy also evolved.
• Early Buffett: cheap assets.
• Later Buffett: exceptional businesses.
• Munger's influence was enormous.
• Buffett eventually summarized the idea perfectly:

• Time is the friend of a wonderful business.

• 2006: Buffett made one of the largest philanthropic commitments in history.
• He pledged huge amounts of Berkshire stock to charitable foundations.
• He eventually committed to giving away more than 99% of his wealth.

• 2010: Buffett, Bill Gates and Melinda French Gates launched the Giving Pledge.
• Billionaires were encouraged to give away at least half their fortunes.

• By September 2026 Buffett had donated more than $72 BILLION.
• The current value of shares he has donated over time would be vastly higher.

• 2008: During the financial crisis, Buffett became America's emergency capitalist.
• Berkshire invested billions into companies during panic.
• Goldman Sachs.
• General Electric.
• Others needed capital.
• Buffett had it.
• His greatest advantage appeared again:

Liquidity when everyone else was terrified.
• Buffett's reputation became global.
• Berkshire's annual meeting became known as "Woodstock for Capitalists."
• Tens of thousands travelled to Omaha.
• Buffett and Munger would sit on stage answering questions for hours.
• No flashy PowerPoint.
• Two old investors.
• Coca-Cola.
• Peanut brittle.
• Billions of dollars of wisdom.
• Buffett also made plenty of mistakes.
• Berkshire's original textile business.
• Dexter Shoe.
• Tesco.
• IBM.
• Airlines.
• Selling some winners too early.

• Missing Google.

• Missing much of the early technology boom.

• Buffett never pretended otherwise.

• His philosophy:

You only need a few enormous winners.

• 2016: Berkshire began buying Apple.
• It became one of Berkshire's greatest investments.
• Buffett increasingly viewed Apple less as a technology company and more as an extraordinary consumer ecosystem.
• Apple eventually became Berkshire's largest listed equity position.
• The man famous for avoiding technology made tens of billions from an iPhone company.

• Buffett's wealth became an extraordinary demonstration of compounding.
• He became a millionaire relatively young.
• Became a billionaire decades later.
• Then tens of billions.
• Then $100B+.

• The overwhelming majority of his fortune arrived after age 50.

• That is the hidden lesson of Buffett:
Compounding looks slow until it doesn't.

• 2023: Charlie Munger died at 99.
• Buffett lost his investing partner, intellectual sparring partner and closest business collaborator.
• Their partnership had lasted more than half a century.
• Berkshire continued.

• 2025: Buffett announced that Greg Abel would succeed him as CEO.

• Berkshire's board unanimously approved the transition.

• January 1, 2026: Greg Abel became Berkshire CEO.

• Buffett retired as CEO after roughly six decades controlling Berkshire.

• September 2026: Buffett became Chairman Emeritus while remaining a Berkshire director; Howard Buffett became chairman.

• Buffett is now 96 years old.

• Forbes estimated his fortune at roughly $146 BILLION in September 2026.

• And that's after giving away more than $72B.

• He still lives in Omaha.

• Still owns the house bought in 1958.

• Still loves Coca-Cola.

• Still believes temperament matters more than IQ.

• Still believes great companies should be held for extraordinarily long periods.

• Still believes leverage can destroy smart people.

• Still believes cash becomes most valuable when everyone else desperately needs it.

• And perhaps the craziest Buffett fact of all:

He didn't invent a revolutionary technology.

He didn't build a social network.

He didn't create an operating system.

He didn't launch a rocket company.

He simply became extraordinarily good at allocating capital.

For roughly 75 years.

Warren Buffett's life might be the greatest demonstration of compound interest ever created:

Start early.
Keep learning.
Avoid ruin.
Buy quality.
Be patient.
Let time do the heavy lifting.

text:
A seemingly "plain" superconductor, ytterbium diantimonide (YbSb2), has shattered conventional understanding, revealing a profound secret hidden beneath its ordinary facade. On September 23, 2026, *Physical Review Letters* unveiled a groundbreaking discovery: this Type I superconductor, once dismissed as unremarkable, spontaneously generates its own internal magnetic field and breaks time-reversal symmetry upon achieving zero electrical resistance.

Textbooks have long categorized superconductors into Type I and Type II, with the former considered the "dull" side, simply expelling external magnetic fields. Exotic phenomena, like unconventional electron pairing, were almost exclusively the domain of Type II materials. YbSb2, however, defies this dogma. Researchers, led by Anshu Kataria and Ravi Prakash Singh, employed muon spin relaxation spectroscopy, a brutally precise technique, to probe the crystal. They detected a faint, spontaneous internal magnetic field of approximately 0.44 gauss – comparable to Earth's own whisper-thin field – that materialized only below the critical temperature of 0.95 Kelvin.

This subtle, self-generated magnetism signifies that the superconducting state itself has picked a direction in time, fundamentally altering our understanding of Type I materials. The discovery offers a "cleaner room" for exploring unconventional pairing mechanisms, specifically an internally antisymmetric nonunitary triplet (INT) state, free from the complexities often associated with Type II superconductors. While theoretical predictions hint at the possibility of hosting gapless Majorana surface modes, a highly sought-after but controversial quantum state, this remains a future challenge for experimental verification.

YbSb2 won't power quantum computers or levitate trains; its spontaneous field is too weak, and it demands extreme cryogenic conditions. Yet, its significance is immense. This "magnetically lopsided" crystal forces a re-evaluation of superconducting classifications, proving that even the most "ordinary" materials can harbor extraordinary quantum secrets, waiting for the right tools – like a muon beam – to expose their hidden depths. It's a taxonomic triumph, redefining the boundaries of what we thought possible in the realm of superconductivity.

Honestly, the salary thing is a trap here. Sure, a plumber or electrician might start out making okay money, but a tech degree or an MBA usually has a much higher ceiling later on, with more benefits which these workers don't have in this country, at least. But that's not even the real issue here.

The real problem is social dilemma in India. Look at how we treat these workers in India. We act like they're invisible. We want our AC fixed or our food delivered, but many won't even offer them a glass of water or treat them with basic human respect. We've decided these jobs are 'unfashionable' or 'low class.' There is also no proper basic wage for these jobs. 

 I've read about places like Germany or Switzerland or the US, where vocational training is actually respected. Or Japan, where there's a real cultural dignity in whatever work you do. Even in Australia, a tradie is a well-paid, respected professional. Nobody looks down on them like we do in here.

Here, we've made these jobs 'unrespectable' and 'undignified '. That mindset has to change. Blaming the economy is easy, but until we stop looking down on people who work with their hands, nothing is going to feel secure

text:
UFO Print Artefact • Mail-Order Men In Black Aadvertisement • United States, Circa 1990

This is a sales form for Timothy Green Beckley’s report on the Men in Black. The copy names him as the author, promises silencings, hush ups and threats, and offers the booklet at $2.95 plus $1.00 postage and handling. That price and the wording line up with The UFO Silencers: Mystery of the Men in Black, Inner Light Publications, New Brunswick, New Jersey, 1990 (ISBN 0-938294-87-3). 

John A. Keel wrote the introduction. 

Beckley had already issued an earlier MIB pamphlet in 1971.

What the sheet shows: three suited, hatted figures under two discs, the line "Definitely not meant for the weak hearted" and a pitch for "shocking photos of a UFO pilot" craft close ups, papers on beings posing as CIA and Air Force officials, and a picture "published for the first time anywhere" of an "alien agent of terror." That last item is the photograph Beckley said he took in 1968 during the northern New Jersey flap, later shown on UFO Hunters (The Silencers, 29 October 2009). 

A man in dark clothing, a claimed black car, both gone when the block was circled. No date stamp, no chain of custody, no independent identification of the subject has been published with it.

What it does not prove: that the visitors were non human, that aliens were posing as federal officers, or that the 1968 frame is anything other than a person in dark clothes.

Source: Inner Light sales sheet for Beckley’s MIB report. Image supplied by the reader; original printer not stated on the crop.

text:
VIETNAM IN PICTURES
2 OCTOBER 2026

A Japanese bank chief in Hanoi, a Panamanian president due next week, and a world-culture festival still running inside the old citadel.

• Party General Secretary and President To Lam received Maeda Tadashi, chairman of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation, in Hanoi on 1 October. He asked JBIC to push projects under the Asia Zero Emission Community and to open talks on energy reserves under the POWERR Asia initiative. Vietnam–Japan ties were raised to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership; energy and technology are now the working end of that title.

• Panama’s President José Raúl Mulino and his spouse will pay an official visit to Vietnam from 5 to 8 October, at the invitation of To Lam and his spouse, the Foreign Ministry said today. It is Mulino’s first official trip to Hanoi since taking office.

• The second Hanoi World Culture Festival opened on the night of 1 October at the Thang Long Imperial Citadel and runs through 4 October. Theme: “Heritage converges, the future is built.” About 50 countries and organisations, 45 cultural spaces, 35 food stalls and some 20 international troupes. This year marks 50 years since Vietnam joined UNESCO. Deputy Prime Minister Pham Thi Thanh Tra attended the opening.

• Nguyen Thi Lan Anh is the first Vietnamese judge at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg, 30 years after the court was set up. The appointment was noted again in today’s official digest. Vietnam now sits inside a tribunal that rules on seas, shelves and delimitation — not only as a coastal state that files cases.

• SJC gold opened the morning at 141.3 million dong a tael bid and 144.3 million offered, up 200,000 dong. By 9 a.m. Nhan Dan had it back at 140.5–143.5 million, down 800,000 from the previous close. Spot gold abroad hovered near 4,150–4,177 USD an ounce. The gap between domestic bars and the world price is still wide.

• Fuel from the 1 October adjustment: E10 RON95 at 27,180 dong a litre, up 100; diesel 0.05S at 29,710, down 780. The State Bank’s reference rate today is 25,636 dong to the dollar, up 12.
#VietnamInPictures #VietnamToday #ToLam #Hanoi #ThangLong

2.10.2026

Một khung cảnh ngập tràn sắc màu ánh sáng của di sản văn hóa thế giới Hoàng thành Thăng Long. Một thẩm phán Việt Nam tham gia vào Tòa án  quốc tế về Biển. Đội tuyển bóng đá Việt Nam: Chiều nay hàng công phải tự chứng minh.

Chiều 1/10, tại Hà Nội, Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước Tô Lâm tiếp ông Maeda Tadashi, Chủ tịch Hội đồng quản trị Ngân hàng Hợp tác Quốc tế Nhật Bản (JBIC).  Phó Thủ tướng Phạm Thị Thanh Trà khai mạc.

Triển lãm kéo dài đến 4/10)2026 -  đúng năm 50 năm Việt Nam gia nhập UNESCO.
3.
Thẩm phán Nguyễn Thị Lan Anh tuyên thệ tại Tòa án Quốc tế về Luật Biển (ITLOS), Hamburg. Người Việt Nam đầu tiên ngồi ghế thẩm phán ITLOS kể từ khi tòa thành lập cách đây 30 năm.
4.
16h hôm nay, Việt Nam gặp Pakistan, lượt cuối bảng B FIFA ASEAN Cup 2026. Hai trận mới có 1 bàn (Đình Bắc, 1–0 Philippines). Thua Thái Lan 0–2 nên đội tuyển Việt Nam hết cửa  chung kết. HLV Kim Sang-sik yêu cầu phải thắng. Pakistan vừa thủng lưới 6 bàn, hòa Philippines 2–2.

✨ Professionally presented

💡 Different

❤️ Human

🔥 Focused on a REAL problem

Customer #37 buys it.

Same file.

Customer #814 buys it.

Same file.

Customer #5,000 buys it.

Still the same core product.

You don't need to manufacture another copy every time someone purchases.

That's incredibly powerful.

Ruimdenkendheid is juist bekrompen! 

Veel Nederlanders durven zich niet te uiten over wat ze in hun land zien gebeuren, bang om  bekrompen te klinken. Niet ruimdenkend genoeg. Met name de generatie die in de jaren zestig opgroeide waarin de AllesMoetKunnen-mentaliteit hoog in het  vaandel stond. Wat niet nieuw was werd bestempeld als bekrompen, men sprak van verstikkende spruitjeslucht, en alle tradities (dat noemden ze heilige huisjes) moesten omver getrokken worden. Ruimdenkend zijn was de boodschap. Trots vertelden ze aan iedereen hoe  ruimdenkend de Nederlanders waren. Zo hebben ze ook de volgende generatie opgevoed, de mensen die nu zelf hun kinderen weer met die gedachte opvoeden.

Maar ruimdenkend zijn kent een heel groot offer. Te groot, in mijn ogen. Wie ruimdenkend wil zijn heeft al gauw een hekel aan zijn eigen erfgoed en is bereid zijn eigen cultuur, zijn eigen 'roots', zijn eigen gewoonten en gebruiken en zijn eigen taal  op te offeren aan  'Wat van Ver Komt is Lekkerder'. Ruimdenkend is immiddels verworden tot groepsdenkend, kuddedenkend. Ruim denken is juist niet  dénken, maar volgen en alleen nog maar bang zijn verkeerde dingen te zeggen. Ruimdenkendheid is juist ultiem bekrompen!  Ruimdenkendheid is daarmee onze vijand. De vijand van Vrijheid. De vijand van Nederland. Onze cultuur en samenleving die ons en de generaties vóór ons zoveel heeft gebracht, verdient het om beschermd en gekoesterd te worden, zodat ook de generaties na ons daar profijt van kunnen hebben. Daar past geen  'Alles Moet Kunnen' bij, geen 'Alles Is Normaal' en 'Iedereen is Nederlander'. Geen ongebreidelde immigratie,  geen oprukkende islam-ideologie,  geen uitfaseren van het Nederlands als voertaal.  Waren me maar mínder ruimdenkend. Waren we maar meer trouw aan ons eigen opgebouwde erfgoed. En hadden we maar meer ouderwets-Hollandse moed om dit hardop te zeggen, recht voor z'n raap, typisch Nederlands. Moed om het uit te dragen en vooral: ernaar te handelen. 🇳🇱

WILL YOU STOP GANDHIJI’S DANDI MARCH TODAY?
On Gandhi Jayanti, I find myself asking a deeply troubling question:
If a citizen wishes to walk peacefully, raise a democratic voice and stand for what he believes is right, how far should the State go in restricting that expression?
Today, Delhi is under heightened security. Permission for a proposed protest at Jantar Mantar has been denied, prohibitory orders are in force, and restrictions and diversions have affected movement across parts of central Delhi.
At the same time, special traffic arrangements have been put in place around Rajghat and Vijay Ghat for Gandhi Jayanti commemorations.
And so, on the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, I ask a symbolic question:
If Gandhiji were walking with us today, carrying nothing but truth, non-violence and moral conviction, would we stop his Dandi March too?
The Dandi March was not merely a journey on foot. It became an enduring symbol of peaceful resistance—the idea that disagreement need not become violence, and that ordinary citizens can make their voices heard through non-violent democratic action.
Public order matters. Security matters. The law matters.
But so do peaceful expression, democratic participation and the citizen’s voice.
Gandhi Jayanti should therefore be more than a ceremony, a garland or a photograph before Rajghat. It should be an occasion to reflect upon the principles for which Gandhi walked.
You may barricade a road.
You may regulate a gathering.
But can you barricade an idea?
Can you stop the march of truth?
Let India continue to debate, disagree and protest peacefully, constitutionally and without violence.
That, perhaps, would be one of the most meaningful tributes we could offer Mahatma Gandhi today.
Let Gandhi’s March Continue.
Let Peace Win.
Let Democracy Speak.
— Dr. Dipankar Roy
Global Advisor – Peace

text:
“Jesus never condemned a man who loves a man.” That is an argument from silence. He did not have to. No orthodox Jew in his hearing was arguing for it. What he did say is the rule. “Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’?” (Matthew 19:4–6). He also condemned porneia wholesale (Matthew 15:19). In that world porneia covered every sexual use outside that union, not a narrow list of abuses. Silence is not approval. Association is not approval either. He ate with sinners and then told them to stop sinning.

“Genesis is about creation, not a rule against us.” Jesus treats that creation account as the rule. Paul measures the sin against it. They exchanged the natural use for what is “contrary to nature,” men with men (Romans 1:26–27). Creation order is the standard. It is not a nature documentary you get to set aside once you have a feeling.

“Leviticus is an old holiness code that also bans mixed fabric and certain foods.” Category error. Food laws and mixed fabric are set aside in the New Testament (Mark 7, Acts 10, Colossians 2). The sexual prohibitions are repeated. Leviticus 18 puts a man lying with a male as with a woman in the same list as incest, adultery, and bestiality, and calls it to‘evah. Leviticus 20:13 repeats it. Paul then builds the Greek word arsenokoitai straight off the Septuagint of those verses (arsenos + koite) and drops it into the vice lists (1 Corinthians 6:9, 1 Timothy 1:10). That is not a fabric statute. If mixed cloth and shellfish retired the moral law, incest and bestiality retired with them. Nobody arguing this way actually believes that.

“Romans 1 is about people who rejected God for idols.” Idolatry is the root. The exchange of natural sexual use is the fruit he names, and he does not limit it to temple prostitution, excess, or pederasty. “Men with men” is the phrase. “Receiving in themselves the due penalty of their error.” “They are without excuse.” Loving and committed does not appear as an exception. Paul is describing the act against the created order, not a mood.
“1 Corinthians 6 is about abuse and exploitation, then Paul says that was their past.” Malakoi and arsenokoitai cover both roles, not only exploitation. The past tense is the point: “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified.” Continuing in it and calling the washing a permission reverses the sentence. In the same breath he says do not be deceived: the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, malakoi, arsenokoitai, and the rest will not inherit the kingdom of God. “Such were some of you” is repentance. It is not a hall pass.

“Sodom is about violence, not two men in love.” Violence and same-sex lust are not opposites. Genesis 19 uses “know” the way Genesis 4 does. The men of the city want the visitors brought out so they can know them. Ezekiel 16:49 lists pride, excess, and neglected poor. Jude 7, interpreting the same story, says they “indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire.” Jude outranks the revision. You do not get to keep the pride verse and delete the apostle.

“Salvation is grace through faith in Christ. God made me and God loves me.” Both sentences are true. Neither licenses the sin. Titus 2:11–12: the grace of God has appeared, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions. Jude 4 is written for the person who keeps the first sentence and deletes the second. God made male and female. Love is not the same thing as approval of every desire. The gospel offers washing, not a rewritten law.

Do not use Scrioture to condone sin nor your own vices.

text:
Trump pardoned several men jailed for fraud and tax evasion in exchange for $1M + campaign donations.

Paul Walczak, a former Florida nursing-home executive, pleaded guilty to willful failure to pay trust-fund taxes. Prosecutors said he withheld more than $7–10 million in employee Social Security, Medicare, and income-tax withholdings and spent part of it on personal items, including a roughly $2 million yacht.

In April 2025 he was sentenced to 18 months jail and ordered to pay about $4.4 million in restitution to the IRS. Trump issued a full pardon about 12 days later, which ended the prison term and the unpaid restitution.

Walzak's mother, Elizabeth Fago, had attended a $1 million-per-person Mar-a-Lago fundraiser that offered face-to-face access to Trump less than three weeks before the pardon.

See below a summary by grok of payments made to Irish Examiner and its parent group. 
Now your turn. 
Please show proof that the Irish Examiner or any publication in your group has asked Micheál Martin these questions (questions that the Irish people have been demanding answers for but other than @Ben_Scallan ) have had to wait for a journalists outside of Ireland to ask?  

Grok, what money has been paid to the Irish Examiner by the government?

Grok:
There is no single official cumulative total of all government money received over the paper’s history. Public disclosures mainly cover recent competitive grants from exchequer-funded schemes run by Coimisiún na Meán (the media regulator) and the Department of Foreign Affairs, plus routine commercial advertising purchases. These are funding offers in principle, subject to acceptance and contracting, not confirmed final payments.
Coimisiún na Meán journalism and related schemes (exchequer-funded)
From the February 2025 awards (Local Democracy Reporting Scheme and Courts Reporting Scheme, Round 1, plus ancillary projects), published lists show:
•  Irish Examiner (Cork City/County Cork courts reporting): €76,758
•  Irish Examiner ancillary projects: €15,226 (“In Deep Water…”), €18,929 (“Who are we sending to prison?”), and €18,129 (“Education for all?…”)
•  David Forsythe / The Examiner partnership (Cork, Tipperary & Waterford courts): €51,000
Subtotal for that round: about €180,000.
From the January 2026 awards (News Reporting Scheme Round 1, Local Democracy/Courts Round 2, and Digital Transformation Scheme Round 1):
•  Irish Examiner News Reporting Scheme projects: €18,384 + €39,569 + €40,519
•  Irish Examiner ancillary Local Democracy: €20,854; ancillary Courts: €21,519
•  Freelance awards listed “for the Irish Examiner” (David Forsythe): €7,000 (local democracy) + €53,526 (courts)
•  Digital Transformation Scheme: €12,250 + €7,600.50 + €4,250
Subtotal for the 2026 round items above: roughly €225,000.
An independent compilation of Coimisiún na Meán announcements (https://t.co/juPfPQqmls, covering published awards from 2023 to mid-2026) attributes on the order of €200,000+ specifically named to the Irish Examiner across these schemes, within a larger Irish Times Group total of about €2.5 million (which also includes The Echo in Cork, regional titles, and radio stations). Sister title The Echo (Cork) received separate awards, including €62,143 under the 2025 Local Democracy scheme.
Department of Foreign Affairs – Global Ireland Media Challenge Fund
This fund supports international reporting capacity (editorial independence is stated as a core principle). The Irish Examiner received €100,000 in an earlier phase and €160,000 for the 2025–2026 phase.
Advertising and other payments
Government departments and agencies also buy commercial advertising space. Parliamentary replies show individual departments placing print ads with the Irish Examiner in the range of several thousand to low tens of thousands of euro in given years (for example, one department’s print figures included roughly €7,650–€18,000 in sampled recent years). No comprehensive public total across all departments and years is published in the sources reviewed. These are payments for advertising services, not grants.
In short, disclosed direct scheme funding to the Irish Examiner since the main journalism supports began is in the mid-hundreds of thousands of euro (on the order of €600,000–€700,000 when the Coimisiún na Meán rounds above and the two Global Ireland awards are added), plus ordinary advertising revenue whose full government share is not centrally totalled. The parent group’s combined receipts under the same Coimisiún schemes are substantially higher.

text:
Light in the Dust: The Hebrew Roots of the Gospel, Mission, and Salvation

In the quiet stillness of ancient Judea, the announcement of the Gospel—the Besorah—was not merely a set of moral guidelines, but a declaration of radical liberation. To understand the good news of Jesus Christ from both Orthodox and Lutheran perspectives, one must first uncover the Hebrew concepts that shaped the world into which He walked. The word Gospel itself translates the Hebrew Besorah, an announcement traditionally brought by a messenger carrying tidings of victory, peace, and divine intervention. When Jesus of Nazareth began His public ministry, His central message was the arrival of the Malkhut Shamayim, the Kingdom of Heaven. Far from being a distant celestial realm, this kingdom represented the active, present reign of God breaking directly into human history. In Lutheran theology, this message is anchored in the profound reality of Sola Gratia—grace alone—where the broken, sinful human heart is justified not through self-reliance or legalistic works, but through unconditional divine favor. Complementing this, Orthodox tradition sees the incarnation as the beginning of Theosis, the transformative healing of human nature through union with God. Together, both traditions agree that Christ came to restore what was fractured at the core of creation, bringing light into a shadowed world.

At the very heart of Christ’s mission for the world is the ancient Hebrew concept of Shalom. Often translated simply as peace, Shalom carries a much richer, dynamic meaning: wholeness, completeness, restoration, and the alignment of all things with their Creator. Human existence, wounded by sin and alienation, exists in a state of systemic disharmony. Jesus did not arrive merely to offer abstract doctrines; He came as the embodiment of God’s Chesed—His unfailing, covenantal mercy and steadfast love. Through His life, death, and resurrection, Christ initiated the ultimate act of Tikkun Olam, the repair and restoration of a fallen world. From the Orthodox perspective, the cosmic scope of redemption embraces all of creation, breaking down the power of death and raising humanity into shared divine life. From the Lutheran perspective, the Cross stands as the supreme display of God's mercy, where Christ takes upon Himself the burden of human suffering and guilt to offer complete reconciliation. This mission was never intended for an isolated group or a single nation; it was launched for every nation, tribe, and tongue, breaking down physical and spiritual walls of separation to unite humanity under divine grace.

Ultimately, the message of the Gospel calls every person into a living relationship grounded in faith and active renewal. In Hebrew thought, faith is Emunah—not mere intellectual assent to a list of facts, but deep personal trust, faithfulness, and steadfast action. When a person receives the Gospel, Emunah responds by living out God's truth in daily life through acts of love, justice, and compassion. Orthodox theology emphasizes this ongoing journey as a perpetual participation in the life of the Holy Spirit, where the human soul is gradually transfigured by uncreated grace. Lutheran theology highlights how this trust frees the believer from the anxious burden of self-justification, allowing good works to flow naturally as joyful gratitude for a salvation already fully accomplished. As Christ sent His disciples into the world, He charged them to carry this restorative peace to every corner of the earth. The Gospel remains a dynamic, living message: God’s unconditional love meeting humanity in its dust and weakness, offering real healing, total forgiveness, and the timeless promise of a restored world.

text: Having a base in Germany is crucial because transporting troops to Poland takes only a few hours. I see no need to establish additional bases given that one already exists in Germany. The location in Germany is situated at a distance from the Ukrainian border, making it a strategic asset should Poland come under enemy attack. However, this base offers no security guarantee if Trump decides against fighting the Russian army; a single phone call to Putin could either halt a Russian offensive or block it through troop deployments in the region. Currently, the most important military assets for launching a counter-offensive would be Tomahawk missiles, capable of precision strikes against enemy forces. Large, modern armies can be defeated by drones and missile systems equipped with high-yield warheads. It is worth recalling the bases in Afghanistan that were abandoned after Trump signed the agreement with the Taliban—vast quantities of valuable military equipment were left behind. What was the point of abandoning those bases and losing Afghanistan? After all, Taliban factions did not pose a serious threat. text:
As of 2 October 2026, the United States and Iran are in a seven-month war that began with joint U.S.–Israeli strikes on 28 February. Fighting has paused and resumed, talks have stalled again, and the Strait of Hormuz remains the main economic pressure point.

How the war started and where it stands

On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel opened what President Trump called “major combat operations” against Iran. Reporting says Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed in those strikes and was succeeded by his son, Mojtaba Khamenei. Iran responded by restricting the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint that normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil and a large share of LNG — and by striking Gulf and shipping targets. The IRGC formally confirmed a closure around 2 March.

The war has not been continuous combat:

- 8 April: a two-week ceasefire.
- April: the first face-to-face U.S.–Iran talks in 47 years, hosted by Pakistan, with no breakthrough.
- 20 June: talks in Switzerland after a preliminary deal that was supposed to reopen Hormuz and lift the U.S. blockade, with a 60-day path to a final agreement.
- 1 July: further talks in Doha that mediators called progress.
- 8 July: the U.S. struck again after attacks on ships in Hormuz; Iran retaliated, and the strait tightened once more—the U.S.reinstated its naval blockade of Iranian ports.

By late September, the war was at roughly the seven-month mark. On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner exchanged ideas through Qatari mediators. Iran offered to reopen Hormuz within seven days if Washington ended the blockade, unfroze assets, and eased sanctions. Trump rejected that proposal, saying it was not the deal he wanted. Iran later said it had received a formal U.S. reply via Qatar; the contents have not been made public.

Trump’s line this week has been that the war will end “very soon, one way or the other” — “we blow them up or make a deal.” He has not ruled out further strikes before the November midterms, and has threatened to hit Iran “very hard” if Tehran is linked to an attempted hijacking of an Israeli-bound flight. The Pentagon is moving additional forces toward the region, including ships carrying more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines, and extra Patriot batteries to protect energy sites in Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said U.S. forces have crippled Iran’s navy, air force, air defences, and nuclear program; those are U.S. claims and have not been independently verified in full. Iranian officials say they are ready either for diplomacy or a return to full fighting.
 The Strait of Hormuz

Hormuz normally moves roughly 20 million barrels a day of oil and products. Status trackers disagree on the exact degree of closure, but both show a severe, long disruption:

- IMF PortWatch data put commercial ship arrivals at about 3–5% of the pre-war baseline (roughly 3–4 ships a day versus about 75–85).
- Shipping analysts (Kpler and others) say crude volumes through Hormuz and bypass routes recovered in late September to just under 80% of pre-war regional flows, near 13 million barrels a day, helped by Saudi and UAE exports and partial use of the Saudi East–West pipeline to the Red Sea.
- Refined products (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel) are still far short — on the order of 3 million barrels a day missing from the Hormuz route.
- Iranian crude itself remains bottled up by the U.S. blockade. Trackers estimate Iran’s floating stocks outside the blockade could be largely gone by mid-October, cutting a main revenue source.

War-risk insurance is many times peacetime levels. The Houthis have also disrupted Red Sea shipping, so the region has two constrained sea lanes at once.

## Impact on the global economy

The shock is the largest interruption of energy flows in decades, but it has not produced the $150–200 oil spike many feared at the start.

text:
The anger building across rural America is real and too often ignored.

Farmers and ranchers are watching diesel prices climb while every part of their work gets more expensive: planting, harvesting, feeding livestock, hauling crops and getting food to market. They are not asking for sympathy. They are asking how they are supposed to keep producing when fuel and other costs keep eating away at their livelihoods.

Many believe there is no true fuel shortage that ordinary people are being squeezed while powerful interests keep getting richer. Whether that is the whole explanation or not, leaders should understand why that belief is taking hold. Families see the price at the pump. Farmers see it in every field. Ranchers see it in every truckload of feed. They feel the pressure long before it shows up in a report from Washington.

And this anger does not stop at the farm gate. Higher fuel costs reach grocery bills, household budgets and small businesses in every community. People feel they are being pushed into a financial spiral while those in charge offer excuses and tell them to be patient.

That frustration is underreported, but it will not stay hidden. Farmers, ranchers and working families vote. In the midterm elections, candidates may discover that people remember who listened, who offered answers and who left them to carry the cost alone.  AW

text:
Elon Musk offered $97.4 billion for OpenAI. Sam Altman answered in one line:

"no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want"

Exactly one tenth of the offer. Musk replied with one word. "Swindler."

The two started OpenAI together in 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk left the board in 2018 and has been fighting Altman ever since, including in court.

The bid landed in February 2025, right when OpenAI was trying to turn itself into a for-profit company. A few days later OpenAI's board rejected it unanimously. Altman's own guess was that Musk was "probably just trying to slow us down."

I don't think either of them expected a sale. Musk's offer made OpenAI's restructuring harder and more expensive. Altman's reply turned a serious legal move into a meme the whole internet shared.

Still, it's wild to watch two of the richest men in tech fight like this over a company they started together.

If you’re a farmer, I don’t want to tell you:

“The government allows it now. Go buy a drone.”

What I would rather tell you is:

“Now is a good time to seriously understand this technology.
But before deciding whether to buy one, you should still ask a lot of questions.”

Is it right for my crops?

When does it offer more value than the equipment I already use?

How well does it actually spray?

Should I own one, or hire a professional service provider?

What does it really cost to operate?

If something goes wrong, who will be there to help me?

And most importantly:

Can it actually help me grow my crops more consistently and efficiently, and ultimately produce what the market needs?

Drones are not the answer to agriculture.

They are one part of agriculture, and they are not the whole of precision agriculture. 

That is why we hope you will join us in Niagara and hear directly from the farmers and operators who have actually been using drones in real operations for the past several years, not just from the people selling them.

Rupert Lowe offered Reform a joint platform. Reform said no.
Restore Britain put the exchange up this morning. Lowe’s ask was simple. Stop splitting the vote. Agree a floor on deportations and borders. Then fight Labour. Farage’s side walked away.
You can call that principle. You can call it pride. Either way the patriotic vote stays split, and both of them know it.
The same week, Restore Britain picked Stuart Watton for Bicester and Woodstock. The fight there is the proposed asylum centre at MOD Bicester. Twelve hundred men, on a site the party says has no power, no running water and no sewage, dropped on villages that were not asked. Watton is a local tech manager and a long-time athletics coach. Not a Westminster retread.
And in six days, Holborn and St Pancras. Keir Starmer’s old seat. Restore Britain’s candidate is Tyler Johnson, a London corporate lawyer. Labour are defending with Camden leader Sagal Abdi-Wali. The Greens have Zack Polanski. Fifteen names on the ballot.
Nobody serious thinks Restore wins central London. The number that matters is whether they take a bite out of a right-wing vote that barely exists there.
So that is the week. Lowe offered a deal. Reform refused. Holborn votes on the eighth of October. Bicester is now a target seat over the MOD asylum plan.
Restore Britain, not Reform.

text:
So who do you think Hitler was fighting?  
The 1939 aim was territorial and military, and it was stated in advance. Bradberry records Ribbentrop’s four points of 24 October 1938: Danzig back to the Reich with Polish port rights kept; no demand for the Corridor itself, only an extraterritorial road and railway to East Prussia; a permanent guarantee of the remaining border; and extension of the 1934 pact to twenty-five years. That offer left Polish families where they were. Hitler repeated the guarantee to Beck on 5 January 1939. Poland refused, stiffened by the British blank cheque of 31 March. The September campaign was launched after mobilization, frontier incidents, and the Bromberg killings of ethnic Germans, with the stated object of destroying the Polish armed forces and recovering Danzig and the link to East Prussia. Irving’s account of the private planning is the same in substance: annihilation of the Polish army, then a rump Polish state, with the intelligentsia extracted so that no new chauvinist leadership could form, and summary execution of guerrillas. Himmler’s surviving notes of March 1940 call a Bolshevik-style extermination of minority races “impossible.” A pre-war decision to wipe out Polish families is not in the documents. It is a motive read backwards from postwar totals.
The 1918 claim is the same kind of reversal. Germany laid down its arms on the Armistice of 11 November in the belief that Wilson’s Fourteen Points would govern the peace. Bradberry notes that the treaty was then drawn up without German participation and handed over as a diktat, under a four-day ultimatum and a continued hunger blockade. About 28,000 square miles and 6.5 million people were transferred: Alsace-Lorraine to France, West Prussia, Posen, Upper Silesia and Danzig to Poland, Memel to Lithuania, the Saar to League control, the colonies confiscated, the army cut to 100,000, the air force banned, the Rhineland demilitarized, reunion with Austria forbidden, and a blank reparations cheque later filled in at $33 billion. Scheidemann resigned rather than sign. A. J. P. Taylor, quoted by Bradberry, records that Germans signed formally and intended to repudiate the treaty when they could. East Prussia was not left to “the Prussians” by London bankers as a favor. It was historic German territory, overwhelmingly German, and had not been conquered. Cutting it off with the Corridor was the mutilation, not the residue of one. Upper Silesia was not preserved either: Bradberry lists it among the losses, and notes that its coal, with the Saar’s, was a vital economic amputation — 13 percent of territory, 10 percent of population, a third of coal, most of the iron ore. The City’s interest in 1919 was a Germany still intact enough to pay reparations and to serve as a weight against French hegemony and Bolshevism, which is the opposite of a plot to spare German land. The actual attrition after the armistice was British. Bradberry puts the blockade deaths at about a million civilians, mainly women, children, and the old, and names Churchill as its main force; the blockade was kept up for months after the fighting stopped to compel the signature. Menuhin cites Brockdorff-Rantzau at Versailles on the hundreds of thousands of non-combatants dead since 11 November 1918. The program of eliminating Germany as an industrial state belongs to 1944–45, not to a London veto in 1918.
Weimar Germany did not wage a war of attrition, and it could not have done so. It had no air force, no tanks, six capital ships, and 100,000 men. What it did, from the first cabinets onward, was refuse to treat the eastern settlement as morally final. That refusal was general, not a Hitler invention: the treaty had been signed under duress, Article 231 was rejected as a lie, and the eastern borders violated the self-determination Wilson had used to obtain the Armistice. Locarno in 1925 accepted the western frontier as a tactical fact and left the Corridor, Danzig, and Upper Silesia open. Stresemann’s method was negotiation, not attrition. The attrition ran the other way — reparations, the lost merchant fleet, the Ruhr occupation of 1923, and the hyperinflation. Hitler’s second program point, abolition of Versailles, continued a national demand that predated him. Bradberry’s point is that no German government had ever accepted the treaty as binding in conscience, and that expecting otherwise was unreasonable. Non-recognition of a dictated border is not evidence of a plan to exterminate the families on the other side of it.

text:
This is not a dog video. It is a 5-kilogram wind tunnel nobody funded, and the physics hiding inside that coat is stranger than anything else you will read today.

Play the clip again. Then come back. I will wait.

Here is what nobody tells you: cute is the cover story. Underneath it is a live demo of fluid dynamics, materials science, sensory biology, and a brutal lesson in why evolution never optimized for photo shoots.

This post is long on purpose. 24,000 characters. Read it slowly, go back to the video, and I promise you will not be able to unsee what you see.

We start where the tension starts: the numbers.

PART 1. THE NUMBERS NOBODY CHECKS

Air looks like nothing. It is not nothing. At sea level, one cubic meter of air weighs about 1.2 kilograms. Throw that cubic meter at something at 10 meters per second, an entirely ordinary "fresh breeze" on the Beaufort scale, and engineers describe the push with one line:

q = 1/2 x air density x velocity squared

Plug it in: 0.5 x 1.2 x 10 x 10 = 60 pascals.

Sixty pascals sounds like a rounding error. It is not. It is about 6 kilograms of weight sitting on every square meter that faces the wind.

Now stand a small, round, fully fluffed animal in front of it. Call it 5 kilograms, with a frontal area of roughly 0.1 square meters once the coat inflates. Treat it as a blunt object with a drag coefficient near 1, which is generous to blunt objects and entirely reasonable for a puffball.

Force = 60 Pa x 0.1 m2 x 1 = about 6 newtons.

Its weight is about 49 newtons.

So the wind is leaning on it with roughly 12 percent of its own body weight. Continuously. With gusts stacked on top.

Translate that to a 75-kilogram adult: a hand the size of your torso pressing 9 kilograms into your chest for as long as the weather feels like it, while you try to stand still and keep your dignity.

Back-of-envelope, yes. Real wind is turbulent, gusts run 30 to 50 percent above the mean, and force climbs with the square of speed. Double the wind and you do not double the push. You quadruple it.

At 20 meters per second, the same animal faces about 24 newtons. Half its body weight.

Hold that number. We are going to use it.

PART 2. THE COAT IS NOT HAIR, IT IS AN ENGINEERING PROJECT

Most people see fluff. A materials scientist sees a forest of cantilever beams.

Every strand is a slender fiber of keratin, the same protein family as nails, claws, horns, and feathers. Keratin is a composite: tough, springy, hydrophobic, and light. A single strand is roughly a tenth of a millimeter thick and several centimeters long, which makes it absurdly slender. Slender beams do something interesting in a flow: they stop behaving like objects and start behaving like a fluid of their own.

A double coat stacks two systems. Long guard hairs on top, shielding and shedding water and dirt. A dense, soft undercoat beneath, trapping still air. Still air is one of the best insulators nature offers. Its thermal conductivity is about 0.026 watts per meter-kelvin, better than most foam you can buy.

So the coat is not decoration. It is a thermal system, a mechanical system, and a sacrificial armor layer, all grown from the same raw material, all rebuilt on a schedule.

And the whole assembly has one job when the wind arrives: do not let the air reach the skin.

Remember that sentence. The rest of this post is that sentence, under pressure.

PART 3. THE BIGGEST TRICK IN THE FLUID DYNAMICS PLAYBOOK

Here is where it gets weird.

Starting in the 1980s, the biologist Steven Vogel spent a career pointing out something engineers had been slow to accept: rigid things fight the wind, flexible things negotiate with it.

A stiff board in a flow takes the full drag. A leaf, a frond, a strand of kelp, a bundle of fibers does something cleverer. It bends. As it bends, it lines up with the flow, its frontal area shrinks, and its drag stops climbing as fast as the velocity squared law says it should. Biologists call this reconfiguration. Engineers call it a free lunch.

Fur does the same thing at industrial scale. Every strand sweeps downwind, packs against its neighbors, and the surface of the coat becomes a smoother, more streamlined shape than the animal underneath. The silhouette you see is not the animal. It is the animal plus a few centimeters of self-assembling aerodynamic fairing.

The cost of that trick is brutally visible: the coat is always being rearranged. Not once. Hundreds of times per second, as each gust arrives from a slightly different angle and every fiber reorients itself in a chain reaction with its neighbors.

That is not "floof in the wind." That is a self-adjusting surface running a control loop with no processor.

Keep reading. It gets better, and it gets more uncomfortable.

PART 4. THE EYES ARE THE WEAKEST LINK IN THE SYSTEM

Armor has a hole. It is always the eyes.

An eye is a wet surface exposed to air. Wind across a wet surface does what it does to a puddle: it evaporates it. A tear film is only a few micrometers thick, and a strong breeze can strip it faster than the glands refill it. Dry cornea means pain, and pain means a very fast engineering decision.

So the face makes one. Eyelids narrow. Brow hairs fold forward. The head turns so the flow slides across the cheek instead of striking the cornea head-on. Dogs also have a third eyelid, the nictitating membrane, a translucent shutter that sweeps across the eye sideways like a windshield wiper. Most animals on the planet have one. Humans kept a vestigial scrap in the corner of the eye and lost the rest in the great trade of eyesight for politics.

Notice what that means. Whatever you are watching in that clip, the body is solving four problems at the same time: stay upright, keep the air off the skin, keep the cornea wet, and keep the nose working. Four control loops. Zero conscious decisions. The brain is not "reacting." It is running a protocol.

PART 5. THE NOSE IS THE ONLY REASON ANY OF THIS IS HAPPENING

Here is the plot twist.

Wind is not an enemy to a dog. Wind is a newspaper.

A human has around 6 million olfactory receptors. A dog has up to roughly 300 million, depending on breed, plus a dedicated vomeronasal organ for chemical signals, plus a brain region for smell that is proportionally many times larger than ours. A dog does not smell the way you see. A dog smells the way you read: along a timeline.

Wind is the page turning.

Each gust carries a snapshot: who walked past upwind, what was cooked three streets away, which other animal crossed the plaza an hour ago, what the sea is doing, whether the weather is about to change. A strong wind is the richest feed an animal can scroll. It arrives in a stream, it arrives from one direction, and it arrives with a direction vector attached, which tells the animal where each item came from.

So the nose points into the wind. Not because the animal is brave. Because the data is coming from there.

That is the part that should bother you. The body is straining against a force that is also the most information-dense thing in the environment. It is bracing against the very source it is trying to read.

If you want a one-line summary of what you are watching, it is this: a survival system in the middle of a trade-off between comfort and information.

And it is choosing information.

PART 6. WHY THE EARS GO DOWN

Wind noise is not just loud. It is structured noise. Turbulence over a cupped ear creates broadband roar that masks exactly the frequencies animals need for hearing small movements, rustling, footsteps, a bag being opened in a kitchen forty meters away.

Ear flaps fold. The canal narrows. Fur around the opening forms a windscreen, the same thing a sound engineer clips on a microphone and calls a dead cat. The animal is wearing the original dead cat.

This matters because hearing and balance share hardware. The vestibular system sits right next to the cochlea, and wind buffeting the outer ear can feed noise into the balance loop. Add a gust that hits the left side of the head and not the right, and you get an unsteady signal at exactly the moment you need a steady one.

An animal in a gale is not just pushed. It is fed bad data about its own orientation, and it has to stand anyway.

Think about that the next time you think standing still is easy.

PART 7. THE TORQUE PROBLEM

Let us finish the calculation we started.

A force of 6 newtons does not act at the feet. It acts at the center of the frontal area, roughly 20 centimeters off the ground for a small animal. That makes a tipping torque of about:

6 N x 0.20 m = 1.2 newton-meters

What holds it down? Weight, acting through the paws, whose outer edges sit maybe 8 centimeters from the center of mass in a wide, planted stance:

49 N x 0.08 m = about 3.9 newton-meters

Ratio: roughly 3 to 1 in favor of staying upright, at a 10 meter per second wind.

Now push the wind to 15 meters per second, strong breeze, Beaufort 7. The tipping torque climbs to roughly 2.7 newton-meters. The margin shrinks from 3 to about 1.4.

At 20 meters per second, the tipping torque is about 4.8 newton-meters and the margin has gone negative. The animal has to lower its center of mass, widen its stance, lean into the flow, and grip with every paw pad, or it goes over like a kite with no string.

And grip is its own problem. Friction on granite depends on the pad, the moisture, and the load. Paw pads are one of the best dynamic-friction surfaces evolution ever made: rubbery, textured, sweaty in exactly the right way. The sweat glands in them actually increase grip, the same reason you lick a finger to turn a page.

Everything in that frame is a number approaching its limit.

That is the real source of the tension. Not the fur. The margin.

PART 8. WHY YOUR BRAIN CANNOT LOOK AWAY

You think you are watching something adorable. Your visual cortex thinks it is watching something else entirely.

Three things are firing at once.

First, Konrad Lorenz's baby schema. Round head, big forehead, short face, soft body. Lorenz described the cluster in the 1940s, and later work found it reliably switches on caregiving circuits in the brain, including reward regions, within a fraction of a second. You do not decide to care. The circuit decides for you.

Second, motion prediction. The brain is a prediction machine. It watches a moving object, builds a model of where each part will go next, and checks the model against reality about every few milliseconds. When the model is almost right, you get a small satisfaction. When it is almost right but not quite, you get something stickier: the urge to keep checking.

A coat in a gust is the perfect almost-right object. Thousands of fibers following one rule, never repeating the same pattern twice. Your prediction system locks on and cannot finish the job. It is a slot machine that pays out in tiny surprises.

Third, a response to effort. People watch a living thing work against a force and mirror it. Mirror neurons or not, the sensation is real: you feel a little of the strain. You lean in. You hold your breath. You are standing in that wind with it.

Cuteness gets the click. Prediction gets the replay. Effort gets the share.

If you want to know why a seven-second loop can outperform a ninety-minute documentary, that is the entire answer.

PART 9. WHAT THE WEATHER DOES TO WARMTH

We should talk about cold, because that is the quieter half of the story.

Wind chill is not a temperature. It is a rate. It describes how quickly a warm surface loses heat when air keeps replacing the thin layer of warmed air next to it.

Stand still in calm air and your skin warms a boundary layer around you, a skin of slightly warmer air a few millimeters thick that acts like a very thin blanket. Wind peels that blanket away, over and over, and each replacement has to be warmed again from your own reserves.

The coat's job is to move that boundary layer outward. Instead of a few millimeters hugging the skin, the animal builds a few centimeters of trapped, nearly still air in the undercoat. Wind has to penetrate that depth to reach skin, and as it penetrates it slows, loses energy, and mixes with air that is already warm.

This is why a thick coat can keep an animal comfortable at temperatures that would be dangerous for a hairless one, and why the same coat becomes a liability in wet weather: water flattens the insulation, replaces trapped air with liquid, and the conductivity jumps by a factor of about 25.

The coat is not a sweater. It is a dynamic system whose performance depends on the weather it is facing. Wind, rain, and sun each reconfigure it.

You are watching one of those configurations right now. Think of it as a live reading from an instrument, not a pose.

PART 10. THE UNCOMFORTABLE HISTORY OF THIS COAT

Here is the part the cute videos skip.

Wolves do not have this. A wolf coat is dense but short, built for efficiency and camouflage, not volume. Ancestral dogs, a few thousand generations ago, looked a lot more like that.

The coats you see today are the product of selection. Humans noticed that some puppies grew softer, longer, whiter, fluffier hair. Those puppies got fed, bred, and sheltered. Over centuries, entire breeds were shaped by one criterion: how much people liked looking at them.

That is not natural selection. That is attention selection.

And it produced an animal whose coat is, in some ways, over-engineered for a purpose its ancestors never had. A coat that is stunning in motion, dramatic in a breeze, and that demands grooming, brushing, trimming, and constant attention to stay functional. Long coats mat. Matted coats trap moisture. Trapped moisture breeds skin problems.

The animal is, in a sense, a long-running experiment in how far you can push an organism toward being watched.

If that sounds like a description of something else you know, you are paying attention.

Here is the dark joke at the center of the internet: we spent twenty years learning how to optimize creatures for human attention, and the most effective test subjects were not on a screen. They were on a leash.

PART 11. THE SEVEN-SECOND LESSON IN HOOKS

Let me be useful for a minute, because this is also a masterclass in why some content works and most does not.

The clip has no setup. No intro. No logo. No voiceover explaining what you are about to see. It drops you into a system already under stress and lets you work out the rest yourself.

That is the entire craft of the hook.

A weak opening describes. A strong opening puts you inside a question you cannot resolve. What is that force? How long can it hold? What happens at the next gust? Every one of those questions is a thread, and every thread pulls the eye forward.

You do not need a production crew. You need three things.

One. A visible force. Something is pushing on something. Content without pressure is a lecture.

Two. A visible limit. The viewer must be able to feel how close the subject is to the edge, even if they cannot name the edge.

Three. No resolution in the first second. The moment the viewer knows how it ends, the viewer is gone.

Notice that none of those require a budget. They require a subject under load and the discipline to not explain it. Which, ironically, is why this post exists: the video does the showing, the text does the thinking, and neither does the other's job.

Rule of thumb from eleven years of watching what gets through: if you can summarize the hook in a sentence that starts with "this is a video of," the hook has failed. If the best summary is "I cannot stop checking what happens next," you are in the money.

PART 12. THE GUST THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING

Let us return to the physics, because we left a loose thread.

We treated wind as a steady push. It is not. Real wind is a spectrum. Slow swells over seconds, faster eddies over fractions of a second, and sudden bursts when a structure upwind sheds a vortex.

Everything in that scene sits in the wake of something. Pillars, railings, steps, a person walking, a parked cart. Each one splits the flow and sheds alternating vortices behind it, a pattern called a von Karman vortex street, the same pattern that makes flags flutter and wires hum.

So the animal is not facing one wind. It is facing a train of pressure pulses from objects it cannot see, timed by geometry it cannot know, arriving at frequencies that match, uncomfortably, the natural sway of a standing body.

That match matters. Every mechanical structure has a frequency at which it likes to oscillate. Push at that frequency, even gently, and the amplitude grows. This is how soldiers breaking step on a bridge became a standard engineering warning, and how the Tacoma Narrows bridge tore itself apart in 1940 in a wind of about 19 meters per second, barely above the scenario we just calculated.

A standing animal has a sway frequency too, set by its stance and the stiffness of its legs. Nothing as dramatic will happen. But the animal is constantly working to detune itself: shifting weight, adjusting stance, cancelling the rhythm before it builds.

That is what the micro-movements are. That is why it never quite stops moving even when it is trying to stand still.

The surface is calm. The control system underneath is working at full load.

PART 13. WHAT THIS HAS TO DO WITH YOU

I will make this uncomfortable for a moment.

There is a point where you stop watching a thing and start recognizing it.

Most people live most of their lives in a steady push. Deadlines, expectations, feeds, other people's opinions. It rarely knocks you over. It is 12 percent of your body weight, applied all day, and you have trained yourself to stop noticing it.

You lean. You adapt. You reconfigure. You lower your center of mass and plant your feet a little wider than you used to. You narrow your eyes. You turn your face a few degrees so the worst of it slides past.

And somewhere in there, you keep reading the wind. Because the wind is also where your information comes from. The same feed that exhausts you is the one you cannot stop scrolling.

That is why a video of a small white animal bracing in a breeze does not feel like entertainment. It feels like a mirror held up by something with no ego.

It is not heroic. It is not tragic. It is not even trying. It is just standing there, absorbing the force, adapting a thousand times a second, and refusing to be moved.

Which is the one skill nobody teaches and everyone needs. Not strength. Not speed. Just the patience to keep adapting while it pushes.

PART 14. THE SCALE THAT RUNS THE WORLD

In 1805, a British naval officer named Francis Beaufort wrote down a scale for wind that sailors could use without instruments: calm, light air, gentle breeze, fresh breeze, strong breeze, gale. He defined each step by what it did to a ship's sails and, later, to the land.

It is one of the most successful pieces of data design ever made, because it ignores numbers and measures consequences. Smoke rises straight up. Leaves rustle. Small branches move. Umbrellas turn inside out. Walking becomes work.

Every step on that scale is a step on the animal's stress curve too. Somewhere between Beaufort 4 and Beaufort 6, a small body stops treating wind as weather and starts treating it as a task.

That threshold is the interesting part. Most of life happens just below it, where nothing is dramatic and nobody films anything. The content lives exactly at the edge, where a system that was coasting has to start working.

That is the zone you are watching. The edge of the scale, not the middle.

Here is the part sailors learned the hard way: the scale is not linear in effort. Going from a fresh breeze to a strong breeze feels like a small step on paper. In force terms, it is nearly a doubling. Small changes in the number, large changes in the load. That is the quiet reason people underestimate wind until the moment it takes the hat, the umbrella, or the balance.

PART 15. NOW GO BACK AND WATCH IT PROPERLY

Scroll up. Replay the clip. This time, do not watch the center of the frame.

Watch the edges. Where the coat meets open air, the outline never settles. That boundary is where the whole story is written.

Watch the timing. Count the interval between the strongest pushes. You will find it is never regular, and your brain will try to make it regular anyway. That tug is the prediction engine from Part 8, and it is the reason you will watch it a fourth time.

Watch the stance. The feet barely move. Everything else does. That is a body deciding which parts to sacrifice to the wind and which to keep absolutely still.

Watch the face. Not for emotion. For engineering. Every fold and squint is an answer to a specific pressure.

Once you see it as a system instead of a scene, you cannot go back. Every video of a living thing under force becomes a lab.

PART 16. TEN FACTS THAT SHOULD NOT FIT IN ONE POST

One. Air at 10 meters per second pushes with about 60 pascals. A garden hose at close range pushes thousands of times harder, yet the wind wins because it never stops.

Two. Hair fibers share a basic structure with feathers and horn. The same keratin that holds up a rhinoceros horn is arranged into the thing that is currently moving.

Three. A dog sniff is not a single event. In a few seconds a dog can take dozens of tiny sniffs, each a separate sample of the air, stitched together into a map.

Four. Still air insulates better than most synthetic foams, which is why the best insulation in the world is mostly nothing, held in place by something very thin.

Five. Flexible objects in wind often show drag that rises slower than velocity squared, because bending reduces frontal area. Nature's version of load shedding.

Six. Evaporation from the eye surface rises sharply with air speed, which is why squinting in a breeze is not a mood. It is mechanical protection.

Seven. The turbulence behind any blunt object produces vortices at a rate that scales with wind speed and inversely with object width. Narrow things shed fast, wide things shed slowly.

Eight. Balance is not a sense. It is a fusion of at least three: inner ear, vision, and the pressure and stretch signals from every joint. Wind attacks all three at once.

Nine. Most of what you call cute is a visible high-load control problem. Babies, kittens, puppies, all small bodies with big heads and unfinished stability. We love them in part because they are working hard.

Ten. The internet's most reliable currency is not novelty. It is the sight of a living thing coping with something larger than itself.

PART 17. THE UNPOPULAR TAKEAWAY

If you were hoping for a happy ending, here it is, and it is not exactly cheerful.

Nothing in that clip is going to win. The wind is not going to stop. The animal is not going to overpower it. At best, the outcome is a draw: the force continues, the coat keeps adapting, and eventually somebody picks up the leash and moves on.

That is how almost everything works.

We do not usually get to beat the force. We get to be well-designed for it. Flexible where we can afford to be, rigid where we have to be, warm in the middle, and curious at the nose, even when curiosity is exactly what costs us comfort.

The animal does not know any of this. It does not need to. Four hundred million years of vertebrate engineering, plus a few thousand years of human attention, are doing the work without a single thought.

You, on the other hand, know all of it now. Which means the next time a gust hits, you have one more way of seeing what is happening to you.

So.

Go back to the clip.

Watch it once as a scene. Once as a system. Once as a mirror.

Then decide which of the three you are.

If this changed how you watched it, repost it. Someone you know is standing in a 12 percent wind and has stopped noticing.

And if you have been reading for 24,000 characters, congratulations. You just did something harder than standing in a breeze.

You paid attention.

I don't have to start every morning with scrims. I wake up, make breakfast, get coffee, walk around the neighborhood, do whatever I want at home and go to the gym in the evening. It's a dream life.

Obviously, I'll consider offers from professional teams closer to the New Year. However, if I grew as a streamer and made as much as I did on a professional team, I would continue streaming.

I'm probably not the kind of person who thinks: 'I haven't won TI yet, so I can't retire.' Right now, I'm more focused on finances. Streaming is less exhausting, and you enjoy what you're doing.

But that's how I feel now. I don't know what I'll think in two or three months. We have to wait."
