text:
Jean-Paul Marat and the Media That Know They’re Saving You

Jean-Paul Marat would have understood a particular habit in American media: the conviction that being on the right side of history gives you permission to get ahead of the facts. He lived during the French Revolution, published a newspaper called The Friend of the People, and became famous for identifying the people’s supposed enemies. The name promised friendship. His denunciations offered something considerably less pleasant to everyone else.

Before becoming a revolutionary journalist and politician, Marat worked as a physician and pursued scientific recognition. Beginning in 1789, his newspaper gave him a platform to champion ordinary people and attack those he believed were betraying them. His political writing eventually included demands for the execution of perceived enemies of the revolution. He offered readers an explanation for their suffering, named those responsible, and urged action against them.

There were genuine reasons for anger in revolutionary France. An unjust social order does not become imaginary because an inflammatory writer describes it. That is what makes Marat worth studying. His radicalization shows how defending people against abuse can turn into demanding punishment for their supposed enemies. A righteous starting point does not guarantee a righteous destination.

That warning deserves attention in America’s liberal and far-left media, particularly where reporting becomes an extension of activism. These are different political traditions, with considerable disagreement between them. But whenever moral conviction weakens standards of evidence, the same question applies: does believing you represent the public good make you less willing to examine your own conduct?

The resemblance to Marat becomes strongest when a publication claims to speak for ordinary people while deciding in advance which people deserve a fair hearing. Someone classified as privileged, reactionary, or an obstacle to progress can become a character in a political lesson before anyone has established what that person actually did. Once the lesson takes priority, inconvenient details start looking like editorial clutter.

Consider Rolling Stone’s 2014 University of Virginia rape story. The magazine pursued a serious subject: sexual assault and universities’ responses to it. But a Columbia Journalism School investigation found failures in reporting, editing, supervision, and fact-checking. Essential verification was neglected, and the published narrative concealed important gaps in the reporting. The investigation also found that the failure could not adequately be explained by the magazine’s desire to protect its source.

The case illustrates a temptation that should particularly trouble publications committed to social reform. When a story appears to expose an injustice you already believe exists, skepticism can feel disloyal to the cause. Yet a cause cannot establish whether a particular accusation is true. The existence of sexual assault does not verify every account of it, just as the existence of racism does not settle every disputed encounter. The more serious the accusation, the greater the obligation to get it right.

Failure can also damage the cause itself. Columbia’s investigation described harm to those implicated in the UVA article and concerns that its collapse would make sexual-assault survivors less likely to be believed. Good intentions did not prevent those consequences. They certainly did not repair them.

Marat’s demands for executions were vastly more extreme than contemporary American commentary. But that difference should not become a convenient excuse to ignore lesser versions of punitive thinking: deciding that people associated with a condemned political cause deserve punishment before examining their individual conduct. A comparison can recognize enormous differences in severity while still identifying a dangerous habit.

January 6 provides a test of that principle. A person who assaulted a police officer, a person who unlawfully entered the Capitol without committing violence, and a person who attended a lawful rally did not do the same thing. Responsible reporting must preserve those distinctions. Whenever coverage rolls them into one undifferentiated category of enemies, it encourages readers to substitute collective condemnation for individual judgment.

Nonviolent defendants did receive jail sentences. Jenna Ryan, for example, received 60 days after pleading guilty to a misdemeanor arising from her entry into the Capitol. That was an actual offense, not merely attendance at a political demonstration. But acknowledging the offense still leaves room to question whether incarceration was proportionate. A journalist should be capable of asking that question without being accused of endorsing the violence committed by somebody else.

The government’s judgment also proved open to challenge. Matthew Martin was acquitted in 2022 after a judge accepted that he reasonably believed police had permitted his entry. In 2024, the Supreme Court’s decision in Fischer v. United States rejected the government’s expansive interpretation of an obstruction statute used in January 6 prosecutions. Neither decision established that everyone prosecuted was innocent. Both demonstrated why government accusations required scrutiny rather than automatic endorsement.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson joined the majority in Fischer. Her concurrence emphasized that even abhorrent conduct must be judged under the criminal law Congress actually enacted. That principle should be easy for every newsroom to defend: outrage cannot expand a statute, and dislike of a defendant cannot replace proof.

The criticism also extends to anti-Trump conservative commentators—the “RINO right,” as their critics call them—whenever they abandon those distinctions. A conservative label provides no protection against guilt by association or enthusiasm for excessive punishment. The same standard applies to a liberal editorial board, a far-left activist publication, and a Republican commentator eager to demonstrate distance from Trump: explain what the individual did, establish what the evidence proves, and consider whether the punishment fits.

Journalists do not hand down prison sentences. Prosecutors bring cases, and courts decide them. But media help shape the public climate in which prosecutions are understood. There is a serious difference between reporting an allegation and treating it as a verdict, between defending accountability and applauding punishment without examining its proportionality. A press that claims to hold power accountable should retain that skepticism when the government is prosecuting people its readers despise.

This is where the Marat comparison has force. Once an accused person becomes a symbol of everything an audience hates, fairness can begin to look like weakness. Asking for evidence becomes helping the enemy. Questioning a punishment becomes excusing the offense. Under that reasoning, basic protections gradually become privileges reserved for sympathetic defendants.

The problem extends beyond criminal cases. Political frameworks can help journalists ask useful questions about wealth, discrimination, government power, and institutional failure. But an investigation must be allowed to produce an inconvenient answer. If the facts cannot change the conclusion, the reporter is illustrating a belief.

Moral labels require the same discipline. Racist, fascist, and extremist can describe real conduct and real political movements. They should carry the weight of evidence. When used as substitutes for explaining what someone said, did, or proposed, they ask the audience to accept a verdict without examining the case. Publications that encourage skepticism toward powerful institutions should welcome scrutiny of their own power to assign those labels.

The audience can make that difficult. A writer who repeatedly promises to expose the wickedness of the opposition can become dependent on that promise. Readers arrive expecting confirmation, and an account that complicates their beliefs may receive a colder welcome than another satisfying denunciation. Eventually, even an independent writer can end up taking instructions from the crowd without anyone formally issuing them.

Research gives that concern some substance. A 2021 study examining more than 2.7 million Facebook and Twitter posts from news organizations and members of Congress found that posts about political opponents were shared roughly twice as often as posts about their own political group. The pattern included liberal news accounts. The study was observational, but it identified an incentive any editor should recognize: hostility toward the other camp can attract attention.

For a publication that considers itself a force for progress, this creates an uncomfortable possibility. What feels like educating the public may become the business of keeping an audience morally agitated. Every controversy supplies another villain, and every correction threatens to disappoint the paying congregation. Marat needed a printing press. We have managed to automate much of the distribution.

Strong opinions and rigorous reporting can coexist. A journalist can investigate racism, defend civil liberties, expose corporate wrongdoing, or criticize conservative politicians with considerable force. The obligation is to show the evidence, distinguish fact from interpretation, and correct the record when the evidence changes. Those duties should become more demanding when the target is someone the readership already dislikes.

Marat was murdered by Charlotte Corday in July 1793, and his supporters made him a martyr. His image outlived him, most famously in Jacques-Louis David’s painting of his death. The public champion became a political symbol, another reminder of how readily a complicated person can be turned into a useful story.

His warning to today’s media is uncomfortable because it challenges the flattering stories institutions tell about themselves. Caring about justice does not make anyone immune to unfairness. Distrusting someone else’s authority does not make your own judgment infallible. And defending due process only when the defendant belongs to your political tribe reduces a constitutional principle to a membership benefit.

The Friend of the People sounds splendid over a newspaper. Before subscribing, the people would be wise to find out whether that friendship survives an inconvenient fact.

$IPGP 
tldr
The market is pricing a partial recovery and a better business mix, not a return to the high-margin monopoly-like years. Bulls focus on order momentum, the medical pivot, technology position, and the balance sheet. Bears focus on structural margin pressure, cyclicality, and a valuation that already assumes a meaningful earnings rebound.

- - - - Long form view solution - - - -
[ Open the post in its own view or                      ]
[ Click on the post versus show more and then you can use X's browser back to collapse the long form ]

IPG Photonics (NASDAQ: IPGP) is a Massachusetts-based maker of high-power fiber lasers, amplifiers, diode lasers, and laser systems. It is the longtime leader in industrial fiber lasers used for cutting, welding, marking, and cleaning metal, with smaller but growing exposure to medical, micromachining, semiconductor, additive manufacturing, and defense applications.

The company is vertically integrated: it designs and produces its own pump diodes, specialty optical fiber, and many of the subsystems that go into the lasers. That has historically been a cost and technology advantage versus competitors that buy more components. Headquarters are in Marlborough, MA; manufacturing is in the U.S., Germany, and elsewhere. Founder Valentin Gapontsev built the business around fiber-laser technology that displaced older CO₂ and solid-state lasers in many materials-processing uses.

Recent financial picture
Revenue peaked near $1.46 billion in 2021, then fell with weaker industrial and China demand, competition, and inventory destocking, bottoming around $977 million in 2024. Trailing-twelve-month revenue is about $1.07 billion, up roughly 13%. Trailing net income is only about $28 million (EPS around $0.65), so the trailing P/E is very high (around 130). Forward P/E is nearer 40, reflecting expected earnings recovery.

The balance sheet is a clear strength: roughly $870 million in cash and short-term investments and almost no debt, or about $20 of net cash per share, against a book value near $50. Market cap is about $3.6 billion at a recent price around $84. The 52-week range is roughly $69–$156.

Q2 2026 revenue was about $279 million, up 11% year over year and the third straight quarter of double-digit growth, led by industrial solutions (battery welding and related demand). Adjusted EPS of $0.58 beat consensus by a wide margin; adjusted gross margin was about 40.7%. Book-to-bill stayed above 1.0. Management has guided continued recovery, with tariffs still a modest margin drag.

In 2026 the company also agreed to buy Lumibird Medical (binding offer around €300 million plus up to €50 million earnout), expected to close in Q4 2026. The deal is meant to scale a medical laser platform (pairing IPG’s urology work with Lumibird’s ophthalmology position), expand the addressable market by about $1 billion, and be accretive to gross margin, EBITDA, and adjusted EPS.

Why the market likes it
Cyclical rebound is showing up in orders and sales. Battery manufacturing, industrial welding/cutting, and some advanced applications have improved, and management has pointed to a multi-year demand roadmap.
Earnings beats have moved the stock sharply at times (shares rose more than 40% in February 2026 after a large Q4 beat).
Strategy is shifting mix toward higher-value areas—medical, micromachining, semiconductor, and defense—rather than relying only on commodity high-power cutting lasers, where Chinese competition is intense.
The cash-rich, low-debt balance sheet limits financial risk and funds the medical expansion and buybacks or investment.
Sell-side consensus is Buy, with average price targets in the low-to-mid $120s (roughly 45–50% above recent prices in early October 2026 data), though individual targets range widely.

Why the market remains skeptical
Profitability is still far below the old peak. Gross margins that once sat well above 50% are now in the high 30s to low 40s. Analysts generally do not expect a full return to prior margin levels because of competition, especially from lower-cost Chinese fiber-laser suppliers, and a changed mix in core welding/cutting markets.
The stock is well below its 52-week high and has lagged over multi-year periods as industrial demand and margins compressed. Trailing valuation looks expensive until earnings normalize; if the recovery stalls, the multiple can compress.
End markets are cyclical (autos/EVs, machinery, general manufacturing, China). Tariffs have delayed shipments and pressured margins.
Short interest has been elevated at times (recently around 8% of shares outstanding / low-teens of float), reflecting doubts about the durability of the margin and growth story.
The Lumibird deal adds integration and execution risk even if it improves the longer-term mix.

text:
Why did housing prices skyrocket suddenly.  I have a friend who made several full-price offers but investors made over asking price and bought out from under her:
Did investment firms drive up the cost of housing by purchasing so many residential homes?  

The evidence on whether investment firms significantly drive up housing costs is **mixed and context-dependent**, with the consensus suggesting they are **one contributing factor among many**, rather than the sole cause.

**Arguments that investors increase costs**
Research indicates that institutional investors, particularly during the pandemic boom, **accelerated price growth** by competing for limited inventory. A Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis study found that higher shares of institutional ownership increased price-to-income ratios, especially for entry-level homes. In specific markets like Charlotte and Atlanta, large-scale purchases by Wall Street firms targeted affordable neighborhoods, reducing owner-occupied stock and raising local prices. During the 2020–2021 boom, investors (including large portfolios) nearly doubled their share of purchases, which economists linked to the surge in home prices as they outbid individual buyers.

**Arguments that investors have a modest or neutral impact**
Conversely, other analyses argue that institutional investors own a **very small share of the total housing stock** (less than 1% of all single-family homes and ~3% of rentals), making their aggregate impact on national prices minimal. A 2023 study by Coven found that while large investors slightly raised purchase prices, they **reduced rents** by increasing the supply of single-family rental units, often by renovating distressed properties that individual buyers avoided. Critics of the "investor blame" narrative note that investors are drawn to markets with strong fundamentals (population and job growth), meaning correlation does not equal causation, and that their cash purchases can actually lower transaction costs compared to mortgage buyers.

**Broader Context**
Most experts agree that the primary drivers of the housing affordability crisis are **chronic underbuilding, restrictive zoning, and rising interest rates**, not investor activity alone. While investors may exacerbate local shortages in specific hot markets, they are generally viewed as a **secondary factor** compared to the structural lack of new housing supply.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Mel Robbins Podcast: How One “Golden Moment” Can Transform Your Entire Life

Overview
A single courtroom moment can redirect an entire life, but only if it is backed by relentless daily work. John Grisham’s story is not a tale of signs or destiny. It is a case study in rejection, routine, and clarity. He sold 500 million books and saw nine feature films made from his work, yet his career began with roughly 20 rejections from New York, years of five in the morning writing sessions, and a first novel that flopped. The lesson is blunt and repeatable: write one page a day, know where the story is going before you start, and do not talk your ambition to death. The same principle applies far beyond writing. Momentum comes from small daily actions, not from waiting for inspiration or permission.

Key Themes
- Consistent daily output beats waiting for inspiration, big blocks of time, or perfect conditions.
- Repeated rejection is the norm for successful writers, not the exception, so persistence matters more than early validation.
- Knowing the ending and outlining before drafting prevents the wasted 50,000 words that get tossed when a writer backs into a corner.
- A story idea must survive a brutally honest 30 second pitch, ideally tested on someone who will shoot it down.
- A false plagiarism accusation shaped a lifelong pull toward justice, wrongful accusation, and courtroom morality.
- Two golden moments, one in college and one in a courthouse, gave sudden clarity after years of drifting.
- Studying admired practitioners, reading widely, and watching great trial lawyers in court builds skill and motivation.
- Focusing on what you can control, one small action a day, is the practical response to hopelessness and injustice.
- The good outnumber the bad, and small individual actions in home, marriage, friendship, and community drive broader change.

Detailed Summary
John Grisham’s career did not begin with a breakthrough. It began with roughly 20 submissions to New York, split between 10 agents and 10 publishers, that all came back rejected. He checked rejection letters on Friday afternoons after returning from the state capital. His first novel, A Time to Kill, was a flop when it was first published. He kept writing anyway.

Mel Robbins credits The Firm with changing her life in 1991. Reading it showed her she did not have to remain trapped in law school or a legal career. That personal debt sits behind the conversation, because the book that freed her almost did not exist.

The Firm grew from a real law school anecdote. At Ole Miss law school in the early 1980s, Grisham was not heavily recruited by law firms. He planned to return to his hometown, marry his sweetheart Renee, and open his own practice. A close friend who was a top student interviewed with regional firms in Houston, Kansas City, Memphis, and New Orleans. The friend returned and described a weird firm that felt like once you joined, you never left. Grisham had the story in mind from 1980, long before he thought of becoming a writer.

After A Time to Kill, a tough book to write and to read, Grisham wanted something more fun. He turned to the firm story his wife Renee had always loved. The Firm took two years to write. His first novel took three years. A Time to Kill was almost a thousand pages once typed, and his first editor cut a third of it. Grisham says the editor was right and there was too much junk in it. Cutting a third felt like losing a year of his life. After that, he decided to know where he was going, organize, and outline before writing.

The daily discipline became the core lesson. Write at least one page a day, preferably at the same time and same spot. Do not talk the book to death by telling people what you plan to do. Grisham wrote early work by hand on legal pads and often woke at five in the morning to write. As a rookie lawyer about 40 years ago, he got up at five o’clock every morning. His first novel took three years, the second two years, written back to back over a five year period. His wife repeatedly asked, where’s the latest chapter, when he had not written.

He still follows the same time, same spot, same coffee routine after more than 50 books. He cites John Irving saying he does not write the first sentence until he writes the last one. Grisham says he does not write the first scene until he knows the last scene. Writers often write 50,000 words, stop, back themselves into a corner, and toss the work. He pitches ideas to his wife and gets about 30 seconds. She is brutally honest and usually shoots them down.

The plagiarism accusation left a lasting mark. In freshman college English, Grisham had straight A’s but received a D minus after the teacher accused him of plagiarizing his term paper. He denied it. The teacher had written a big F on the back of the paper. He received an F on both the term paper and the final exam, resulting in the D minus for the course. He became emotional and cried in an empty men’s restroom. He left that school afterward and continued transferring. The episode happened when he was 19, and it shaped his later interest in writing about falsely accused and wrongfully convicted people.

Two golden moments gave sudden clarity. The first occurred in 1975 at Mississippi State in a finance course. A Vietnam vet student, about three years older and wounded in Vietnam, challenged a conservative professor who argued the U.S. should have stayed in Vietnam and could have won. The vet advised Grisham not to study general business but to study accounting, because it was the toughest business major, prepared students for law school, and was a route there. At age 20, Grisham stopped drifting, found a place on campus and in a major, and began thinking about law school. He had been drifting after high school, shaped by a strict Southern Baptist upbringing and the shadow of Vietnam and draft anxiety.

The second golden moment came when Grisham was a 30 year old lawyer dreaming of becoming a big trial lawyer. In a local courthouse, he watched a trial involving a young girl, around 10 or 12, testifying that she had been raped by a defendant described as a hardened criminal. The judge cleared the courtroom and posted deputies at entrances. Only necessary people, including Grisham as an officer of the court, remained. The girl testified for about an hour, moving through extreme emotions. Jurors were wiping their eyes, the judge hid his face, and lawyers were emotional. After a recess, Grisham returned for a forgotten briefcase and saw the defendant sitting unmoved, with only a deputy guarding him. He had a violent vengeful thought about what he would do if the victim were his daughter and he had a gun. That experience became the origin of A Time to Kill, envisioned through an idealistic young attorney appointed to represent the defendant. He had not written fiction before and began with chapter one.

Grisham practiced law for 10 years and did not enjoy it, but says he would not be a writer if he had not been a lawyer. He says writers should try different jobs, live different places, travel, and experience success, failure, love, hate, and broken hearts to have something to write about. He describes odd jobs including laying asphalt, driving a bulldozer, digging ditches, working for a plumbing company, and selling underwear at Sears. At 18, working at Sears, he refused to accept a return of a suspicious three pack of white briefs because they looked used, and his boss worked out a compromise. Tough construction and summer jobs made him appreciate college and realize what he did not want in life. His parents were not college graduates but wanted their children to go to college.

Reading is the most important habit. Grisham says he has never known a successful writer who was not an avid reader, and vocabulary, grammar, and technical skills can be self taught. He grew up with storytellers. His father, grandfather, and uncles told stories on the front porch in rural Arkansas while listening to Cardinals games on the radio. His mother disliked television, so the family went to the library often and read. He keeps a notebook of story ideas. Most do not work or fade, but the good ones stick.

The Firm’s path to Hollywood was accidental. Grisham’s agent wanted changes to The Firm, and he refused, leading to a months long stalemate. The agent called around Christmas 1989 saying nothing was happening and he would sell the book in January. A person pretending to be his agent ran 25 copies of The Firm and sent them to studios and production companies, generating offers. His agent called on a Sunday morning asking authority to accept the highest film rights offer from Paramount, Universal, or Disney Touchstone. The film rights sold to Paramount Pictures for $600,000, more than Grisham had made in 10 years of practicing law. The Firm was published in 1991 and hit the New York Times list. He went to New York for a victory lap and appeared on the Today Show with Bryant Gumbel.

A young Waldenbooks executive changed his output. The comment that the big guys come out every year motivated Grisham to publish annually. He returned to Oxford, Mississippi and wrote around the clock to finish The Pelican Brief for 1992 publication. Book a year has continued for roughly 35 years, with the motto page a day, a book a year. He advocates patterning yourself after admired practitioners, watching great trial lawyers in court and reading popular fiction to learn technique and find motivation. He was inspired both by books he felt he could surpass and by books he felt he could never match.

On hopelessness and injustice, Grisham focuses on what he can control. Take baby steps. Do one thing daily to make the world a little better. Publishing needs new talent every year, so he tells discouraged writers to read debut novels and keep writing as long as they have a story. His Innocence Project involvement began with a New York Times obituary about a man his age from his region who came within five days of execution in Oklahoma. He traveled to Oklahoma, met the family, and wrote a book about it. That work opened his eyes to thousands of innocent people in prison roughly 20 years ago. He still writes about wrongful convictions and advocates for criminal justice reform while frustrated by lack of reform. He and his wife are active with nonprofits addressing childhood hunger, homelessness, and wrongful convictions.

The closing message is forward looking. The speaker feels hopeless looking at the wider world but empowered by focusing on their own community and asking what one positive thing they can do today. Small individual actions in home, marriage, friendships, community, and the world are the mechanism for broader positive change. The good outnumber the bad. Listeners are encouraged to act on the advice and tools shared, and to start writing a new chapter.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett: Most Replayed Moment: I Met An Uncontacted Tribe! The Secret World Hidden In The Amazon Rainforest - Paul Rosolie

Overview
Paul Rosolie has spent most of his adult life in the Amazon, and his story moves from teenage adventure to a life mission: protecting a rainforest that supplies roughly a fifth of the planet's fresh water and oxygen. After watching loggers burn ancient forest, he and his mentor JJ built an organization that turns former loggers and gold miners into conservation rangers and now protects 130,000 acres. The centerpiece is a rare encounter with an uncontacted, nomadic tribe, told not as spectacle but as a lesson in fear, survival, and what protection actually requires. His larger argument is blunt: humans removed themselves from nature and are paying for it in loneliness, anxiety, and lost purpose. This is the last generation that can restore what remains.

Key Themes
- The Amazon functions as a planetary life-support system, not a regional resource, which makes its destruction a global risk rather than a local one.
- Conservation works when local people are paid to protect what they know, converting former loggers and miners into rangers instead of outsiders imposing rules.
- Uncontacted tribes survive by keeping the outside world out; their violence is a response to encroachment, and their only realistic hope is external protection of their forest.
- Contact with isolated peoples is reliably destructive through pathogens, alcohol, and money, capable of erasing a language and culture within a single generation.
- Modern disconnection from forests, deserts, mountains, and oceans shows up as loneliness, anxiety, and a lost sense of purpose.
- Voluntary difficulty builds resilience; doing hard things you do not want to do is framed as a trainable capacity tied to longevity.
- Reputation damage from a misrepresented TV stunt cost years, and the recovery came through returning to field experience rather than chasing redemption.
- Fear of snakes and of the wild is mostly learned and disproportionate, which matters because that distance feeds the broader disconnection.

Detailed Summary
Paul frames the Amazon as a system the whole planet depends on. He cites about one-fifth of fresh water and one-fifth of oxygen, which makes protecting it irreplaceable rather than optional. His personal arc began at 18 with a need for adventure and moved toward meaning once he understood what was being destroyed.

He has lived mostly in the Amazon for 20 years and says he has slept more nights outdoors than indoors in adult life. He befriended indigenous people of the upper Amazon and learned under indigenous experts during what he calls the barefoot machete days. One teacher, JJ, did not have shoes until age 13 and lived a life where fishing meant going to the river and eating meant entering the forest.

As a young teenager he camped with one match, one steak, and a golden retriever, with a rule of no shelter. He describes being suspended and in detention while also being in American Mensa, and feeling school was controlling and counter to his nature. He dropped out, took the GED, and agreed to attend university between Amazon trips. At 17 he arranged work at a remote research station two days by boat from the nearest city in Peru.

The station was run by JJ, a Peruvian indigenous man from the Seaha tribe and son of Don Santiago. JJ's knowledge covered medicinal plants, piranha fishing, Barbasco root to stun fish, and tracking deer, jaguar, and people. Paul traded snake-handling knowledge for JJ's broader jungle knowledge. A pivotal scene arrives when JJ points at a beach and asks him to read the news, interpreting jaguar tracks, scat, vultures, and a fresh deer kill.

The turning point came when loggers burned ancient forest. JJ asked whether he saw anybody, then told him he had to do something. Paul was around 19 or 20 with no PhD, no trust fund, and no media presence, only a machete and bare feet. He and JJ became directors of Jungle Keepers, which has protected 130,000 acres and is on the cusp of creating a national park. The stated mission is to save the entire watershed.

Jungle Keepers turns loggers and gold miners into conservation rangers and offers local indigenous communities sustainable work as rangers, boat drivers, guides, and handymen. The point is to give people cash alternatives so they do not become loggers, countering outsiders who take trees and fish and sell things not worth what people think. The reserve contains two indigenous communities.

Paul argues people are alive at the most important moment in history because global society now faces the same problem: if ecosystems collapse, life on Earth is not possible. He calls this the last generation that can restore them. He links modern disconnection to screens and anxiety and calls humans a fish perpetually out of water. He says he personally needs trees, frogs, stars, and rivers, and feels stressed when locked in concrete or composite-material rooms. He describes a hotel room where everything was unnatural and he could not open the window.

A related theme is voluntary difficulty. He cites the anterior midcingulate cortex as a region that grows when people do hard things they do not want to do, noting it tends to be smaller in younger doom-scrolling generations and in obese people, and bigger in athletes and longer-lived people. He references Sebastian Junger on community, tribe, and mission, and Teddy Roosevelt going to the Badlands after losing his mother and wife on the same day, returning transformed. He also mentions Native American vision quests and Aboriginal initiation practices.

He describes 10-day solo survival trips deep in the Amazon, off the map, to verify destruction firsthand rather than through a screen. His body carries scars from crocodile bites, tiger bites, infections, near-crushing by elephants, and being hunted by narco-traffickers. He rejects finding out through a screen what the wild actually looks like.

The river stayed wild for hundreds of years because it was protected by the Mashco-Piro, described as nomadic and uncontacted and as the original jungle keepers. A distinction is drawn between indigenous communities outsiders can interface with and uncontacted tribes; the president of Peru had called the uncontacted tribes a myth. A BBC piece had flown a plane over an uncontacted tribe.

About a year before the account, the community called Jungle Keepers to report the tribe was coming out and urged the directors to come because they feared they would not be believed. Paul and JJ were in town with lawyers when they heard the tribe is out. They traveled a two-day boat journey in one night, from 6 p.m. to 9 a.m., through a severe thunderstorm in an open-top canoe, navigating by caiman eyes shining back at a flashlight because the storm hid the river edges.

When they arrived the tribe had left. A man had been shot at with a 7-foot arrow while fishing; the arrow ricocheted off the boat and hit his thick leather belt, blunting the tip. Ignacio, now a Jungle Keeper ranger, carries a scar from being shot in the head by a 7-foot arrow while trying to make peaceful contact and give a gift. A native anthropologist from another region arrived, said he was known as the grandfather, and claimed he could speak a little of their language. Paul says he learned to always believe locals in the Amazon, and Ignacio insisted the tribe was coming and that leaving would be idiotic.

The tribe appeared across the river: naked, with string around waists, carrying 7-foot bows and arrows, crouched and watching. The anthropologist said they do not have stones and are still in the bamboo age, describing them as hunter-gatherers isolated for centuries like a time capsule. Paul describes a thousand years between them while standing on opposite sides of the river. The tribespeople held up their hands and said no mole, meaning we are the brothers, and the other side repeated it. The first request was to send bananas and plantains. The contacted side responded that they would talk if the tribespeople put down their weapons, saying they did not want it to end violently.

Both sides were primarily motivated by fear. The group asked how to tell the bad guys from the good guys, saying they are hunted by traffickers, gold miners, and loggers. They accused all outsiders of cutting down their trees and said our trees are our gods. The group demanded plantains, and anthropologists gave bananas and plantains from a boat in the river. They rushed desperately for them and held their own portions. Archers stayed hidden in the shadows while others in front put down bows. The group worried cameras were guns and asked for cameras to be put down. Communication was difficult because many spoke at once. The interaction lasted several hours.

The group said some of you shooted us with guns and fire sticks. They were all men, with women hidden in the forest who allegedly raided a farm behind the observers, taking yuca, plantains, and sugarcane. The farm was ruined afterward, and smaller footprints were cited as evidence. The group reportedly eats primarily turtles and monkeys and does not fish, and they deny cannibalism rumors. Rope is highly important for bowstrings, arrows, and lashing. They have large, wide, calloused bare feet. They appeared to range from roughly ages 12 to 45, with no one who looked in their 50s.

The anthropologist said he had met an uncontacted tribe before in the region but none of these men. At the end he told them to go in peace. The group asked to see the speaker with the big beard, and they acknowledged each other with raised hands. As they left, one man showed a machete over his shoulder; another warrior shot an arrow toward them, smiled, and left. Millions of butterflies swarmed the beach as the tribe walked across it.

A man named George was shot the day after the encounter while driving a boat; an arrow entered over his scapula and exited near his belly button, collapsing his right lung. He was helicopter evacuated and survived but was permanently changed. Police have no jurisdiction outside the city, and Paul says there is no law in the wild. The tribe reportedly emulates animal calls, including capuchin monkeys, birds, and tinamou, to communicate and surround prey. Don Santiago told them that if animal sounds seemed off or something felt wrong, the tribe had surrounded them and were watching. A friend's father was shot in the stomach and died in a similar situation.

Paul rejects framing the tribe's reality around happiness and describes it as desperate, closer to Cormac McCarthy than Downton Abbey, concerned with calories, the blood cost of travel, and stealing women from other tribes. He says little is known about birth rates, infant mortality, treatment of the elderly, creation myths, and beliefs. He doubts some have seen water boil, since they lack pots, and says they certainly do not know water freezes. He describes them as living in a 4D jungle environment beneath the canopy and notes they make fire, evidenced by cooking and camps.

He argues contact must be gradual, led over time, and must preserve the tribe's agency, which requires protecting their forest. Releasing the footage was sensitive because it could encourage others to seek out isolated people who have long asked to be left alone. An invisible mist river above the Amazon is described as larger than the Amazon River itself. A treehouse was built on a promontory at the edge of the terra firma overlooking the jungle so donors and visitors can see the reserve and the forest they are protecting. Paul says he is not jealous of the tribes' lives, has no romanticism about their state, and values modern medicine, photography, a camera roll, and FaceTime with family. He frames the relationship as being at the stage of learning which questions to ask, not receiving lessons.

A separate thread covers snakes and a costly TV stunt. Paul learned snake handling from Steve Irwin: catch a snake by the tail, and if you have the head, you have control. He agreed to a Discovery Channel stunt where he would attempt to be eaten by an anaconda, motivated by reaching millions with a conservation message. He believed snakes would not actually try to eat him, but producers wanted the spectacle. His first big anaconda catch nearly killed him; he grabbed it by the head instead of the tail, the snake wrapped around his wrists like handcuffs and then his shoulders, and he could hear his collarbone flexing. JJ grabbed it by the tail and pulled it off at the last second. The snake was about 12 feet long and at least as thick as Paul's leg.

He had a breathing tube and a special suit for the stunt. The show was filmed for six weeks and called Expedition Amazon, with the call sheet abbreviated EA. The anaconda used was named Eleanor, after his grandmother. Eleanor was the largest snake ever verifiably, scientifically measured at the time: 18 feet 6 inches and over 100 kilos, and skinny because she had not eaten recently. The team caught her while filming. They fed her a transmitter she consumed and retained until defecation, which for snakes can take months, to learn how she moved through the environment, research Paul calls never done before.

Jane Goodall was a formative influence and he credits her with making his career, books, and conservation work possible. He gave her printed chapters, including one about caring for a baby giant anteater and one about searching for his first anaconda, with a cover letter asking for an endorsement. About 48 hours later her team reached out; she had read the chapters and said she would endorse his book if he found a publisher. The endorsement helped him get in the door. She is quoted on the front of his book: on behalf of the forests that I love, thank you, Paul, for writing this book. His parents read him and his sister stories about Jane Goodall and Gombe at night. She broke rules by naming her study subjects, saying they have names and personalities.

The show was changed from a science and conservation working title into a stunt-driven special titled Eaten Alive, dropping the science and conservation messaging. The stunt used a captive snake and handlers, not a wild encounter. The fallout damaged his reputation across multiple groups: the public felt misled, PETA objected to the snake's treatment, and scientists dismissed him as a thrill-seeker. He says the backlash put him out of work and set him back about 10 years, and he left for India and lived with a herd of elephants. He reframes the failure as a turning point that sent him back to the field for years of experience and led him to develop technology as a forest-saving strategy.

For the first 15 years of his 20-year journey he had no support, living out of a backpack and a boat in the Amazon, barefoot, with no paycheck, health insurance, or clear path. He describes himself as a high school dropout who was never going to be a conservation biologist and was trained and adopted by local people. He cites a quote attributed to Alex Hormozi: confidence comes from giving people irrefutable proof that you are who you say you are.

In a studio segment he introduces a baby ball python and a larger ball python of the same species. He explains snakes are ectotherms dependent on environment for body temperature, and calls ball pythons the golden retrievers of snakes: docile, low-risk, and handleable even near the face. On a smooth table they struggle and use an inchworm motion, showing they need ground contact and friction. Burmese pythons are described as obligate carnivores, pretty placid despite their size, capable of reaching 18 feet, and in Florida they have no predators that can handle them and are eating alligators, birds, and native wildlife. Reticulated pythons are described as the longest snakes and the only ones confirmed to have eaten humans, while anacondas are described as the biggest snake on Earth. His core message is to be respectful of snakes the way one is respectful of heights, rather than afraid.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Joe Rogan Experience: JRE MMA Show #186 with Sean Sharaf

Overview
A massive underdog score and a hard look at what it costs. Sean Sharaf knocked out Gable Steveson with a first-round left hook, possibly the biggest betting upset in sport history, after a camp with no sponsors, no promotion, and almost no money. He now questions whether to keep fighting at all. The wider conversation covers motivation, damage, coaching, rules, peptide regulation, surveillance, and political discourse.

Key Themes
- A historic upset was built on desperation, not resources, and the win immediately raised the question of walking away.
- Chasing glory is framed as a bad motivation; glory finds the greats, it is not something you catch by hunting it.
- Elite wrestling does not translate automatically to elite MMA, and neglecting your best skill is fatal.
- Sudden fame invites resentment, accusations of changing, and opportunists appearing after the breakthrough.
- The regional-to-UFC jump is enormous; many fighters need several UFC fights before their real skills show.
- Fighters face an endless title treadmill, and knowing when to stop can matter more than one more win.
- The oblique kick to the knee is debated as a career-ending technique that should be banned.
- A purist rule set is proposed: no stand-ups, no position resets, one continuous fight.
- Peptides like BPC-157 and creatine are discussed as recovery and performance tools, with purity risks.

Detailed Summary
The win itself was a shock. Sharaf, a heavy underdog, landed a left hook and Steveson fell. He says he cursed in disbelief. Coming off two losses and a minus-2400 line, he had no sponsors and got only a $4,000 advance from management. He stayed in cheap fighter houses in Las Vegas where rooms cost about $40, slept on a mat and later an air mattress, and gambled in casinos. At one point he texted Strickland about the situation.

The camp was brutal and unusual. He went eight weeks abstinent, calling it Marine mode. He trained with a broken nose in headgear that felt suffocating, repeatedly put in bad positions, picked up and slammed. His camp included Sergey Spivak, a coach named Bloy, and Wan Coutaba. A planned fight with Tai Tuivasa was canceled in April. He had already been in camp for Tuivasa and pulled out after breaking his nose.

The White House card was floated as a possible venue around June. He said yes and never heard back. The fight landed in LA roughly six weeks after he was told. He only got the main card spot after Ortega fell out, which he describes as divine intervention. Without the press conference, he doubts he would have gotten in Steveson's head.

Steveson came in as an Olympic gold medalist, one of the best U.S. heavyweight wrestlers ever, undefeated in MMA, trained by Jon Jones, with only about a year and a half of striking. Dana White praised his striking after his first fight. He booked a RAF wrestling match during camp a few weeks out. He did not attempt takedowns in either the first fight or the title fight.

Sharaf argues the loss came from neglecting the number one skill. Steveson tried to stand and strike instead of wrestling. Sharaf says his own plan was simple: do not over-respect the wrestling, put hands on him, and land the left hook. He says Steveson reached and closed his eyes. He also brought up Steveson's past at the press conference intentionally, and admits the same punch might have landed anyway.

Rogan frames the moment as potentially life-defining and urges letting it settle before deciding anything. Sharaf is openly questioning whether to walk away. He cites a CT scan showing brain matter concerns, stitches head to toe, and multiple injuries. He wants to go to the mountains or desert, take mushrooms with his dog, and process everything.

He compares himself to Justin Gaethje's upset over Ilia Topuria at the White House, called one of the greatest moments in combat sports history. Gaethje had nothing left to prove and could walk away as an all-time great. The difference between chasing the dream and chasing the high is a central tension, especially for wealthy, established fighters. Conor McGregor's last fight is described as wanting to prove he could still beat a world-class fighter like Max Holloway despite being worth half a billion dollars.

On the regional scene, Steveson reportedly got wheel-kicked in Mexico by a 1-0 opponent. A good manager protects fighters from being fed to elite wrestlers too early. Hanging around an all-time great like Jon Jones can lead a fighter to believe he is the next Jon Jones before earning it. A lack of dungeon experience, hard grinding regional fights and being in the fire repeatedly, was a decisive gap.

Jon Jones is praised as a one-of-one athlete and the GOAT. His win over Ciryl Gane is described as dominant: takedown, strangle, not scratched. He became the youngest UFC champion at 22. His run through Gusmao, Stefan Bonner, and Shogun is recalled, along with choking Machida unconscious. Kamaru Usman vs. Leon Edwards is used as an example of how one head kick can change a career forever.

Sharaf says people accused him of going Hollywood about five days after the win. He was bombarded by texts. He did interviews all day while wanting to walk his dog. He did the Bisping interview while walking Apollo, his German Shepherd, now nearly eight, who has been with him through moving to Vegas alone and knee surgeries, including driving himself to PT two days post-op.

He calls the lucky punch criticism an attempt to diminish accomplishment. He says there is no such thing as a lucky punch: he stepped in, threw a left hook, and landed it perfectly. He cites Charles Oliveira, who had a reputation for quitting and losses to Cub Swanson, then became undeniable and a world champion. He criticizes commentators with no high-level accomplishments diminishing fighters performing with millions watching on Paramount Plus and 16,000 in the arena.

He explains his post-fight prayer as the opening prayer of the Quran, recited for his late father, and rejects the idea that this makes him anti-American. His father passed when he was 15. The Marine Corps taught him to tie a tie, shave, press his uniform, and articulate himself. He has the prayer memorized since childhood and recites it for the dead and in daily prayer. He says he is not a perfect Muslim, mentions gambling, and says many Muslims hide things. He chooses not to conform to one side or the other. He notes he has America tattooed on his arm and says there is no nuance anymore, giving the example that supporting Palestine supposedly conflicts with being a Marine.

He describes being on the journey alone for a long time and now seeing snakes in the grass offering to manage, help, or sponsor him. Rogan reframes sponsor interest as a consequence of success and elevation, not necessarily exploitation. Rogan notes Sharaf was 0-2 in the UFC before the breakthrough and says the gap between the regional circuit and the UFC is gigantic. Some fighters are phenomenal in camp but cannot be themselves under the bright lights.

The heavyweight division is described as insanely shallow, giving heavyweights a better chance of not being cut if they fight hard. Tai Tuivasa is mentioned as having seven losses in a row. A fighter with three UFC fights is fighting for the title. Herb Dean is criticized for stopping a fight. Sharaf prefers fighters who go out on their shield rather than stay too long and get hurt badly. He relates to Dustin Poirier stopping to preserve his health and brain. He says he has a lot of life left and wants to prioritize health and family.

His original goal was just to hear and new once. He is torn because the UFC is the biggest stage and he is only 30, but he just had a newborn daughter and a son, and wants to be able to play with them. His college wrestling coach told him the most important thing you can do is play with your kids. He now realizes that message has come full circle. He wants to go out on top, not be one of those guys who stays too long. He references Tony Ferguson as someone who just wants one more win. He thinks Tai Tuivasa should retire. He mentions bare-knuckle fighting as an option after the UFC because it pays.

He paid for every private session and never got free privates, which contributed to financial struggle with no sponsors. He sought coaches like Cus D'Amato but did not find them. He bounced around gyms including Pillo, Nick, Freestyle MMA, and Pada. He recommends fighters move to a big gym like Syndicate MMA for proper coaching, noting gyms give free privates to top prospects. He started MMA in 2016, so he is 10 years in. His friend and manager Rocky will present him with options, and he will decide when ready.

On brain damage, MRI and CT scans reportedly found white specks and white matter changes from unclear causes. Sparring is described as a major source of brain damage, not just fights. Camp was built around an opponent crawling forward like Jones and using the oblique kick. In the fight, the opponent walked forward instead. Jon Jones is credited with destroying opponents' knees, including Thiago Santos, who had both knees reconstructed, and Rampage Jackson, who said his knee was never the same. MVP blew out an opponent's knee with a sidekick, requiring surgery right after the fight.

The proposed ban would target only straight kicks that hyperextend the knee, not leg kicks or round kicks to the leg. Andy Foster, a California athletic commission director, reportedly thinks the kick should be banned, and the UFC also thinks it should be banned. The anti-kick argument compares it to banned eye pokes and biting: the sport already restricts permanently injurious actions. A counterargument is that heel hooks can be tapped to, but a sidekick to the knee cannot be tapped out of. MVP is presented as proof that elite point-fighting karate can translate to MMA if combined with grappling and leg-kick defense. Ian Garry was cited as the only fighter who figured out how to handle MVP.

On rules, Sharaf favors a purist set where fighters are never stood up and rounds do not reset position. If you get taken down, you must earn your way up, and failure to do so means you lost that fight. A fight is one continuous fight, not five separate fights. Pride's early-2000s heavyweight division is called the most stacked heavyweight era ever, with Mirko Cro Cop, Mark Coleman, Minotauro Nogueira, and Fedor. Fedor reportedly lost to Blagoi Ivanov in combat sambo by points. The concern with 25 minutes straight is a battle of attrition and horrific damage for heavyweights. Cain Velasquez vs. Junior Dos Santos is cited: Dos Santos won the first by knockout, Velasquez dominated the next two.

On peptides, BPC-157 is described as the best peptide for soft tissue injuries and used heavily by the speaker. Unregulated online peptides are risky because purity and content may be unreliable, with tests finding some contain only about 20 percent of what is claimed. Creatine is strongly endorsed as one of the few legitimate supplements for athletes and mental performance, citing benefits under sleep deprivation. Dosage is commonly 5 grams, not milligrams. Creatine makes people hold more water, which may matter for fighters cutting weight. Ryan Garcia vs. Conor Benn was mentioned, with Conor Benn reportedly rehydrating from 146 to 178.4 pounds less than 12 hours after weigh-ins.

Ryan Garcia is seen as a different level than Conor Benn, based on competing against elite opposition like Javvante and Roelly, and his extreme speed and left hook. Conor Benn is in severe financial distress, filing bankruptcy and in debt from fight-related expenses, viewing fighting as his way out. He says his only goal was getting his hand raised in the octagon; now that he has achieved it, he is unsure what is next and is taking things as they come. The argument is that fighters should be fully committed or not fight at all; a half-committed fighter will eventually meet someone fully committed. The recommendation is that Conor Benn get a legitimate technical coach like Trevor Whitman or Faras Hobby rather than just sparring, to develop as a fighter.

On coaching, the idea that you must have competed to be a great coach is disputed. Analytical understanding and dedication can matter more than personal competition history. John Danaher is cited as the greatest jiu-jitsu coach despite not competing, due to unparalleled analytical understanding and dedication, training seven days a week. His injuries, two hip replacements and a knee replacement, are cited as why he could not compete. Athletes credited to him include Gordon Ryan, Garry Tonon, Craig Jones, and Nicky Rod. Craig Jones is described as the funniest guy in jiu-jitsu.

The conversation then turns to politics and surveillance. The term anti-Semitic is argued to be misapplied to criticism of Israel. Many Palestinians are themselves Semites and many Jews oppose the actions in Gaza. Clips and narratives strip nuance, causing people to react to fragments rather than full speeches. The Macklemore speech is presented as clear evidence that Free Palestine and criticism of Israel are not anti-Jewish messages.

Gaza is described as around 90 percent destroyed, with amputations without anesthesia and thousands or tens of thousands of women and children killed. The claim is made that the Biden administration funded Israel's actions. In Iraq and Afghanistan there were rules of engagement requiring looking someone in the eyes, contrasted with drone and missile strikes. Mamdani is cited as winning NYC mayor partly because he was the only candidate who said he would not visit Israel. Some members of Congress are said to have dual citizenship and receive funding, with the correction that all of Congress is not accurate. A banned documentary clip is shown alleging pro-Israel curriculum in American schools, with a speaker saying Israel and the Jews are better than all of us, described as indoctrination starting in childhood. Something similar reportedly just passed in Texas. Fauci pleading the fifth and a pardon are cited as examples of being lied to.

A preacher argues Christians have a spiritual obligation to support Israel, citing Genesis 12's promise that God blesses those who bless Israel and curses those who curse it. The speakers push back on the idea that any group is better than others, calling that teaching to children insane and asserting all people are God's children deserving dignity, respect, and love. There is disagreement over surveillance. Flock cameras have helped catch criminals, but the technology is widely abused. Liberty should not be traded for security. The tension is surveillance as a tool to catch terrorists versus documented misuse and the risk of a self-censoring surveillance state.

Immigration is discussed: the border should not be open, immigrants should be vetted to exclude terrorists, criminals, and cartel members, and enforcement is complicated by a four-year window before a possible 2028 political reversal. ICE is said to offer a $50,000 signing bonus, leading some recruits into debt when background checks disqualify them and ICE seeks repayment. The border was open for four years, letting in at least 10 million undocumented people. The census counts all people, not just citizens, so undocumented populations could shift congressional seats. Open-border motives are claimed to include cheap labor for construction and meatpacking companies and alleged census-based seat rigging.

Flock camera misuse examples include a Franklin County detective fired for tracking a private citizen, a North Carolina deputy fired and the system suspended in Franklin County, five Indianapolis officers charged with misuse, one allegedly tracking women to interact with them, and one Florida officer tracking his ex-wife roughly 500 times. Mark Andreessen reportedly argued Flock cameras helped catch shooters in Austin who were apprehended after leaving city limits where Flock is disallowed. Palantir is referenced as using face recognition in Gaza, with a system fusing satellites, radars, and cameras into real-time tracking. Benjamin Franklin is invoked: those who give up liberty for security deserve neither. The call is for serious punishment, including firing squad and public hangings, as an alternative deterrent.

Throughout, the throughline is the cost of the moment. A fighter achieved the only thing he ever wanted and immediately faced the question of whether it was worth it. The sport rewards that kind of sacrifice, then asks for more. Sharaf sounds like a man who knows the answer might already be no.

📖This morning I read in the book of Jeremiah about those whose ancestors turned against the Lord and did not keep the law.  They acted more wickedly than ancestors, so God threw them out of the country and restored the land to the Israelites because this land was promised o their ancestors!
 
“Then the word of the LORD came to me: “You must not marry and have sons or daughters in this place.” For this is what the LORD says about the sons and daughters born in this land and about the women who are their mothers and the men who are their fathers: “They will die of deadly diseases. They will not be mourned or buried but will be like dung lying on the ground. They will perish by sword and famine, and their dead bodies will become food for the birds and the wild animals.” For this is what the LORD says: “Do not enter a house where there is a funeral meal; do not go to mourn or show sympathy, because I have withdrawn my blessing, my love and my pity from this people,” declares the LORD. “Both high and low will die in this land. They will not be buried or mourned, and no one will cut themselves or shave their head for the dead. No one will offer food to comfort those who mourn for the dead—not even for a father or a mother—nor will anyone give them a drink to console them. “And do not enter a house where there is feasting and sit down to eat and drink. For this is what the LORD Almighty, the God of Israel, says: Before your eyes and in your days I will bring an end to the sounds of joy and gladness and to the voices of bride and bridegroom in this place. “When you tell these people all this and they ask you, ‘Why has the LORD decreed such a great disaster against us? What wrong have we done? What sin have we committed against the LORD our God?’ then say to them, ‘It is because your ancestors forsook me,’ declares the LORD, ‘and followed other gods and served and worshiped them. They forsook me and did not keep my law. But you have behaved more wickedly than your ancestors. See how all of you are following the stubbornness of your evil hearts instead of obeying me. So I will throw you out of this land into a land neither you nor your ancestors have known, and there you will serve other gods day and night, for I will show you no favor.’ “However, the days are coming,” declares the LORD, “when it will no longer be said, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of Egypt,’ but it will be said, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of the north and out of all the countries where he had banished them.’ For I will restore them to the land I gave their ancestors. “But now I will send for many fishermen,” declares the LORD, “and they will catch them. text:
A Beluga Had Pneumonia Antibiotics Couldn’t Cure. Doctors Sent Viruses Down Its Blowhole Instead | Tudor Tarita, ZME Science

When antibiotics failed an 11-year-old beluga whale with stubborn pneumonia, her veterinarians reached for something that sounds, at first, counterintuitive: viruses.

Jetta, a beluga at Mystic Aquarium in Connecticut, had developed chronic pneumonia caused by a multidrug-resistant strain of E. coli. Powerful antibiotics had done little to clear the infection. So veterinarians at the aquarium, working with researchers at the University of Florida, selected bacteriophages—viruses that prey specifically on bacteria—capable of attacking the strain infecting her.

But how do you get virus-based medicine deep into the lungs of a whale?

Their answer was a custom nebulizer built for a blowhole.

Caretakers taught Jetta to swim to the edge of her pool three times a day and inhale deeply through the device, breathing in a mist containing the phages. More than a year after treatment, her care team says it has found no evidence that the pneumonia has returned and no apparent adverse effects from the therapy.

The treatment appears to represent the first use of bacteriophage therapy against a bacterial infection in a marine mammal via nebulizer. Given the odd case, it’s no surprise this is a world-first operation. But the case has not yet been described in a peer-reviewed scientific paper, so important clinical details remain unavailable for independent assessment.

Bacteria Busters

Bacteriophages, or simply phages, infect bacteria rather than animal cells. A phage attaches to a susceptible bacterium, inserts its genetic material and turns the cell into a factory for producing more phages. Many eventually burst their bacterial host apart.

That specificity is both their strength and their weakness. A phage capable of killing one bacterial strain may be ineffective against another, meaning researchers often need to find phages closely matched to the pathogen causing an infection.

For Jetta, that precision provided another option when conventional drugs faltered.

“Whales, dolphins and seals, in the wild and under human care alike, are especially prone to gram-negative bacterial infections, a category of pathogens notoriously difficult to cure with antibiotics,” Molly Martony, senior veterinarian at Mystic Aquarium, told Popular Science.

“That’s the opposite of most land mammals, which more commonly battle gram-positive infections with a wider range of treatment options. As a result, marine mammals face multidrug-resistant infections far more often.”

According to the University of Florida’s Phage Across One Health Symposium page, Martony will present the case at the symposium on Oct. 30, 2026.

A Life Jacket

Phage therapy itself is not new. Scientists have experimented with it in humans for years, particularly against infections that no longer respond reliably to antibiotics. What makes Jetta’s case especially intriguing is how the treatment reached the infection.

“Administering the phages via nebulization, essentially having her breathe them in, proved remarkably effective and stress-free,” Martony explained. “Human researchers have also started to show that it’s a route worth exploring in human medicine, potentially offering a faster, less invasive way to fight multidrug-resistant infections in people.”

Previously, a 2026 review of inhaled bacteriophage therapy identified 31 human studies, including six clinical trials, testing nebulized, aerosolized, or dry-powder phages against lung infections. Most reported clinical or microbiological improvements without major adverse events.

Jetta’s successful treatment does not mean inhaled phages will become standard medicine for whales—much less people. But her case offers an unusual demonstration of what such treatment can look like: a carefully selected virus inhaled through the blowhole of a cooperative whale.

And for Jetta, the treatment was a life jacket.

SMOKING GUN: Fulton County Quietly Ordered 1,058,910 Absentee Ballots With No Stubs and No Envelopes — More Than Every Registered Voter in the County
By Jonathan Gregory 

Fulton County, GA - October 1, 2026
President Trump’s allies say a paper trail that Fulton County never wanted found has blown the 2020 Georgia election wide open. County records, uncovered only after a receipt was produced and shoved in front of officials, show Fulton ordered 1,058,910 absentee ballots at the last minute, without the stubs used for chain of custody tracking and without the envelopes required to mail, verify, and later audit a ballot. Official tallies put total ballots cast in Fulton at 528,777, of which only about 148,000 were absentee, and most of those were printed and sent to voters by Runbeck Election Services under the state’s own program. The late county order, skeptics argue, could not have been folded, stuffed, and mailed in the days remaining, which leaves one question hanging over every recount Georgia has ever offered; what were those ballots for?

The math gets worse the closer you look. The Election Assistance Commission listed Fulton County with 836,563 registered voters in 2020, a figure already equal to 113.8 percent of the county’s citizen voting age population. The blank absentee stock Fulton took in still blew past that number, landing at roughly 126 percent of every name on the rolls, active and inactive combined. Georgia law only requires counties to keep emergency ballots equal to 10 percent of registered voters, about 83,656 in Fulton’s case. Nothing in that statute explains a seven-figure print run with the audit features stripped off, placed after the realistic mailing window had closed, and kept quiet until the invoice surfaced.

Trump supporters say the conclusion is no longer a theory. A county that certified a Biden win did so after ordering more unmarked absentee ballots than it had voters, more than six times the emergency stock the law contemplates, and far beyond the 148,000 absentee ballots that were actually counted. Those ballots, the argument goes, were the raw material for the fraudulent votes that flipped Georgia. Until Fulton accounts for every sheet in that 1,058,910 order, ballot by ballot, the certified result remains what Trump has called it from the start; a stolen election.
