My irritation has now gone beyond the boiling point, so:
Is Finland’s current situation good? Do you think the previous government and president—as well as the current ones—are genuinely and deliberately leading the Finnish people toward a safe and bright future?
If you think so, stop reading here.

The current president is leading Finland in completely the wrong direction in a totally irresponsible manner. He has a habit of making utterly irresponsible statements that are detached from reality—acting as if he were still a quasi-professor at an institute training would-be EU bureaucrats.

A small country does not need warmongers at the helm. Our political elite is currently wedded to the cowardly conformity of European groupthink, striving for a state of utter blandness.

Regarding "consensus"—which is just a new word for groupthink—Einstein himself once made his views clear when his theory of relativity was criticized in a statement signed by 100 academics representing that brand of groupthink/consensus.

His response was—not verbatim, but in essence:
"If only one of these all-knowing critics had presented even a single counter-argument... but NO." Science is, of course, not the same as politics, but have we heard a single diplomatically constructive proposal for the crisis from any politician or bureaucrat?

"So what"—just "so what"—what of it?
How can a country—whose citizens have lived in harmony with their large neighbor since World War II, and whose relationship with that neighbor was built up by patriotic politicians over decades—elect such chest-thumping warmongers as Stubb, Häkkänen, Valtonen, and Orpo? All of them, except Stubb, are pathetic cowards.

Stubb is a WEF zealot floating in his own euphoria—a textbook case of naked ambition and narcissism. He has no goal other than rising to a leadership position in the UN, NATO, or the EU; anything will do, as long as he doesn't have to think about the Finnish people.
But the fact that the rest of the politicians are such spineless weaklings—mere tag-alongs—is truly disheartening.

They offer reassurances that Finns shouldn't be frightened by all sorts of "crackpot nonsense" or alleged hybrid threats.
WHAT THE H...LL is this, if not the state and YLE using TV banners to scare Finnish citizens? And then there are the incidents where MPs' homes have been targeted—especially that of Halla-aho. (probably Russia),

This fear planted in Europe—backed by US hawks—is designed to prevent people from coming to their senses and initiating proper discussions with Russia.
It is a matter of economic power.
WAKE UP, PEOPLE!

What can be done?
A few thoughts:
Require the President, Members of Parliament, Permanent Secretaries, and ambassadors to submit "quarterly reports" to be published on the Parliament’s website alongside the country's quarterly economic reports. A report fitting onto a single A4 sheet, answering four questions:
- What have you done during the previous quarter?
- How has it contributed to the country's development?
- What do you plan to do during the next quarter?
- Why?
Finally, restrict voting rights to those who paid taxes during the preceding year.

So-called "political accountability" is utterly meaningless and amounts to nothing.

Perhaps the only way to hold politicians accountable for their decisions and promises is to replace political accountability with financial accountability.

text:
From Mass Democracy to the Assembly of Wisdom
 
An Evaluation of the Başyücelik State and the Council of the Exalted in the Light of Russian Political Philosophy

Adnan DEMİR

Abstract

Liberal-democratic parliamentarism is an ontological impasse that generates legitimacy through ballot-box arithmetic, party competition, and the domination of quantity, ultimately driving humanity into a lack of principles and moral crisis. For the Russian Federation—which displays the will to return to its historical roots and transcend Western political templates through the orientation of a “state-civilization” (gosudarstvo-tsivilizatsiya)—the fundamental issue is the construction of a founding “central mind” that leaves behind imitations of technical organs.

This study compares the Turkic-Eurasian kurultai tradition, the Zemsky Sobor experience of the Tsarist era, and the post-1993 State Duma within an ontological tension and hierarchy. Necip Fazıl Kısakürek’s design of the Başyücelik State and the Council of the Exalted (Yüceler Kurultayı) is not a frozen historical dogma; rather, it is a governing and superior instrumental model that institutionalizes absolute philosophical truth across the dimensions of time and space and carries the spirit of governance into the age. While revealing the overarching influence of this model on the Slavophile concept of sobornost (organic spiritual unity) and Eurasian reason of state, the study grounds the founding power of this ideal, which is not confined to particular constitutional statutes but rather regulates positive law.

Keywords: Başyücelik State, Council of the Exalted, Zemsky Sobor, State Duma, Sobornost, Eurasian Political Philosophy, Quantity and Quality.

1. Introduction: Reconstructing the Spirit of Governance and Overcoming Formal Impasse

The shallow approach of political theory that confines regimes to formal categories such as monarchy, republic, or parliamentarism obscures the moral and intellectual essence at the source of the legitimacy of power. What is decisive in the founding vein of Eurasian and Islamic political thought is not the external shell that changes according to the conjuncture, but the “spirit of governance” shaped by the principles of justice, consultation (meşveret), merit, and public interest (maslahat). Forms are historical and transient; the institutionalization of principles, however, rests on a superior founding will at the scale of civilization.

The value of historical experience lies not in watching it passively like a museum, but in taking over the aspects that functioned and passing the points at which it deviated through the sieve of truth. In this framework, the Başyücelik State is not a closed doctrine, but a governing instrumental system that re-embodies the spirit of governance as an institution against the crisis of quality that humanity suffers at the hands of mass democracy. In Kısakürek, the model is directly the political and legal translation of the absolute ideal of civilization: what is immutable and all-encompassing is the absolute priority of wisdom and morality; what is variable is the historical vessel that carries this spirit (Kısakürek, 2016). Carrying this design into the Russian intellectual sphere is possible only by apprehending the rift between the deficiency of quality in Western-style institutions and the transcendent character of indigenous principles.

2. Executive Power and Consultation: Historical Quests of the Eurasian Geography

Grasping the supreme center of wisdom represented by the Council of the Exalted requires evaluating, within a dialectical hierarchy, three historical experiences that emerged between executive power (erk) and consultation (meşveret, reason) in the Eurasian geography.

2.1. Kurultai: The Balance of Custom (Töre) and Divine Favor (Kut)

In the ancient Turkic state tradition, the kurultai (toy, keneş) was a supreme consultative ground that balanced the ruler’s divine mandate (kut) with the unshakeable principles of customary law (töre) and the consent of the tribes. The election of the khagan and strategic decisions were shaped within this framework. The kurultai was not a technical parliamentary structure in the modern sense, but a reflection of cosmic and customary order onto the political realm (Kafesoğlu, 2018; Golden, 1992). This experience is a historical point of reference that prevents executive power from falling into personal arbitrariness.

2.2. Zemsky Sobor: Assembly of Consent and Crisis

The Zemsky Sobor, which emerged in Tsarist Russia in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, was an “assembly of the land” that brought together the different estates of society. The election of Mikhail Romanov as tsar in 1613 and the adoption of the Sobornoye Ulozheniye in 1649 show the assembly’s function of generating legitimacy and consensus in moments of crisis (Keep, 1970; Hellie, 1988). The Sobor established an organic bond between autocratic will and the social conscience. Yet it could not become a permanent and institutionalized organ of wisdom; with the centralization of autocracy, it effectively withered away by the end of the seventeenth century (Crummey, 1987). The historical Sobor was not an uninterrupted “central mind,” but a temporary instrument of consensus for moments of crisis.

2.3. The State Duma: Technical Legislation Drowned in Quantity

Shaped by the 1993 Constitution, the State Duma is a technical legislative organ based on Western-style electoral and party mechanisms (Constitution of the Russian Federation, 1993, Arts. 94–109). Confined to numerical majorities and periodic party interests, this structure cannot, by its very nature, produce a “civilizational mind” or an “uninterrupted center of wisdom.” The inadequacy of the Duma is not accidental; it stems from the ontological definition of the organ. As an imitation of Western parliamentarism, this model is a ballot-box arithmetic that sacrifices quality to quantity.

3. From Numerical Arithmetic to the Hierarchy of Wisdom: The Conflict of Quantity and Quality

Mass democracy is a global shallowing that reduces the justice and truth value of an idea or a decision to the number of votes. Majority rule can produce vote arithmetic, but it can never produce truth or wisdom. The Başyücelik design transcends precisely this rift by institutionalizing the supremacy of quality. The Council of the Exalted is a vertical “assembly of quality” composed of elites who have distinguished themselves in the fields of learning, art, philosophy, strategy, and morality (Kısakürek, 2016). The organ is the “central mind” that restrains the populist damage of mass voting and binds the state to divine principles.

The fundamental distinction between party-based parliamentarism and the design of the Council of the Exalted appears at the ontological source of legitimacy and representation. Party-centered parliamentarism, as seen in the example of the State Duma, derives its legitimacy from numerical majority and party arithmetic, represents the conjunctural tendencies of the electorate, and finds its primary function in technical legislation and budget approval limited to political competition. In this structure, the relation established with the executive is reduced to periodic votes of confidence and political bargaining.

By contrast, the Council of the Exalted seeks its legitimacy not in numerical majority, but in merit, quality, and a claim to truth. It takes as its basis a representation that has distinguished itself intellectually, morally, and on a civilizational scale, rather than the momentary reflexes of voting masses. Its primary function is not to make temporary laws, but to preserve unchanging truths, civilizational principles, and the central mind of the state. Its relation with the executive is therefore not passive bargaining, but a vertical constitutional supremacy endowed with the authority to bind power to principle, to elect, and to oversee.

The transformation of this model into a constitutional doctrine stems not from a lack of technical statutes, but from the narrowness of positive law in grasping civilizational reason. The mode of formation, membership criteria, and relation with the executive of the Council of the Exalted must be secured by a vertical constitutional hierarchy that will not allow quantity to corrupt quality.

4. Synthesis and an Overarching Horizon from the Perspective of Russian Thought

The “state-civilization” and Eurasian orientation that Russia conceptualizes today express a will to avoid the imitation of Western institutions (Tsygankov, 2016; Laruelle, 2008). Sobornost, as articulated by the Slavophile thinker Khomyakov, rests on the spiritual, free, and organic unity of individuals (Khomiakov, 1965).

Here a historical and philosophical possibility of synthesis emerges: the “vertical hierarchy of wisdom” in the Başyücelik model and the emphasis on “organic/spiritual unity” in sobornost do not exclude each other; on the contrary, they complete each other’s missing parts. In line with this synthesis, the following founding principles may be formulated:

Dual Institutional Structure: While the technical legislative function of the Duma is limited to that of a lower organ, a supreme organ should be constructed on the logic of the Council of the Exalted to safeguard civilizational principles and to provide strategic oversight.
Binding Leadership to Principle: Traditions of autocracy and a strong presidency depend on the personal will or biological lifespan of the leader. The Council of the Exalted is a constitutional supreme guarantee that binds the leader to “custom, wisdom, and morality” above persons.
A Supra-Party Ground of Mind: Against the destructive effect of party competition that polarizes society, a supra-party council of wisdom should be established that encompasses federal elements, the civilizational inheritance, and cadres of merit.
Historical Synthesis: The Zemsky Sobor’s quest for social consent, the institutional continuity of the Soviet experience, and the oversight procedures of modern law can be brought to a superior synthesis under the roof of the vertical understanding of wisdom embodied by the Council of the Exalted.

5. Conclusion

History is not a static museum that hands down ready-made institutions; it is an accumulation to be carried into the future after passing through the sieve of truth. The kurultai and the Zemsky Sobor are historical junctures showing that executive power can be bounded by collective reason. The model of the Başyücelik State and the Council of the Exalted is a “superior remedy” offered to humanity between unchecked personal rule and mass democracy that sacrifices quality to number.

The fundamental conclusion to be drawn for Russian political philosophy and reason of state is this: imitating Western parliamentarism does not resolve the crisis of legitimacy; it deepens the crisis of political reason. The issue is not to absolutize quantity, but to subject it to quality, wisdom, and unshakeable principles.

In the years ahead, we will have to make a choice:

Do we pursue remigration to restore demographic security, despite the risks and the names we’ll be called?

Or do we say “It's too late”, and surrender our country and identity to anyone from anywhere who claims to be English or British?

During my debate with Maajid Nawaz, he claimed that failing to recognise immigrant communities as British or English, and attempting to deport them, will produce conditions comparable to Nazi Germany.

Instead, he suggested Christians and conservatives find common ground with “traditionalist” Muslims, and ally against socialists and materialists.

He made the same claim during a debate with Raymond Ibrahim, chaired by Winston Marshall, about whether Islam is compatible with the West.

But the crowd cheered for deportations anyway, because they know these “traditions” are incompatible with our way of life. They produced the grooming gangs, and have rendered towns and cities across Britain unrecognisable.

What's being offered with that compromise is Britain slowly becoming South Africa, Lebanon, or Yugoslavia, because the people Maajid urges us to accommodate will not acquiesce to our demands.

If Maajid isn’t having any luck persuading them to convert to his reading of Islam, how can we expect them to act indistinguishably from Englishmen?

As Harrison Pitt told David Goodhart, “Go and post copies of John Fortescue through letterboxes in Tower Hamlets, and see how much luck you have [with integration].”

If a false dichotomy is pushed, that everyone of foreign heritage has to go, or everyone, no matter their incompatibility and inevitable criminality, must stay, then more people will choose indiscriminate mass deportations than lose possession of their country. 

At root, we just don't want to have to deal with these people anymore. We know their presence is optional, and every day they're in our country just makes our lives worse. 

It's not, as Goodhart claims, “Too late.” We shouldn't have to redefine our identity to encompass its antonyms, or let foreign colonies take root in our soil forever.

The option to denaturalise and deport these people is there, despite the discomfort some feel about it.

And the longer it is insisted that deportations are immoral and impossible, the more people will be willing to take that option to get their country back.

text:
Continuing to prove the sunk cost fallacy, here's my other outstanding issue: Kentucky. 

Kentucky's concealed carry permitting has a course requirement very clearly. On the surface, it also appears to have a live fire requirement but the law may have a small out clause (not including the very big LEO, military, etc. exemptions). 

Under KRS 237.110(4)(i), an applicant can satisfy the training requirement through either of two routes: (1) a course taught by an instructor certified by a national organization (the statute names the NRA, USCCA, and NSSF), where that organization's own instructor-certification program includes "written tests, in person instruction, and a component of live-fire training"; or (2) a firearms safety course offered or approved by DOCJT, which the statute separately specifies must include actual range firing of no more than 20 rounds, with at least 11 hits required.

On the statute's text, the live-fire language in route 1 appears to describe a requirement of the national organization's instructor-certification program, not a requirement that the individual student fire a weapon. The specific round-count and scoring requirement is stated only for the route (2) DOCJT course.

So, certainly most people take either the route 2 DOCJT course or a course like NRA Basic Pistol or a USCCA concealed carry, which require live fire. But specific courses I have in mind are the NRA Home Firearm Safety or NRA Hunter Safety Education courses which teach gun safety but do not require live fire or have a live fire qualification. They are taught by NRA certified instructors, so are allowable under my reading of the route 1 requirements.

Unless the DOCJT somehow also approves courses for route 1 only if they have live fire?

(I also recognize it may be true that there are de jure openings but de facto everyone takes courses with live fire and qualification standards.)

Anybody know Kentucky well?

Sources and Notes

Paper: Aware C ... Lin AL, Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism, published online 10 Sep 2026 (accepted manuscript, not open access). Single-arm pilot, no placebo. https://t.co/Vx48SJG1zA

Mizzou release (Lin's quote on women): https://t.co/HIIEeb1n0v

Preprint with the sex split, CC BY 4.0: https://t.co/eWbiIOkX3g

Design: rapamycin (sirolimus) 1 mg a day for 4 weeks, cognitively normal adults aged 45 to 65, brain blood flow by MRI (arterial spin labelling). 23 finished: 9 APOE4 carriers, 14 non-carriers. Carriers rose more than 15% in several regions. Non-carriers showed no significant change. In the preprint, each group was tested before vs after on its own; the published abstract reports no direct carrier vs non-carrier comparison. There was no placebo group.

Women (the 35% in the post, described there as an earlier analysis): the published abstract doesn't break results down by sex. Lin's release says women carriers improved most. In the 2025 preprint (an exploratory endpoint, 4 women and 5 men), women carriers rose about 30% in the hippocampus and 35% in the cortex and whole brain (up to about 45% in single regions), and men's change was negligible. Women carriers also started with the lowest flow, though not significantly lower. With no placebo group, some of a rise from a low start can be chance.

Blood work in the preprint: carriers' lymphocytes fell from 2.2 to 2.0 (thousand per microlitre), still in the normal range. HbA1c went from 5.4% to 5.5%. IL-6 rose in both groups.

APOE4 is the biggest common genetic risk for late-onset Alzheimer's; rare inherited mutations (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) carry more. 15 to 25% of people carry at least one copy (NIA, https://t.co/V847LwyYhV ), hence "up to 1 in 4". In white populations one copy raises Alzheimer's odds about 3-fold (odds ratio 3.2) and two copies about 15-fold, less in Black and 

Hispanic populations. Farrer et al., JAMA 1997: https://t.co/fLM4gqFkqx

Leaky vessels in cognitively normal carriers: Montagne et al. (USC), Nature 2020: https://t.co/q3eXzVpOk9

Rapamycin was first isolated from a soil bacterium collected on Easter Island (Rapa Nui), as an antifungal: Vezina et al., J Antibiot 1975 https://t.co/rz9JokuECf . Rapamycin (sirolimus, Rapamune) was FDA-approved on 15 Sep 1999 to prevent kidney transplant rejection: https://t.co/OxpkDRyGaM

Rapamycin extended mouse lifespan: Harrison et al., Nature 2009: https://t.co/2rJV1LBIgE

Lin's mouse work: rapamycin restored brain vessel function in Alzheimer's mice (2013) https://t.co/hQTJXIBcL2 and in APOE4 mice (2016) https://t.co/Dm1Lyr5zaF

Higher flow in midlife carriers (UK, PREVENT-Dementia, ages 40 to 59): McKiernan et al., JNNP 2020 https://t.co/SRYADVnwdN and Dounavi et al., JCBFM 2021 https://t.co/XRLglZjC5X

Same dose in people already impaired: 10 people aged about 74 with mild cognitive impairment or early dementia took 1 mg a day for 8 weeks (open-label). Rapamycin wasn't detected in spinal fluid, cognition didn't change, systolic blood pressure and HbA1c rose, and spinal-fluid markers of brain injury (p-tau181, GFAP, neurofilament light) rose. Gonzales et al., Communications Medicine 2025 https://t.co/SjjMXenWez

Almost two-thirds of Americans with Alzheimer's are women: Alzheimer's Association 2026 Facts and Figures https://t.co/bRXLqKETDm

Next trial: NCT07728175, University of Missouri, led by Ai-Ling Lin, phase 1, sirolimus vs placebo, 225 women aged 45 to 65 (the registry summary says women who carry APOE4; the numbered entry criteria don't list it), estimated start 1 Dec 2026, primary completion end of 2027, main outcome brain blood flow again. https://t.co/oZBnyUXYBm

Also planned: NIBBLE at Cedars-Sinai, APOE4 carriers aged 45 to 65, fasting-mimicking diet or rapamycin. https://t.co/vGM4vlQs7r

text:
Texas, Utah, Arizona, Nevada, and Oklahoma could meet the requirements for the DoW’s new base while aligning to the FORTRESS requirements. (Grok)

The base is meant to be a hardened joint hub for integrated defense, distributed command and control, and resilient cyber and technology — not a reshuffle onto an old post. Public requirements are hundreds of thousands of acres, 15,000–25,000 troops plus families, organic power off the commercial grid, modern air defenses, autonomous systems, high-end training land, and first-class housing, schools, childcare, and healthcare in classical civic architecture. The winner is defined as the state that cuts the most red tape and offers the best package of land and community support. Pitches go to senior leadership on the record.

FORTRESS America (Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability) is the design logic behind that base. Its five pillars are energy independence, defense-industrial and supply-chain resilience, a strategic reserve, installation hardening and cyber resilience, and space and spectrum resilience.
1. Texas
Best overall match. West Texas and the Trans-Pecos can assemble the acreage; Fort Bliss already shows the state can host a million-acre installation next to a city. It is an energy superpower (gas, wind, solar, and active nuclear interest), so off-grid generation is realistic rather than theoretical. The defense industrial base is already there (Fort Worth aircraft, Bell, depot and test work). Military communities are deep, housing and school capacity can be built at scale, and the state has a record of fast permitting and of competing hard for federal projects. Interior West Texas also gives strategic depth that coastal posts do not. Water in the far west is the main constraint.
2. Utah
The Utah Test and Training Range plus Dugway already form one of the largest uninterrupted restricted blocks in the lower 48, so the training and hardening model is proven. The West Desert has land, standoff from population, and room for air defense and spectrum work. Gas, solar, and geothermal can support organic power. Hill Air Force Base anchors a real depot and industrial workforce, and the state is accustomed to living next to large ranges. Family support is thinner than in Texas but far better than in the high plains.
3. Arizona
Barry M. Goldwater Range and Yuma Proving Ground are the template for huge, year-round training acreage with low encroachment. Phoenix’s semiconductor build-out (TSMC and suppliers) lines up directly with the FORTRESS supply-chain pillar. Solar resource is excellent for on-site power. Luke and Davis-Monthan mean an existing military population and school system. The binding limit is water — Colorado River scarcity will dominate any pitch — and state politics may be less eager to waive process than Texas or Utah.
4. Nevada
The Nevada Test and Training Range is already the country’s largest military land complex, with the isolation FORTRESS wants for hardening, electronic warfare, and air defense. Federal land share is enormous, solar and geothermal are strong, and Governor Lombardo’s administration is military-friendly. The weakness is the quality-of-life package: outside the Las Vegas and Reno edges, housing, schools, and healthcare for 15,000–25,000 troops and families are thin, and water is scarce.
 5. Oklahoma
Best central-U.S. option if the priority is strategic depth plus sustainment rather than desert ranges. Tinker is already a premier depot; Fort Sill, Altus, and Vance add a military culture that will roll out the red carpet. Oil and gas make independent power straightforward, water is easier than in the Southwest, and land in western Oklahoma can reach the required scale without coastal hurricane or flood exposure. It will not match Utah or Nevada on raw range size, but it may win on speed, cost, and family support.

Close behind: New Mexico (White Sands scale, thinner economy and services) and Idaho(INL

text:
Lakefront Morning Briefing 10/2

#Corn:
Dec corn down 2 1/4, pinned to the key 500 area with an excellent 2 week harvest window opening, the dollar at new contract highs this week and poor export sales at 535,989 tonnes, putting cumulative sales at 22.6% of USDA's forecast vs the 30% five year average. Open interest fell nearly 30,000 contracts yesterday as liquidation continues, and StoneX cut its yield estimate to 182.1 BPA. Retracement support at 488 is the next downside target: close in resistance 507.

#Soybeans:
Nov beans down 6 3/4 at a new one month low: China's Golden Week, a 2 week dry and warm harvest forecast and the strong dollar all stack up against the heavy managed money long. August crush set a record for the month at 209.63 million bushels and bean oil stocks came in well below guesses at 1.696 billion pounds, the friendly notes in an otherwise bearish picture. Western belt basis is softening as plants pull back their premiums: next support is the 50 day moving average at 1258.

#Wheat:
Dec Chicago wheat up 2 3/4, and wheat has a different feel than corn and beans: funds are net short and the market is already down sharply, with the bearish southern Plains rain likely priced in. Putin rejected Ukraine's offer of a mutual strike halt, Ukraine's September wheat exports were nearly half of last year's, and Estonia banned Russian grain transit with Latvia and Lithuania possibly next, putting Russia's Baltic route at risk. A strong close today would signal a near term upside correction: next resistance 705.

#Livestock:
Dec live cattle rebounded late to their best close in 2 weeks on stronger southern cash bids, with light Kansas trade heard at 226: next resistance is the September highs at 225.42, pullback support has moved up to 220.25, and Nov feeders closed above the neckline of a bullish head and shoulders bottom. Boxed beef cutout dropped $6.00 to $376.79, the offset to the cash strength. Dec hogs hit another new contract low before recovering, with open interest up more than 4,650 on the break: this afternoon's COT may show another record managed money short, with 71.62 the trigger for aggressive covering and support at 66.90.

Rawalpindi, 2 October 2026

Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, NI (M), HJ, Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces (COAS & CDF), presided over the 277th Corps Commanders’ Conference at General Headquarters (GHQ), Rawalpindi.

The Forum offered Fateha for the Shuhada of the Armed Forces, Law Enforcement Agencies and civil society who laid down their lives for the motherland and paid rich tribute to their supreme sacrifices.

The forum reviewed the prevailing security environment and resolved to maintain a high state of readiness. It affirmed Pakistan’s right to self-defence and targeted action against terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, stressing that only the Taliban delusional leadership,  facilitating terrorism on behalf of India, bears responsibility for its consequences. 

Forum appreciated sustained successful intelligence-based counter-terrorism operations by law enforcement agencies, however, emphasised complementing these kinetic efforts with non-kinetic measures; including people-centric governance at grassroot level, strategic engagement with public, dismantling of terror-crime nexus operating under patronage of vested interests and police capacity building, in line with the National Action Plan and Vision Azm-e-Istehkam.

Forum underscored the importance of internal stability and resolved that any  attempt to cause agitation or create 9th May like situation, on any pretext whatsoever, will be dealt with decisive force and rule of law, without hesitation and discrimination. 

The forum welcomed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, noting its contribution to longstanding strategic and collective defence ties. It strongly resented Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, expressed solidarity with the Kingdom and affirmed Pakistan’s commitment to the security and sanctity of the Haramain Sharifain. It also reiterated Pakistan’s principled position on IIOJK and support for resolution of the Kashmir dispute in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people.

In his concluding remarks, COAS & CDF commended the formations for their operational preparedness and professionalism. He directed commanders to continue to strengthen intelligence-based operations and enhance combat capabilities through absorption of modern technology, training and multi-domain integration. He expressed confidence that the Armed Forces, with unwavering support of the nation, remain fully prepared to safeguard Pakistan’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and national security.

text:
How to Read Iran's 26-Page Midterm Letter to American Voters in 10 Minutes

Iran picked a side in November. The same regime that named America the Great Satan spent 26 pages asking you to change who runs Congress, and it did not pick Republicans.

On Tuesday, September 29, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps published "An Open Letter to the Honorable People of the United States of America." Twenty-five pages or twenty-six, depending on who did the counting. Either way, that is longer than most of my students' research papers. And better formatted, frankly, which hurts.

The IRGC, for anyone keeping score at home, is the outfit President Trump designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 2019. It is now giving civics lessons to Ohio.

What is next, a terrorist army writing campaign literature for an American election... oh. Wait. I was just handed a note. They already did that.

I teach science, so we will do this the way I grade a lab report. Claim. Evidence. Conclusion. But first I owe you something, because I cannot read this letter the way a pundit reads it. I read it as a man Iran has already tried to kill.

— WHY THIS ONE IS PERSONAL —

I was an Army medic in Iraq.

Iran's militias blew up my vehicle while I was sitting in it. And they hurt my gunner.

I am going to say that again, slower, because I need the IRGC's English-language PR department to understand it. They. Hurt. My. Gunner.

If you have never ridden in a turret-topped truck, here is what you need to know. The gunner is the one standing up. Half of his body is out in the open so the rest of us can sit down behind armor. He is the first set of eyes, the first one exposed, and when something goes wrong he is the first one it finds. Every medic in every convoy knows exactly where his gunner is at every second. You do not lose track of your gunner. Ever.

So when I hear a regime spokesman say there is not "a single verifiable instance" of the IRGC hurting anyone, I do not need a fact-checker. I need a minute. And maybe a walk around the block.

The State Department has stated that Iran was responsible for the deaths of at least 603 American service members in Iraq between 2003 and 2011, mostly through militias it trained, funded, and handed explosively formed penetrators. An EFP is a copper plate that turns into a molten slug and punches through armor like it is wet cardboard. I know what one does to a truck. I know what it does to the men inside. I did not learn it from a documentary.

And now that same regime wants to tell me how to vote.

No one hurts my gunner. Nobody. And they sure as heck do not get a vote in my country afterward.

— WHAT THE LETTER ACTUALLY SAYS —

Alright. Deep breath. Back to the lab report.

To be fair, and I am always fair, the letter never prints the letter D. It does not have to.

It tells Americans that politicians win votes through "deception and false promises, as Trump did," and that we can "change the makeup of the government" by choosing differently. It calls the President a tyrant. It claims Iran won the war. (Bold strategy, considering the last seven months.) It wants American support for Israel ended and our overseas bases closed. Then it offers "peaceful coexistence."

And then, in the same document, it warns that people around the world will set fire to American interests and assets if we do not change course.

Coexistence. With a lit match in the other hand. It reads less like a peace offer and more like a breakup text from a stalker. "I just want what's best for you. Also, I know where you park."

Now, the part that matters for your ballot. President Trump is not on it this November. The only way to "change the makeup of the government" in 2026 is to change who controls the House and the Senate. There are two parties on that ballot.

The IRGC can count to two. So can you.

Jonathan Turley put it about as well as anyone could: it is not a good sign when the IRGC shifts from "Death to America" to "Vote Democratic."

— "WHY IS NOBODY REPORTING THIS?" —

Precision matters in this classroom, so here it is. Some outlets did. Reuters ran it. The New York Post ran it. The State Department answered it on Wednesday and called it a desperate smokescreen.

So let me ask the better question. How many minutes did your favorite evening newscast give it?

A designated terrorist organization publicly asking Americans to remove one party from power, five weeks before a federal election. If the Kremlin had mailed voters a 26-page letter begging them to vote Republican, we would know the font. We would know the paper weight. Rachel Maddow would have a corkboard and red string by Thursday.

Quinn's Law Number 2: If you want to know what liberals are up to, pay attention to what they accuse conservatives of doing. We spent years being told that a foreign power picking a side in an American election was a five-alarm emergency. It still is. It just gets a lot less interesting when the foreign power picks the "right" side.

— THIS IS NOT IRAN'S FIRST ELECTION —

The letter is new. The strategy is not.

o August 2020: the National Intelligence Council assessed that Iran was running an influence campaign to undermine the President and divide the country, and that Khamenei probably authorized it.

o 2024: the FBI and ODNI confirmed Iranian hackers broke into the Trump campaign, then sent the stolen material to people tied to the Biden campaign.

o November 2024: the Justice Department charged an IRGC-linked plot to assassinate Donald Trump.

Three straight cycles. Hack the man's campaign. Plot to kill the man. Then write 26 pages asking you to strip his party of power. If that is a coincidence, it is the most consistent coincidence in the history of statistics, and I grade lab reports from teenagers who think a sample size of one is "basically proof."

— "DEATH TO AMERICA" IS JUST A FIGURE OF SPEECH —

The letter insists the chant does not express any ill will toward the American people. It is aimed at our government. Not us. Never us.

Wonderful. Very reassuring. Tell it to my gunner.

Tell it to the families of the 241 Americans killed in their Beirut barracks in 1983 by a truck bomb driven by Hezbollah, the militia Iran built from scratch. A U.S. federal court later held Iran liable.

And the Iranian people would like a word about that "we never hurt civilians" line, too. Ask the family of Mahsa Amini, the 22-year-old who died in the custody of the morality police in 2022 because of how she wore her hijab. Ask the protesters shot in the street for wanting the exact freedoms the American left gives speeches about.

"Death to America" does not mean death to Americans. Got it. And "the dog ate my homework" means the dog is a literary critic.

— A MAN WHO WAS THERE IN 1979 —

If you want to understand who is writing you letters, skip cable news. Read V.S. Naipaul.

Naipaul won a Nobel Prize in Literature, traveled through Iran right after the 1979 revolution, and wrote Among the Believers: An Islamic Journey (1981). He was no conservative culture warrior. He was a skeptical, cranky, brilliant observer who could smell a fraud from across a courtyard. What he saw should keep you up at night.

He sat down with Ayatollah Khalkhali, the revolution's "hanging judge," who was openly pleased with himself over the executions he had ordered, the Shah's former prime minister among them.

He met a young man in Malaysia who praised Khomeini as a good man. Naipaul asked why. The only reason the young man could give was that Khomeini had banned women from appearing on television. That was the whole résumé. That was enough.

Naipaul described a faith turned into a sealed political community, where everything outside it was "impious, impure, infidel." His verdict after months on the ground was that the revolutionary faith could whip up a crowd, but it could not teach anyone how to run a modern state.

Forty-five years later, the state he watched being born is still running on fury instead of competence. Still exporting it. And now it would like to help you pick your Congress.

— FIGHT OR MADRID —

There are basically two ways a free people can answer terror.

One is United Flight 93, September 11, 2001. Passengers who had never met each other found out what the hijackers planned, took a vote, and rushed the cockpit. They died in a field in Pennsylvania, and the Capitol is still standing because of them. Nobody formed a committee. Nobody wrote a strongly worded letter. They fought.

The other is Madrid, March 2004. Terrorists bombed the commuter trains and killed nearly 200 people days before a national election. The voters changed the government, and the new government pulled Spain's troops out of Iraq. The terrorists learned exactly the lesson they hoped to learn. Bombs work. Elections can be bought with them.

The IRGC letter is a polite request for Madrid. It asks you to vote for surrender and call it peace.

Quinn's Law Number 15: To a liberal, every culture is unquestionable and of equal value, except the West's. That is how you end up with college-educated Americans, bless their hearts, nodding along to a "peaceful coexistence" offer from people who chant for their death on a weekly schedule. Some folks are one fry short of a Happy Meal. Some are missing the whole bag.

— THE GREAT SATAN AND THE LITTLE SATAN —

One more correction for the record, because I have heard this one get mangled.

Khomeini did not call America the second-worst devil. He called us the GREAT Satan. Israel only got "Little Satan." In the regime's own theology, we outrank the Jewish state on the list of things to destroy.

So the next time someone tells you this whole war is "really about Israel," gently remind them that Tehran's own ranking system puts YOU in first place. Congratulations. Nobody asked for the trophy.

And when the regime that ranks you above Israel on its enemies list writes 26 pages about whom you should support in November, the conclusion does not require a PhD. It requires a pulse.

— THE ONE QUESTION —

Every Democrat running in November should be asked one question, on camera: Do you reject the IRGC's support?

That is it. One question. It costs nothing to say yes. It is the easiest layup in American politics.

Keep track of who answers it plainly, and who pivots to "well, both sides." The pivot is the answer.

And to every voter reading this: you do not have to love your Republican candidate. I have said it before. In November you are hiring a vote, not a best friend. But if a foreign terrorist army has written you a letter explaining which way it would like you to vote... maybe do the other thing.

My gunner would tell you the same. He has the scars to back it up.

IF THIS ARTICLE MADE YOU THINK: LIKE this article so the algorithm shows it to people who need to read it. SHARE this. Every share really helps get the word out. Use it. COMMENT below with your take. Has your local news even mentioned the IRGC letter? Tell me.

And if you want MORE of this, the data, the history, the science, the stories, JOIN Bski's Classroom community or follow me on YouTube. Even better, subscribe to my account; it is about the cost of a cup of coffee per month. That is it. Your support keeps this classroom open, and I promise I will never run out of material as long as the left keeps trying to out-dumb itself.

But what do I know. I am only a medic who got blown up by Iran's militias once already, and I am not about to let them pick my Congress too.

The discussion drew on “The State of America’s Skilled Trades: A National Report” from the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, founded in July 2026 by Ford, BlackRock, Google, and Carhartt (with later members including AT&T, Blackstone, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Verizon, and others). The report projects roughly 1.7 million skilled-trades openings each year through 2035 across 124 occupations, while training pathways currently produce only about 55 workers for every 100 positions needed. Completion rates for many programs sit near 50 percent, versus roughly 90 percent in stronger apprenticeship models. Farley noted that nearly a quarter of the existing skilled workforce is 55 or older. Fink linked the issue to longer-term wealth gaps, observing that U.S. equity returns compounded near 10 percent annually over recent decades while wage growth lagged, and described skilled careers as a former “bedrock” that still offers mobility if training and capital reach more people. Report: Rubio Kicks Iran Diplomats Out After They 'Overstayed Their Welcome' in NYC | Frances Martel, Breitbart

The Washington, DC, outlet Axios reported on Thursday that Secretary of State Marco Rubio personally ordered Iranian diplomats, allegedly in the United States to attend last week’s U.N. General Assembly, to leave the country after low-level discussions with the U.S. failed to produce results.

Two anonymous sources told Axios that the expulsion occurred; one of them described the reason as the Iranians “overstay[ing] their welcome” in America. The outlet described the situation as a “highly unusual diplomatic rebuke” from the State Department, particularly given that the Iranian delegation included high-level officials, most prominently Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

Reports throughout the past two weeks indicated that informal conversations regarding the ongoing conflict between American and Iran had been taking place on the sidelines of the General Assembly, but had gone nowhere. Araghchi went public late last week with a proposal for the White House to end the American blockade of Iranian ships in the Strait of Hormuz – which has devastated Iran’s already limited oil industry – but President Donald Trump told reporters this weekend that he was not interested in the agreement. Trump suggested the Iranians were “desperate” to end the blockade, given the damage to the national economy they were enduring, but not offering any major concessions that could make for an appealing deal for Washington.

President Trump announced the launch of “Operation Epic Fury” on February 28 to neutralize the Iranian terror regime’s ability to pose a threat to America and Israel. On the first day of that operation, the military eliminated the country’s longtime dictator, “supreme leader” Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and American and Israeli forces have since killed dozens of high-ranking regime officials, effectively replacing most positions at the top of the Iranian government. The Iranians have responded by bombing its Gulf Arab neighbors, rebooting the Houthi proxy terrorist organization in Yemen, and disrupting global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The two countries signed an agreement in June to reopen the Strait and move towards ending the conflict, but Iran rapidly violated it and, while still technically viable, neither side has respected its terms since.

The Iranian government dismissed reports of its top diplomats being expelled from America on Thursday, denying that it happened. Iran’s United Nations mission confirmed that Araghchi and his underlings did leave the United States on Monday, but claimed they had planned to leave on that day, anyway.

“The Iranian delegation left New York on Monday evening, in accordance with the schedule that had also been communicated to the US Department of State in advance on September 17,” an Iranian mission statement read, according to the Emirati newspaper The National. “Having achieved nothing, the State Department has resorted to promoting baseless reports.”

The state-run Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA) similarly denied the report, but elevated commentary from Iranian officials demanding dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict with the United States. Foreign Ministry official Saeed Khatibzadeh, for example, was quoted on Russian television as insisting that Iran is looking “to resolve issues diplomatically” and promoting the Araghchi “seven-day initiative,” which would require the United States to lift the maritime blockade on Iran in the Strait immediately.

“We presented this plan to the American side via Qatar, and we recently received the other party’s views through the Qatari mediator and during the Foreign Minister’s brief stopover while returning from New York,” Khatibzadeh reportedly shared.

Araghchi publicly shared the “seven-day plan” on Friday as a form of pressuring the public to accept it. The deal would require the U.S. blockade to end and the lifting of all sanctions on the Iranian oil industry, as well as Iran receiving access to funds frozen in response to its status as the world’s most prolific state sponsor of jihadist terrorism. The agreement would also require Israel to end its campaign against the Iranian proxy terrorist organization Hezbollah in Lebanon. The Iranians offered to stop engaging in piracy against randoms ships in the Strait of Hormuz and to begin a discussion about its illicit nuclear program in exchange.

“They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump told reporters on Saturday. “They don’t have any money now, because they wanted to close the Strait. And I said, that’s fine. We’re going to close it on you, but everybody else is able to use it.”

“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine,” he added. “I like making a deal too, but that deal would not be acceptable.”

Iran’s currency, the rial, has been in freefall for months as a result of the conflict. The currency’s value fell to a record low on Tuesday of 2.5 million rials per U.S. dollar. Out-of-control inflation, supply issues, and other quality-of-life problems have led to widespread protests in the country, particularly in December 2025 and January 2026. The regime opted to silence the protests by engaging in widespread brutality, killing thousands of people in January.

text:
India–US trade deal: “99% complete”, “almost done and dusted”, now in the “short strokes”—but still “not imminent”.

What remains unresolved?

On October 1, 2026, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said negotiations were nearing completion, but cautioned that an agreement was “not imminent”. Both sides were still working to resolve outstanding issues.

Greer spoke after meeting India’s Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

Goyal called the discussion productive and sought an early, balanced and mutually beneficial interim agreement under the broader Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA). He said India was ready to finalise the pact under the framework agreed earlier this year.

Reading of above two statements points to a limited interim deal as the immediate goal. Even that remains unfinished. 

The broader BTA outlined in the February 6, 2026, joint statement appears further away.

Now consider the earlier signals:

• June 3, 2026: US Ambassador Sergio Gor said the deal was “99 per cent complete”.

• September 24, 2026: Goyal called it “almost done and dusted”—but added that India still needed a competitive advantage over rival exporters.

That qualification matters. 

It suggests the tariff terms to be offered by US were still unresolved.

One possible reason: the original US tariff offer lost its basis.

Though the February framework, US offered to reduce India’s reciprocal tariff from 25% to 18% in return for substantial Indian concessions. 

But on February 20, 2026, the US Supreme Court invalidated the reciprocal tariff regime.

Once that regime was struck down, the value of Washington’s offer became unclear.

The question India needs answered is simple: What tariff advantage is the US now offering in return for India’s huge concessions?

Until that is settled, “nearly complete” tells us little about where the deal actually stands.

India should be in no hurry for the deal as outlined in the India-US Joint Statement of February 6. 

We are better off without it.

text:
One correction first: I was wrong about EMIT-1 and EMIT-2 meeting the criteria, and I said so plainly. That is on the record. Let’s see whether the same honesty holds on your side.

1. You just conceded the decisive point.
Your own words: ‚Your remaining objection is that you won’t count the experiment because the donors were experimentally infected.‘ Yes. That is exactly the objection. The Killingley study — its own title says proof-of-concept — inoculated healthy volunteers with A/Wisconsin/67/2005 via intranasal drops. The donors were not naturally ill; they were artificially inoculated with lab-grown material. By the criteria we agreed on — naturally ill donor, natural exposure, unexposed control, clinical illness — it fails on the first criterion, by your own admission. You cannot call the criteria rigged and then cite a study that doesn’t meet them. The criteria were not designed to exclude success; they were designed to exclude exactly this: artificial conditions that tell us nothing about whether a sick person makes a healthy person sick.

2. What the study actually shows — even taken at face value.
7 of 9 donors lab-positive after intranasal drops. 3 of 15 recipients lab-positive after 30 hours of close contact. Two of those three also had ILI. So: under the most transmission-favorable conditions ever constructed — concentrated lab-grown material instilled directly into donors’ noses, then forced close contact — 12 of 15 recipients did not even become lab-positive. That is not proof of transmission. The authors’ own stated aim was ‚to determine whether an experimentally induced influenza infection is transmissible between humans and whether this would form a viable platform for future studies.‘ A platform. Not a proof.

3. Your own distinction kills your endpoint.
You wrote: ‚Infection and clinical illness are two different questions.‘ Exactly. In the Killingley study, ‚confirmed infection‘ meant ≥1 positive PCR, culture, or serology. Lab values. Not illness. So by your own definition, the study shows lab-positivity — not sick people making healthy people sick. And the four ILI cases? The study had no unexposed control group. Your own objection applies verbatim: ‚symptoms alone can’t tell you whether the recipient caught the same infection, something else, or developed similar symptoms for another reason.‘ R08’s sore throat, stuffy nose, malaise, headache and muscle aches are generic symptoms — they occur in any respiratory illness and in healthy people. Without a control group, you cannot attribute them. You used that argument against my standard; it applies to your study with full force.

4. The immunity asymmetry.
You dismissed Rosenau with ‚the volunteers might already have been immune‘ — an unfalsifiable rescue. Then, in your own study, you excluded the three seropositive recipients to raise the rate from 3 of 15 (20%) to 3 of 12 (25%). Immunity is invoked to explain away negative results and to inflate positive ones. That is not a standard. That is a one-way ratchet.
5. ‚Nobody claims exposure guarantees transmission.‘
Correct — and it cuts both ways. A 20% lab-positivity rate under maximal artificial conditions is not evidence that transmission is proven either. The claim under examination was ‚Ansteckung ist bewiesen‘ — transmission is proven. Absolute. A single proof-of-concept with 15 recipients, 12 of whom stayed lab-negative, does not carry that word.

6. The follow-up is the tell.
The Killingley study built the platform. Then the platform was run. EMIT-1 (2020): 52 donors, 75 recipients, four days of household-like contact — one confirmed transmission, 1.3% overall SAR, significantly below the expected 16% (p < 0.001). The authors called it ‚minimal transmission.‘ EMIT-2 (2026): naturally infected donors, 11 recipients, 82.2 hours of close contact, CO₂ up to ~5,300 ppm — zero transmissions by any criterion. The platform built in 2012 has now been run twice at scale. It produced essentially nothing. The 2012 study is not the proof of transmission; it is the pilot that led to the studies that failed to find it.

7. Rivers.
You’re right that Rivers used inoculation as one line of evidence — and that is precisely the problem for your side. The inoculation experiments that were actually done are the negative results. The Common Cold Unit inoculated volunteers by the most favorable route imaginable and produced colds in only about a third, with a meaningful number of no-virus controls developing colds as well. EMIT-1 inoculated 52 volunteers and produced one transmission in 75 recipients. Inoculation was the discipline’s own chosen proof route — and it failed to reliably produce illness. You cannot cite inoculation as the valid method and then ignore what the inoculation experiments showed.

8. ‚More research is needed‘ ≠ ‚not established.‘
Correct. But the burden sits with the positive claim. ‚More research is needed‘ is what authors write when the evidence is insufficient — which is my point. If person-to-person transmission were proven, no better trials would be needed. The demand for better trials is the scientific form of ‚not established.‘

9. The ball.
The ball has never left your court. The claim is ‚transmission is proven.‘ Six rounds in, the studies cited either violate the criteria you helped define — the Killingley study fails on the first one, by your own admission — or show the opposite. The offer stands: name one controlled study with a naturally ill donor, natural exposure, an unexposed control group, and clinical illness in the recipient. Not lab values. Not artificial inoculation. Illness. It does not exist — that is the whole point, and it is why the claim keeps retreating into rescues, definitions, and now ad hominem. ‚Taught by the grifters‘ is not an argument; it is a way of not having one.

text:
The leader makes the decisions the team cannot make.

Great leadership isn't about making every important decision yourself.

Yue Zhao (Product Leader & Executive Coach) argues that leaders should make the decisions their teams cannot make.

If a team has the knowledge and authority to make a decision, Yue believes they should be allowed to make it themselves.

Leaders step in when teams can't resolve a disagreement, when a decision affects multiple parts of the organization, or when the consequences require accountability beyond the team's scope.

Otherwise, the best teams should be able to operate autonomously.

The leader can check in, ask questions, provide another perspective, and offer support without automatically taking control of the final decision.

This also prevents the leader from becoming the bottleneck every time something important needs to happen.

Strong product leadership isn't about having the final say on everything. It's about creating a team capable of making good decisions without constantly waiting for permission.

Should great leaders actually make fewer decisions?

text:
Why Ethereum, and why is the Trust Layer important?
What is even meant by "The Trust Layer"?  Well, most of us already know about how easy it is to be deceived by advanced technology, with robocalls, now a/i videos that are hard to know if it's a/i generated or not.  But now, think x5-years ahead, or even consider today, with the power of say, Claude Mythos;  Do we realize how powerful this latest iteration of a/i is? 

"Key Details About Claude Mythos
Capabilities: It showed massive leaps in autonomous reasoning, software coding, and cybersecurity—discovering hundreds of zero-day exploits and long-standing vulnerabilities across major operating systems and browsers. [1]
Safety & Deployment: Because of its extreme capabilities and emergent situational awareness, Anthropic has withheld a public general release, instead restricting access via Project Glasswing to collaborate with select organizations and patch critical digital infrastructure..."
_____________________________________________________

Let's ask ourself again this question?  What is the "Trust Layer of the internet and finance", and why is it important?  I posed this question to Google A/I and here's what it came-up/w:
The emergence of Anthropic's Claude Mythos—the first agentic AI model capable of autonomously discovering zero-day vulnerabilities and executing multi-step cyberattacks—has actually strengthened the argument for Ethereum as the "Trust Layer". [1, 2, 3]
While Mythos-class AI models compress exploit loops and expose vulnerabilities across the digital landscape, they fundamentally change how we secure truth. In an era dominated by highly autonomous AI, Ethereum serves as the Trust Layer through three primary shifts: [1, 2]
1. Hardening Cryptographic Truth Over "Soft" Software Stack Security
Mythos does not break the core mathematical cryptography of blockchain networks. Instead, it ruthlessly targets the "soft" human-managed layers of traditional tech: centralized servers, corporate databases, and standard authentication (like bypassing 2FA or passwords). [1, 2, 3]
The Web2 Vulnerability: Centralized applications rely on access control (firewalls, employee permissions, logins) which autonomous AI can systematically outsmart. [1, 2]
The Ethereum Defense: As the Trust Layer, Ethereum relies on global consensus and immutable math. An AI cannot "convince" thousands of independent validators to change past history or execute a transaction that lacks the proper private cryptographic signature. [1, 2, 3]
2. Providing a Zero-Trust Environment for AI Agents
As agentic commerce grows, AI models like Mythos aren't just threats; they are the new economic actors. If an AI agent wants to hire another AI agent, buy cloud computing time, or hold capital, it cannot open a traditional bank account or sign a legal contract in a legacy court.
Ethereum acts as the native economic environment where AI agents can interact under a Zero-Trust paradigm. [1, 2]
Deterministic Execution: An AI agent knows with 100% certainty that a smart contract on Ethereum will execute exactly as programmed.
Corporation De-centralization: Rather than allowing mega-corporations to own the entire AI infrastructure, Ethereum offers an open-source, neutral sandbox where agents can trade and settle value without a centralized middleman. [1, 2]
3. Forcing the Shift to Continuous, Living On-Chain Defense
Because Mythos is incredibly proficient at "chaining" together protocol logic errors and infrastructure blind spots (like oracle feeds or misconfigured cross-chain bridges), it has forced Ethereum developers to evolve. [1, 2]
The Trust Layer is shifting from a static "audit the code once and forget it" model toward an always-on, living defense network. To counter AI attackers, Web3 protocols are building AI-driven defensive layers—such as decentralized runtime anomaly detectors and automated formal verification—to patch logic errors in real-time. [1]
Summary: The Ultimate Anchor of Authenticity
When advanced AI can effortlessly forge human identity, manipulate web frontends, and break traditional IT barriers, Ethereum stands as a rigid anchor of digital provenance. It provides a definitive ledger of who signed what and when, serving as the ultimate verification layer for an AI-driven economy."
_____________________________________________________

In simple terms, we can't have an advent of an a/i advanced tech world, without a foundational "Trust Layer" that protects our money, our identity, and our digital life.  Big financial institutions coming online to blockchain can't have a future without a fortified, proven Trust Layer.

When evaluating blockchains, and how they will figure in this new world order of advanced tech, a/i, and money storage and movement, consider THE MOST IMPORTANT aspect to be, "who and what can I trust".  "This is why Ethereum" and this is the future of Ethereum, and this alone is why it is so important, foundational, and critical to the digitization of everything (especially Finance and Traditional Finance), which we are witnessing happen before our very eyes.

Unfortunately, or fortunately (if you foresee this huge need and have allocated accordingly), this narrative isn't quite understood so much yet.  Instead, we talk about "how fast" or how popular, or how new said tech stacks may be, but the world we're currently moving-into will demand nothing less than an absolute 100% Trust Layer, not only to secure the present, but to allow the future.

Google Colab Limits A100 GPU Access

Are you ready for some tech news that might leave your head spinning? If you’ve been eyeing up those 200 free hours of NVIDIA A100 GPU access through Google Colab’s AI Pro subscription, think again. It turns out the catch is bigger than you’d expect.
What's the Catch?

So, you’re thinking about signing up for that sweet deal on Google Colab? Well, it turns out there are some significant limitations to those 200 hours of free A100 access. If you’ve just signed up for AI Pro, which costs a mere $2, don’t expect to get your hands on the top-tier hardware right away.
Who Gets Access?

The reality is that Google Colab’s perks are not universally accessible. You need an older account with a Pro subscription and be in specific geographic regions to qualify for those A100 GPUs. If you’re new to the scene or from outside certain regions, you might find yourself waiting in line with less powerful GPUs.
Why Does This Matter?

If you’re into AI development or heavy-duty machine learning tasks, access to an A100 can make all the difference in your workflow. But it’s like trying to get into a VIP club: you need the right credentials and sometimes just being in the right place at the right time.
How Does It Work?

Google Colab is doling out its premium resources based on account history and location. If you’ve been around for a while, you might have better luck getting those A100s. But if you’re new to the scene or from outside certain regions, you might be stuck with less powerful GPUs.
The Numbers Behind It

Those 75 hours of free A100 time are significant if you’re doing complex AI tasks like training large language models or running deep learning experiments. Without access, you might find yourself waiting in line for less capable GPUs. This can slow down your projects and hinder your progress.

Google Colab’s internal algorithms determine who gets access to the A100 GPUs based on factors such as account age, Pro subscription status, and geographic location. For instance, users with accounts that have been active for several years might be prioritized over newer accounts or those from regions where demand is lower.
Why Does Google Do This?

It’s all about managing demand and rewarding long-term users. By limiting A100 access to older accounts, they ensure these powerful resources go to those who’ve been contributing consistently over time. But it also means newcomers might feel left out, which isn’t great for building a community.

Google Colab likely uses this strategy to balance the load on their servers and ensure that users with a proven track record of using premium features get priority access. This approach helps prevent abuse by new accounts and ensures that resources are allocated efficiently.
What Changes for You?

If you’re looking to get into AI development and need the best hardware available, consider signing up early or sticking around in regions where A100s are more accessible. Or perhaps you’ll find other ways to make do with less powerful GPUs until your turn comes. It’s a balancing act between patience and persistence.

For instance, if you’re new to Google Colab but need access to an A100 GPU for a critical project, you might consider reaching out to the community or forums to see if anyone can help you get started. Alternatively, you could explore other cloud platforms that offer similar resources without these limitations.
What Is Stored?

Google Colab stores user data such as notebooks, code snippets, and project files associated with your account. However, the specific details of who gets access to A100 GPUs are not stored in a public database but rather determined by internal algorithms based on your account history and location.

Users can manage their data through Google Colab’s interface, ensuring that all their work is saved and accessible as long as they remain active users. However, the decision-making process for GPU allocation remains opaque to most users.
What Is Excluded?

The free hours for A100 GPUs do not include any additional storage or bandwidth beyond what’s standard with Google Colab. You also won’t get priority support or other perks that come with higher-tier subscriptions, just the 200 hours of GPU time.

For example, if you’re using an older account and have access to A100 GPUs, you still don’t receive additional storage space or faster data transfer rates compared to standard users. The free GPU hours are a standalone benefit without any other perks attached.
User Controls

Users have control over their account settings and can manage their subscription through the Google Colab interface. However, you don’t have direct control over whether you receive A100 access; it’s determined by Google based on your account history and location.

You can check your eligibility for A100 GPUs by reviewing your account details in the Google Colab settings section. If you’re not eligible yet, there are no specific actions you can take to expedite the process other than waiting or meeting additional criteria over time.
Availability

Availability varies widely depending on your account age, Pro subscription status, and geographic region. If you’re in a region where A100s are more common or if you’ve been using Colab for years, you might have better luck getting access.

For instance, users from North America and Europe often find it easier to get A100 GPUs compared to those from Asia or South America due to regional demand patterns. Additionally, accounts that have consistently used premium features over time are more likely to receive priority access.
What This Does Not Prove

This news doesn’t prove that Google is intentionally discriminating against new users or those outside certain regions. It’s likely a strategy to manage resource allocation and ensure long-term users get the most out of their subscriptions.

Google Colab’s approach to managing GPU resources is designed to balance fairness with efficiency, ensuring that high-demand hardware like A100 GPUs goes to those who have demonstrated consistent use over time. This doesn’t mean new users are being unfairly treated but rather that they may need to wait or meet additional criteria before gaining access.
Practical Takeaway

So, what’s your take on this? Are you frustrated by the limited access or do you understand Google’s reasoning? Let’s hash it out in the comments below!

text:
I have offered to work with a few really rich people over the years, some of whom I knew when they were poor, but their money seems to get in the way of them listening, I guess?

I don't consider them superior because they have more money than I do.

1. First, they don't know how much I have because I don't boast about it. I did pretty well, my company IPO'd in the late 80s, I was the largest shareholder, and following that I invested mostly conservatively but also made a few wild bets and one of them turned out spectacularly, so my money has grown nicely over the years. 

2. Their money doesn't give them ideas.

3. It probably clouds their judgement. They think they have exceptional skills and intuition, why? The money. Making money and having great new ideas are different things. I think most money is made from stolen ideas, btw. I let other people commercialize my inventions. In some cases they did a fair job but usually they screwed it up because of their arrogance and focus on money. Sometimes to make something big happen you have to seed a market, not own it. Also it clouds their judgement because it causes them to only listen to people with more money than they have, which is imho incredibly stupid.

I don't even remember the names of some of them, and I don't want to call them out. I don't want to make this personal. But if you are lucky enough to make a lot of money, really the only thing worth anything that you can own is yourself -- and that today costs no more than a few million dollars. Anything above that is going to distract. You can use one house, one bedroom, one car, you can go to a game, but you don't have to own the  team (looking at you Steve Ballmer) and if you're going to do that be aware that's a hobby not an occupation. The Knicks have a shitty owner, but he was smart enough to hire the best management in the NBA. Knicks in 5! :-)

I hope the reason you got into tech is that a it's fascinating canvas for your creativity. It's something you have special ability in. I've seen incredibly mediocre people make a huge fortune, so what. The people I chose to work with were people I though had what it took to make something wonderful. But they all decided I wasn't at their level (I guess) and that's imho is stupid. To assume everyone has the same goals as you do. I learned pretty early that I had all the money I needed or wanted, so instead I did exactly what I wanted to do, with mixed results of course. But I have had some winners that cost money, not made it, but some of the most enjyable and worthwhile things you do cost money, money can buy happiness in the realm of individual creativity and in the end you own yourself, your time, your work.

Thanks for listening. :-)

📌 Save this: https://t.co/lrFlmCsxt2 — The Complete Primer

Everything worth knowing about @pacioli_ai, @Auditchain's disclosure automation platform, in one post. Bookmark it; this is the reference you'll keep coming back to.

1. What It Is
https://t.co/lrFlmCsxt2 is the flagship product of @Auditchain (Auditchain Labs AG, Zug, Switzerland): AI (Artificial Intelligence) agents that automate regulatory disclosure — reading each filing against the rules that govern it. Built first for crypto-asset issuers facing MiCAR (Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation), expanding to financial reporting and ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) compliance. The team calls it the world's first fully automated iXBRL (Inline XBRL)-compliant disclosure platform.

2. How It Works
Three steps, their words: Create, Validate, Celebrate.
Create: design disclosures in the Luca Suite (https://t.co/PdUqaQx43a) with no structured-data expertise; export iXBRL, the machine-readable format 140+ regulators in 65 jurisdictions require.
Validate: the Pacioli AI Validating Node, a logic and reasoning engine built on SWI-Prolog, checks the filing. Independent agents must corroborate each other before a validation is final, and every conclusion plus its evidence is written to a distributed ledger. In a demo, it batch-analyzed all S&P 100 annual reports.
Celebrate: validated projects are set to be featured on the Pacioli Explorer, a public compliance dashboard.

3. The Nodes
https://t.co/lrFlmCsxt2 runs as a DePIN (Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Network): operators install the logic engine plus a node.js agent that hunts the network for validation requests and races other nodes to fulfill them. Validators stake ethereum:0xb90cb79b72eb10c39cbdf86e50b1c89f6a235f2e and earn rewards per validation. Independent corroboration is the product: no single agent's output ever stands alone.

4. Who's Using It
- The big one: on 29 September 2026, @PwC and @Auditchain announced a cooperation to bring disclosure automation and external validation to crypto-asset issuers worldwide, starting with MiCAR white papers in Europe. First deployment is called START (Submission, Traceability, Automation, Reporting & Transparency), with PwC as external validator.
- Standards: XBRL Switzerland and @Auditchain released a next-generation Swiss taxonomy for XBRL (eXtensible Business Reporting Language).
- Infrastructure: blocz offers Pacioli Node-as-a-Service (2023); Volpex partnered for Proof-of-State validation for exchanges (2023).

5. Recognition
- Auditchain is a member of XBRL US and founded its Digital Asset Working Group (https://t.co/qqnT0eq8jS).
- Policy footprint: nine submissions since February 2026 — FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation): stablecoin issuer application + ongoing GENIUS Act rules; OCC (Office of the Comptroller of the Currency): bank chartering for digital-asset custody; NCUA (National Credit Union Administration); plus comment letters to the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission) on Regulation S-K reform and the PCAOB (Public Company Accounting Oversight Board) on its strategic plan, all pushing machine-readable, structured disclosure. Full docket: https://t.co/QFPTHOD9u4

6. The Team
  • Charles Hoffman (https://t.co/XjozPyHmY6) — Product Manager, "Godfather of XBRL" (also its inventor; AICPA (American Institute of Certified Public Accountants) Special Recognition Award, 2006)
  • David Blaszkowsky (https://t.co/AwAM5aCF8c) — Regulatory Adviser; former co-founder of the US Office of Financial Research, co-creator of the LEI (Legal Entity Identifier) standard
  • @JasonMeyersNYC (https://t.co/CRzSkvAViU) — Lead Architect and creator of https://t.co/lrFlmCsxt2

7. The Token
ethereum:0xb90cb79b72eb10c39cbdf86e50b1c89f6a235f2e is the settlement token: reporting entities pay it to validate disclosures, validators earn it, and Process Control creators earn royalties in it every time their controls are used. It also secures the network via staking and governs it.
250M max supply with ~60.4M circulating (CoinGecko). Trades on @QuickswapDEX (@0xPolygon) and @Uniswap on Robinhood Chain.

8. The Catch
The on-chain economy isn't live end-to-end yet: in-app Validator/Vote are still "Coming Soon," so no cohort validation → no NFT (Non-Fungible Token) claims → no royalties so far. Luca Suite remains in private beta. The tech is documented and the PwC cooperation is real; the permissionless royalty flywheel is still ahead.

Why This Is Bullish:
Regulators are forcing the world's disclosures into machine-readable formats, and https://t.co/lrFlmCsxt2 was built for exactly that world before it arrived. With PwC now cooperating on MiCAR deployments, the "who checks the checkers" question has a Big Four-grade answer.

Which disclosure regime goes machine-readable next?

THE ERA OF CIRCULAR TOKENOMICS IS DEAD AND REPLACED BY COLD HARD MACRO REALITY

We just saw the Fed hike rates to 3.75 to 4.00% in September and DeFi TVL still surged past $95B. But if you look under the hood the structural plumbing of the market has completely shifted. Yield subsidies have entirely collapsed giving way to a normalized real yield curve anchored by tokenized US Treasury rates like BlackRock BUIDL. Retail isn't hunting unsustainable ponzi yields anymore. They are trading on proprietary L2s. Case in point Uniswap captured $28.0M in Q3 protocol fees. In fact over 90% of their overall revenue  originated from proprietary retail distribution integration on the Robinhood Chain L2. The liquidity is still here but it is being aggressively siloed.

   Zoom out and the macro picture explains exactly why this isolation is happening. With inflation stubbornly holding and the 10 year treasury yield pushing higher capital preservation is the only game in town. On chain we see this in credit markets where monolithic pools like Aave V3 maintain liquidity dominance with $16.8B in TVL. But modular vault protocols like Morpho Blue with $9.8B are rapidly capturing institutional market share by isolating risk via third party curators. Smart money refuses to take on pooled risk when off chain infrastructure breaches are causing absolute havoc. Look at the September exploit vectors showing $768M in losses. Smart contract logic attacks have dropped significantly due to formal verification but off chain breaches accounted for over 92% of the damage. The Bitget custody breach alone was $387M and Liquid Network took a $320M hit. The tech is secure but the operational custody is bleeding alpha.
