This lasted a lot longer than I thought it would at launch. Was priced out at mint, checked back a few times but didn’t see anything meaniful to me. And yet I did appreciate the thought that tried to put in.

The fact that it even took the time to make an announcement of the shut down is a sign of respect IMO. On a brand level where budgetary cycles and approvals take time to prepare and ROI is a major consideration of every decision that gets made I think nearly 3 years in a down cycle is a substantial commitment to “long haul”. Brand reputation is critical to these major companies and for them to do something it must be effective as well as profitable. 

Big picture, I don’t know if it’s that big brands don’t stick around, or if adoption and benefit hasn’t caught up to other available technical solutions and known community growth strategies.

Starbucks first piloted mobile ordering in 2014. iPhones barely had ApplePay. They didn’t do that overnight, probably took 2-3 years development. It then took 5 years and a global pandemic to make it make sense. Now every food chain and mom and pop offer it. It’s become an expectation today.

I feel there is a similar shift coming for blockchain tech (especially with AI advancement). And hopefully brands that did take chances learned lessons and can apply them to future offerings.

In the meantime we need to keep the discourse going on what does this technology unlock and how can we help use it to create identity and provenance for brand loyalists that want to participate so that brands can recognize the ROI without diminishing their brand reputation.

text:
Podcast Summary | Financial Audit: The Biggest Losers In Financial Audit History

Overview
This audit cycle exposes a repeat pattern: couples and individuals who describe ambitious goals while their money, habits, and home life move in the opposite direction. A recurring setup is a household where one partner earns a stable paycheck while the other pursues creative or contract work that has not produced reliable income for years. Promises and verbal timelines replace budgets, and the gap between stated values and actual spending keeps widening. The audits land on the same conclusion: without reliable income and honest numbers, big goals like homeownership and retirement stay out of reach, and relationships absorb the cost.

Key Themes
- A five-year entrepreneurship window extended to eight years is nearly up, and the earning partner is preparing to move on if nothing changes.
- Claiming to run a business is not the same as producing income, and domestic duties do not count as entrepreneurship.
- Once kids are in the picture, chasing a dream without reliable income stops being acceptable, regardless of creative talent.
- Partners who control the finances can still carry debt, late fees, and interest, so control is not the same as competence.
- Lying about money, then revising the story when confronted, destroys credibility faster than the debt itself.
- A new car on a high interest loan can single-handedly determine whether debt gets paid off in years or decades.
- Spending on food delivery, games, cards, and subscriptions while loans sit in deferment is a choice, not a shortage.

Detailed Summary
Shannon works as a general manager at a St. Louis tourist attraction, earning $78,000 a year, roughly $5,200 a month after tax. Tanner, her husband of eight years, runs a small security company called Ozark South with a couple of contractors. Party security pays him $35 an hour while contractors get around $700 and employees $25 an hour. Pressed on monthly income, he estimates about $1,200 and adds that some months are more. Shannon says she rarely sees the fruits of his efforts and doubts he knows his own averages, which sets the tone for everything that follows.

The marriage runs on a verbal deal. Shannon gave Tanner five years to build an entrepreneurship career before marriage, then extended it by three years after COVID disrupted the film industry. About four months remain. Tanner started in film and acting at $600 to $1,200 a month, and Shannon says he was around $2,000 a month two years in before the pandemic hit. She describes herself as a little over his entrepreneurship. He says he feels underappreciated and trapped, while she says his resentment surfaces once or twice a year and has held the relationship back for years.

The kids sit at the center of the conflict. Tanner describes them as biologically not his, a phrasing Shannon and the host treat as revealing how he views the family, though he insists he raises them as his own and never calls them stepkids. He grew up without family from age 14 and moved from a bachelor life straight into a full family unit. He stepped in after a live-in babysitter stopped helping, took over school runs and domestic duties, and says he was working 80 hours a week on film projects before that role developed. The host keeps returning to one point: domestic duties are not entrepreneurship, and once kids are involved, a dream without income is no longer acceptable.

Money management is another fault line. Shannon controls the finances and gives Tanner a percentage of his earnings as an allowance for drinks and nicotine, though she stopped funding the nicotine and drink spending after reviewing it. He says he hands over about 75% of what he brings in and resists the framing that he does not contribute. He claims he has never been in debt and says she was the one in debt when they met, which she confirms. She says she manages money because she trusted people in the past and lost financially. He points to 2022 as a year he outearned her and paid all the household bills while she pursued her dream; she acknowledges he stepped up then but says it stopped when she returned to work.

The restaurant and coffee shop mark the turning point. A friend approached Shannon in 2019 about buying the restaurant, and they bought it for roughly $60,000 to $65,000. It did $3,700 to $4,100 a week, enough to sustain a salary but not profit. Tanner went from one day a week to managing the whole operation. Shannon says it failed under his full-time presence because of early closings and missed openings. He says multiple factors were at play and it was not because of him. The damage was real: they took a loan against the equity in her house, sold the house to repay it, and later paid $2,000 a month in rent versus a previous $600 house payment. Shannon calls it a stupid decision they made together and says she does not resent the loss.

Industry changes dominate Tanner's explanation for stalled work. He says his methods are stuck in the way projects came together from the mid-2000s to 2016. He cites AI, fewer voiceover jobs, and commercials produced from text-based programs instead of crews. Shannon says his methods stopped working about five years ago and he has not adapted, and he partially agrees. He says past success came from just going for it, while she says the world changed and he has to change with it. He wants to move to a city with a stronger film and acting scene, naming Atlanta, Toronto, New York, and Washington. She will not move because her kids are there and she has a career path and income.

Shannon sets a strikingly low bar. She says he only needs to bring in about $500 a month for the arrangement to work, and he still does not do it consistently. His income swings from $500 to $1,000 in some months and often covers just his allowance. He had a weekly contract worth $1,200 to $1,500 a month until the venue shut down, and a church drumming job ended as well. He says he built a security company, is trusted countywide, does search and rescue and drone work, though much of that is unpaid. He admits he has slacked off and needs to buckle down but refuses a 9-to-5 because he previously earned more from contract work. Shannon has been saving for a house down payment for a year while he says he is content where they live.

Debt and spending undermine the stated goals. Shannon opened a credit card in May to build credit, has spent $1,984 on it, and at current terms it would take 19 years to pay off. They have about $1,300 in savings, and Tanner thought they had $6,000 but found $1,200. A shady lender offered $20,000 to $25,000 at 3% weekly interest, where a $25,000 loan would require roughly $28,000 back. He says he considered it and backed out. He also acknowledges past gambling and gray area activity when he was younger. Credit card charges include therapy, car insurance, groceries, and restaurant charges, and at least two cards carry late payments and fees.

Disclosure problems get worse under examination. Tanner allegedly described credit card debt as fraudulent during onboarding, then texted the next morning saying he remembered the cards and forgot to pay them. Debt balances discussed include $632 in collections, a Care Credit balance of $5,876 that rose by $1,800 two weeks ago for both daughters' braces, an active account at $420, and maxed-out Capital One accounts at $420 and $382 against $300 limits. He also admits telling his wife he was going out of town for work but staying alone in a hotel for three days, and he claims he has submitted over 300 job applications on LinkedIn in three months.

One audit focuses on a household whose choices contradict their goals. The couple defends a new $33,842 car at 15.4% interest and $756 a month, while the host argues a cheaper car was possible and the vehicle is the main reason they cannot pay off debt. They carry $17,600 in student loans, one deferred, while spending on DoorDash, fast food, games, and subscriptions. The host estimates nine years to clear debt with minimum payments and says a car trade plus consistent work could cut that to about 2.5 to 5 years. Financial scores land at zero for overspending, zero for retirement, and roughly 0.5 overall, with the host saying a house purchase is not happening in March and probably not in ten years.

Another audit ends with $1,000 spent on Pokémon cards, money that was meant for a down payment on a house. The participant scores near zero across overspending, emergency savings, retirement, and real estate, with the emergency fund down to a small amount. The host says the participant is 40, wants to retire, and has no retirement savings, then rates it 0 out of 10. The total score rounds to 0.5 out of 10.

Across every case, the same gap recurs: stated goals on one side, cash flow and daily choices on the other. Without reliable income, honest numbers, and someone willing to confront the spending, the dream keeps winning and the family keeps paying for it.

For two decades, the empire has been desperately trying to shove WikiLeaks - the genie of raw, unvarnished truth - back into its bottle. In two days - on the 4th of October - we celebrate twenty years of WikiLeaks, honouring the rebellious spark that permanently shattered the ruling class's monopoly on reality.

To celebrate this milestone, we must strip away the corporate media propaganda and reckon with the tectonic shifts triggered when classified depravity met public outrage. Here are twenty ways that WikiLeaks and Assange changed the world:

1. Assange showed us that one man could challenge the most powerful empire on the planet. He didn't use bombs, just the sheer force of raw truth bleeding out into the ether for all to see. It is a vital, piercing reality.

2. WikiLeaks demonstrated that the most dangerous weapon against a warmongering empire isn't a missile, but a secure drop-box and courageous whistleblowers willing to risk it all. We've learned you cannot fight a behemoth with polite petitions.

3. WikiLeaks proved that true journalism requires adversarial defiance, effectively rendering the traditional, access-driven corporate media obsolete. We do not need their polished lies.

4. WikiLeaks permanently altered that power dynamic by proving cryptography can be used to protect the powerless instead of shielding the powerful. There is a strange poetry in flipping the script on our overlords. As Assange noted: "Knowledge has always flowed upwards, to bishops and kings, not down to serfs and slaves," the platform systematically dismantled the entrenched barriers of official secrecy.

5. WikiLeaks proved that the "rules-based international order" is merely a rhetorical shield used by powerful nations to violate international law with absolute impunity.

6. Cablegate pulled the curtain back on global diplomacy, revealing that the US State Department operates less like an embassy and more like a global mafia enforcing corporate interests. It’s a dodgy club.

7. The publication of the NSA intercepts targeting European leaders proved that the empire has no allies, only vassals and surveillance targets.

8. The 'Vault 7' releases exposed how intelligence agencies weaponised our own smart TVs and phones against us, turning every living room into an unchecked panopticon. We willingly bought the devices watching us.

9. The 'Global Intelligence Files' unmasked the shadow-CIA firm Stratfor, proving that private intelligence contractors are perfectly willing to spy on peaceful activists for corporate cash. Spooks are perfectly happy to moonlight for the highest bidder.

10. WikiLeaks exposed the insidious nature of financial blockades, proving that when Visa and Mastercard cut off donations, corporate banks act as direct enforcement arms of the state. In 2010 the choked off all funding to the publisher overnight without a single legal charge, simply because Washington snapped its fingers.

11. WikiLeaks gave a masterclass in anti-colonialism by releasing the 'Guantanamo Bay files', documenting the systemic abuse of uncharged detainees in a gross violation of international human rights. The cages in Cuba remain a gaping wound on the world.

12. The 'Yemen files' laid bare the reality of a devastating proxy war, exposing how Western arms actively fuelled a humanitarian catastrophe while diplomats looked the other way. Children starved for corporate profit. We were gobsmacked by the callousness.

13. The organisation showed the world that anti-war activism must be grounded in primary source documents, replacing emotional pleas with undeniable, leaked evidence of state violence. You cannot argue with a massive spreadsheet of innocent corpses.

14. WikiLeaks shattered the myth of the benevolent Western empire by bringing to light the 'Collateral Murder' video, proving that the military-industrial complex treats civilian lives like a twisted video game.

15. The 'Afghan War Diary' permanently stripped the heroic veneer off the occupation, exposing how coalition forces routinely covered up civilian casualties and outsourced torture. The propaganda surrounding the endless occupation was a meticulously crafted mirage.

16. By publishing the 'Iraq War Logs', Julian Assange provided the definitive, unvarnished death toll of a neo-colonial invasion built entirely on manufactured lies. The entire invasion was a grotesque, brutal stitch-up from the very beginning.

17. The formidable WikiLeaks archive has evolved into an indestructible, digital rebel library of Alexandria holding over ten million classified documents that can never be erased by imperial censors. It has become an invaluable resource for scholars, students, lawyers, historians, journalists, and the public fighting for emancipation.

18. The global campaign to free Assange redefined international solidarity, uniting hackers, journalists, anti-war activists and decent, caring, awake people in a massive resistance of millions of people against imperial state power, giving birth to a truly beautiful community.

19. Over twenty years, WikiLeaks has cemented the enduring truth that peace and human rights can only flourish when the war machine is stripped of its primary fuel of absolute secrecy. I have no doubt the legacy of this project will outlive the empires that tried to crush it.

20. Having survived the empire's maximum-security torture cells, Julian is now fully recovered, proudly announcing that he is back, and with Stella carrying a brand new baby on the way, they prove that love is an ultimate act of defiance against a sterile, death-obsessed state. Their flourishing family stands as living proof that the tyrants failed to extinguish the human spirit. It will be nothing short of riveting to see what Julian does next on the global stage.

And here we are in 2026, standing at a new precipice, watching a colonial machine orchestrate a horrific genocide in Gaza. As autonomous AI systems and sterile targeting algorithms are deployed as merciless weapons of slaughter across Gaza and Ukraine, the digital fog of war is being deliberately engineered to suffocate our access to truthful information. We seem to be hurtling toward a dystopian world where silicon-driven death squads operate in total darkness, leaving humanity drowning in a manufactured sea of algorithmic deception.

Now, armed with two decades of undeniable proof of elite criminality, the real question is: What are we gonna do about it? We must tear the blood-soaked gears from their engines of death, lock arms, and fiercely demand a world where humanity finally eclipses empire.

text:
Debbie Solsman spent 14 years working in the cafeteria at New Miami Local Schools in Ohio, quietly breaking policy to protect kids from hunger and humiliation. When students came through the lunch line without money, the rule was to give them a cold cheese sandwich, the “alternate meal” that instantly marked a child as poor. Debbie refused to let that happen. She paid for their hot lunches out of her own pocket, day after day, year after year, never telling anyone and never asking for reimbursement.

In 2024, the district discovered her long‑running act of quiet generosity and fired her for violating food‑service accounting rules. The decision stunned the community. Parents described her as the kind of adult who made school feel safe, and a GoFundMe launched to support her quickly filled with donations and messages praising her compassion. Online, her story went viral, not because she broke a rule, but because she had spent more than a decade shielding children from shame in a system that often prioritizes policy over humanity.

As the public rallied behind her, two nearby school districts reached out with job offers, saying they wanted someone with her heart on their team. Debbie said she was overwhelmed by the support and grateful simply to be recognized for the kindness she tried to give quietly for so long. Her story became a symbol of the tension between rigid school policies and the people who choose compassion anyway, and a reminder that communities often step up to defend those who quietly do good.

text:
I am an Akwa Ibom man. I have no intention of insulting my people. But loving your people does not mean becoming their permanent praise singer.

There is something deeply troubling about our political culture.

Too many of our youths have been taught to look up to politicians not as public servants accountable to citizens, but as political fathers whose crumbs must be received with gratitude.

Give a young man ₦10,000 and he calls you “our leader.”

Give him a bag of rice and he becomes your social-media defender.

Give him a political appointment and suddenly every failure becomes “politics.”

Give him a few motorcycles, sewing machines or empowerment items, and he is expected to forget the thousands of young people without sustainable jobs.

That is not empowerment. That is political dependency.

And here is the part that should worry us most:

The politician gives you ₦10,000 today, and you surrender your voice for the next four years.

He gives you rice, and you defend the indefensible.

He gives you a temporary appointment, and you become his attack dog.

He gives you a bus ride to a rally, and you cheer as though he personally built the roads you are travelling on.

Meanwhile, the same young people are graduating into an economy that cannot absorb them. Hospitals struggle. Schools struggle. Roads deteriorate. Businesses struggle with power and infrastructure. Insecurity threatens livelihoods.

And we are celebrating bags of rice.

My people, rice is not development.

A ₦20,000 handout is not economic empowerment.

A political appointment is not evidence of good governance.

A rally crowd is not public approval.

And photographs of politicians surrounded by thousands of beneficiaries are not a development index.

We need to stop behaving like subjects waiting for favours from our political lords.

We are citizens.

The money being distributed is not necessarily the politician's personal money. Public office comes with access to public resources, public authority and public responsibility.

So instead of asking:

“What did he give me?”

Ask:

“What did government deliver for us?”

Instead of celebrating one person who received a motorcycle, ask how many young people obtained sustainable employment.

Instead of celebrating a bag of rice, ask why families need political intervention to put food on their tables.

Instead of defending a politician because he “remembered us,” ask whether the system he controls is actually producing opportunities for millions who were never remembered.

And to my fellow youths:

Please, don't sell four years of your citizenship for one afternoon of political hospitality.

Take whatever lawful assistance you are offered if you need it. But don't surrender your brain, your conscience or your vote along with it.

Eat the politician's rice if you must.

But don't let the rice eat your sense.

Akwa Ibom deserves citizens who can look a politician in the eye and say:

“Thank you for the gift. Now show us your report card.”

That is how a democracy grows.

Not through political worship.

Not through permanent dependency.

Not through crumbs.

Through citizens who know that government belongs to them too.

- Civic Accountability Without Apology.

text:
Date: 2 October 2026
           21 Rabi‘ al-Thani 1448 AH

As-Salamu alaykum wa raḥmatullahi wa barakatuh. Below is the Hadith of the Week.

The Prophet Muhammed ﷺ said:

- *“Whoever wakes up in the morning secured in his [or her] house, healthy in his body, having his food for the day, it is as if he has been given the whole world*”. _(Narrated by ‘Ubaydullah ibn Mihsan (RA), Jami‘ at-Tirmidhi, 2346; graded Hasan.)_

According to the scholars, this hadith reminds us that safety, good health and enough food for the day are among the greatest blessings a person can have. Saying that someone has “been given the whole world” highlights how valuable these three blessings are.

Notice that the Prophet ﷺ did not mention a large bank balance, a beautiful house, an expensive car or a prestigious position. He mentioned basic blessings that many of us already have, but sometimes forget to appreciate.

We may wake up and immediately start thinking about our problems: the bills we must pay, the work waiting for us, the house we cannot afford, the promotion we have not received or the things we want to buy.

Our concerns may be real. But before counting what is missing, can we first acknowledge what Allah has already given us?

Let’s break it down:

*First: Am I safe where I slept last night?*

Perhaps our house is smaller than we would like. Perhaps we are renting and hoping to own a home one day. But we slept without fearing that someone would attack us, rape our women, or even that we would have to flee during the night. For someone living through war, violence or displacement, one peaceful night in a safe place would mean so much.

When we wake up safely, let us remember to say, “Alhamdulillah” — all praise and thanks belong to Allah.

*Second: Do I have health to be thankful for today?*

Sometimes we only appreciate our health when we become sick. We may complain about getting up early for work, forgetting the blessing of being able to get out of bed, dress ourselves and go about our day. Others are bedridden and need help with these everyday tasks.

Even when we are living with illness, there may still be blessings we can acknowledge: being able to breathe , eat, communicate with someone or receive care.

This does not make illness or pain easy. We can thank Allah for the blessings we still have while asking Him for healing and seeking treatment for the sick.

*Third: Do I have food for today?*

Notice that the hadith speaks about food for the day—not for a week or a month; just one day.

We may not have everything we would like to eat. The meal may be simple. But we have something to satisfy our hunger. 

Sometimes we look into our kitchen containing food and say, “There is nothing to eat,” simply because there is nothing we feel like eating. Meanwhile, another person is wondering whether they or their children will eat at all that day. This should make us pause before complaining or wasting food.

The Prophet ﷺ began his day by remembering Allah. When he woke from sleep, he would say:
 
*الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَحْيَانَا بَعْدَ مَا أَمَاتَنَا وَإِلَيْهِ النُّشُورُ*

*Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi ahyana ba‘da ma amatana wa ilayhin-nushur* (Meaning: All praise belongs to Allah, who gave us life after causing us to die, and to Him is the resurrection. Here, waking from sleep is described as being restored to life.) _(Sahih al-Bukhari, 6312.)_

Our gratitude should also influence how we treat others.

If we have enough food, can we share a meal or help a family buy groceries? If someone is unwell, can we check on them or help them access care? If someone is facing hardship, can we offer practical support?

Sometimes our “Alhamdulillah” can be followed by a simple question: “Who can I help today?”

*LESSONS FROM THIS HADITH*

1. Safety, health and daily food are great blessings.
2. We should acknowledge what we have before focusing on what we lack.
3. We can be grateful while still working to improve our circumstances.

1/2…..

text:
Paul wanted to go to Rome and God gave him a pen instead.

He had longed to stand among those believers, to strengthen them, to be strengthened by them, to preach Christ in the capital of the empire. Again and again the road stayed closed. Circumstances frustrated the journey. Paul could easily have regarded those delays as wasted time.

Instead, somewhere in Corinth, a man drew up a chair, sat down and began to dictate a letter. We have been reading it ever since.

A church Paul had never visited received the letter first. Then believers far beyond Rome began receiving it too. Century after century, Christians have opened these same words and found the gospel waiting for them. The journey Paul could not make became a letter that traveled farther than he ever could.

There is something tender in that. Paul could not give Rome his presence, so he gave them his words. What must have felt like an interruption in his plans became one of the great gifts Christ has given His church. Every Christian who opens the book of Romans now receives what Paul longed to say face to face.

Our frustrations sometimes live inside the providence of God. We see the closed road. God sees farther. Romans begins simply enough: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God.”

Paul tells us immediately who owns him. The word servant carries the sense of a bondslave. He belongs completely to Jesus Christ. His plans, labor, body, mind, future, suffering and preaching stand at the disposal of another. Grace has taken hold of him and grace has given his life a new center. That should wake us up before we ever reach the great arguments of the letter.

We sometimes read NT epistles as though they came from dry theologians tucked safely away from the world, writing about matters that never touched blood or tears. Paul will not fit that picture. He had been beaten and chased from cities. In one place his preaching stirred a riot. In another, people believed and a church was born. He carried the gospel into danger because he believed the message actually saved people.

Romans came from that man. He was a Christian who had received grace. He was an apostle commissioned by Christ. He was a missionary whose life had been separated unto the gospel. He was also a man with the churches on his heart. Though he had never met the Roman believers, he prayed for them without ceasing. He wanted to do them good. He wanted their fellowship to do him good too.

There is something beautifully ordinary about that last part. The apostle who wrote Romans still wanted the company of other Christians. Then Paul tells us who receives the letter: “To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints.”

These were ordinary believers. They had heard the gospel with their ears and by the grace of God they had heard it in their hearts. They turned from sin and embraced Jesus Christ offered to them in the gospel. Paul calls them saints because every Christian belongs to God, set apart for Him.

Their faith had become known far beyond Rome. People were talking about it. These were not men and women who had merely responded to an appeal and gone home unchanged. Their faith endured and here Romans comes very close to us.

This letter was not written for a seminary classroom. Paul did not address a private society of theologians. He wrote to the believers who made up a local church. Romans is the gospel of the pew.

It belongs to the farmer and the mechanic, the widow and the young mother, the teenager opening a Bible at the kitchen table, the old saint who has followed Christ for sixty years and the new believer still learning where the books of the Bible are. This is the gospel ordinary Christians are meant to know, love, live by and carry to their neighbors.

Churches grow weak when the gospel grows thin in the minds of their people. We can learn the vocabulary of Christianity while the realities behind those words slowly fade. Grace. Faith. Righteousness. Salvation. Justification. We recognize the sounds, perhaps even know when to say amen, while our understanding becomes shallow enough to leave us vulnerable to half-gospels.

Romans gives us a plumb line. Lay the message we preach beside this letter. Lay the message we believe beside it. Let Romans expose every substitute that asks Christ to share the center with human merit.

Paul makes the subject plain from the beginning. He was “separated unto the gospel of God.” He was eager to preach the gospel in Rome. He was unashamed of the gospel because it is “the power of God unto salvation.” Romans is an explanation of THAT gospel. Its origin is God.

Paul calls it “the gospel of God, which he had promised afore by his prophets in the holy scriptures.” Paul did not invent it. A council did not construct it. A generation did not improve it. God promised it in Scripture long before Paul sat down in Corinth.

The gospel grows out of everything God had been revealing and promising. The OT reaches forward. The NT opens what had been promised. One story runs through both and at the center stands a Person.

The gospel concerns “his Son Jesus Christ our Lord,” descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God with power by the resurrection from the dead.

Jesus walked through much of His earthly ministry almost incognito. People saw the carpenter from Nazareth. Some saw a teacher. Others saw a threat. By the Spirit’s help, a few pierced the veil of ordinary appearance and saw who stood before them. Peter confessed Him as the Christ. The dying thief looked at a crucified man and spoke to a King. A centurion watched Him die and confessed the Son of God.

Then came the wonderful resurrection! The grave opened, Christ rose and what many had failed to see during His earthly ministry was declared with power. David’s Son is David’s Lord. The man from Nazareth is the Son of God. The gospel fixes our eyes there.

Still, Paul goes further. Christianity is more than declaring who Jesus is. The gospel also announces what He has done. That brings us to the question beneath the whole letter, the question every human being eventually faces whether he speaks it aloud or spends his life trying to outrun it. God is holy. We are sinners. How can we be right with Him?

Paul answers with words that have shaken consciences, opened prison doors in human hearts, stirred reformations, and steadied dying saints: “For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith.”

You cannot earn your way into the favor of God. Good works cannot climb high enough. Religion cannot scrub deeply enough. Regret cannot pay the debt. The gospel reveals a righteousness received by faith in Jesus Christ. The just shall live by faith.

This is why Paul could say, “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth.” He did not mean the gospel merely improves people…t saves them.

A Jew who believes is saved. A Gentile who believes is saved. The wise and the unwise come through the same door. The respectable sinner and the ruined sinner stand before the same Christ with empty hands. Whoever believes receives what he could never produce for himself. That is where our walk through Romans begins.

We are coming to this letter because ordinary Christians need a gospel sturdy enough to live on and clear enough to give away. We need our ignorance driven out. We need false gospels exposed before they settle quietly into our churches. We need half-gospels stripped of their disguises. Most of all, we need Christ set before us again.

Paul wanted to go to Rome. God gave him a pen instead. The road closed, the letter traveled and generations of believers have opened these pages to discover the same good news: Jesus Christ saves sinners, and the righteousness we need is received by faith.

So we open Romans together with one prayer. Lord, make the gospel clear to us again.

FDLE agents took Daughtery into custody on Sept. 10. He was booked into the Santa Rosa County Jail, where he is being held without bond.

text:
Science News: Could Your Own Body Tissue Replace Wireless Connections for Medical Implants?

Researchers at Georgia Tech have introduced SWANS, an innovative bioelectronic system that allows miniature medical implants to communicate directly through the body's naturally conductive tissue. By replacing conventional radio signals with ionic conduction, these micro-scale devices operate on ultra-low power and can be made small enough for simple syringe delivery. Preclinical testing demonstrates coordinated communication between internal sensors and targeted neural interfaces, opening new possibilities for continuous health monitoring and precisely timed therapies. This non-invasive approach offers an exciting glimpse into the future of personalized healthcare and healthy aging.

text:
Now published on the Mary Phagan-Kean Legacy Project website

The Citogenesis of the Knights of Mary Phagan Hoax: The New York Times

At the center of this article is an unusual newspaper report published by The New York Times on Saturday, June 26, 1915, page 4. “Violence Feared in Atlanta Today” carried no named reporter. It appeared simply as a “Special to The New York Times” dispatch from Atlanta dated June 25.

Georgia Governor John M. Slaton commuted Leo Frank’s death sentence to life imprisonment on Monday, June 21, 1915. The Times story appeared five days later, during intense public anger over Slaton’s decision, and 52 days ahead of Frank’s extrajudicial hanging near Marietta on August 17. Slaton was also a partner in the law firm associated with Frank’s legal representation, adding another source of public controversy surrounding the commutation (NYT, 3).

The article is valuable for far more than its paragraph about the supposed “Knights of Mary Phagan.” Read as a whole, it gives us a picture of rumor, fear, military preparation, political anger, secret meetings, and secondhand reporting during Slaton’s final hours in office.

The language and anonymity deserve attention. Throughout the article, the Times uses phrases such as “it is said,” “there are rumors tonight,” “it is generally believed,” “the prophets assert,” “it is an open secret,” and “are said to have met.” For a forensic historian or researcher, such wording signals where the newspaper moves away from identified facts and begins repeating unnamed reports or general talk circulating around Atlanta.

The article opens with Slaton preparing to leave office at noon on June 26. The Times says he planned to leave Georgia soon afterward for an undisclosed destination and might spend several months around the Great Lakes, Canada, and New York. Even the time of his departure remained uncertain. One report placed it on Sunday afternoon, while other rumors placed it on Saturday afternoon shortly after he transferred the executive office to Judge Nat E. Harris of Macon (NYT, 3).

The Times then turns to fears surrounding Harris’s inauguration. Atlanta had remained quiet since the attack on Slaton’s home earlier in the week, but the newspaper said public feeling had not diminished. It reported unusually large crowds arriving from country towns and rural districts and predicted a possible anti-Slaton demonstration at the Capitol over his decision to save Frank from execution (NYT, 3).

The military preparations were substantial. The entire Fifth Regiment of Atlanta had reportedly been mobilized for the inauguration. A regiment from Macon and companies from other locations were also expected. The Times then added another anonymous claim, saying many soldiers disapproved of Slaton’s decision even though they intended to perform their duty (NYT, 3).

Slaton traveled to and from the Capitol with an officer while troops remained stationed at his country home. The Times also claimed sentiment across Georgia strongly opposed the commutation, while acknowledging a minority believed Slaton had acted correctly. No poll, survey, vote, or numerical measurement was offered to support this statewide estimate (NYT, 3).

The article also predicted a political reaction. According to the Times, Georgia governors’ pardon and commutation powers would soon be greatly restricted, with two measures already pending for this purpose (NYT, 3).

Then the article turns to secret meetings.

The Times reported nightly mass meetings in Atlanta and surrounding towns. It specifically named Marietta, Hapeville, and Jonesboro and said Atlanta newspapers had received reports of similar meetings elsewhere in Georgia. No organizers, officers, resolutions, minutes, or membership lists were provided (NYT, 3).

It is in this setting where the “Knights of Mary Phagan” suddenly appear.

The Times said 150 citizens “are said to have met” at Mary Phagan’s grave in Marietta. According to the article, they formed an oath-bound organization to avenge her death, and the body “is to be known” as the “Knights of Mary Phagan.” The report claimed organizers intended to establish lodges throughout Georgia whose members would pledge never to rest until Mary’s death had been avenged (NYT, 3).

But who were these 150 citizens? The Times names none of them. Who organized the meeting, presided over it, administered the oath, or served as officers? No names are given. No oath, charter, constitution, membership roll, minutes, lodge records, correspondence, or announcement from the supposed organization appears in the article. Not a clue.

The New York Times establishes one fact with certainty: on June 26, 1915, it printed a story about a supposed organization called the Knights of Mary Phagan. The newspaper report itself does not establish the organization in the form described. Its claim rests on anonymous, qualified language.

This is where citogenesis enters the story.

Citogenesis is the birth and repetition of a weak, unsubstantiated or unsupported claim. One report enters print. Later writers repeat it. Still later writers cite those writers. Over time, one uncertain report can begin to look like several independent confirmations even when the citation trail keeps circling back toward the same original claim.

The Mary Phagan-Kean Legacy Project’s source review identifies the June 26 New York Times story as the earliest print mention it has located using the name “Knights of Mary Phagan.” The same review reports no use of the name in the three Atlanta newspapers searched for 1915. By contrast, The Jeffersonian used “Vigilance Committee” in its August 19 and August 26 coverage of the men associated with Frank’s lynching (MPKLP, 2).

Another contemporary newspaper provides the same basic terminology. The Bamberg Herald of South Carolina reprinted an Associated Press account on September 2, 1915, based on an Atlanta dispatch dated August 22. The AP report repeatedly called the lynching group the “vigilance committee.” It described the group’s automobiles, journey from Milledgeville, actions surrounding the abduction, and its stated view of the hanging as an unofficial execution. It did not call the lynching party the “Knights of Mary Phagan” (Bamberg Herald, 4).

This creates a serious source problem for later histories. The June 26 Times article gives us an unnamed and undocumented “Knights” organization 52 days ahead of the lynching. Contemporary post-lynching reporting gives us a “Vigilance Committee.” Treating both names as interchangeable requires evidence.

Harry Golden became an important link in the later growth of the Knights story. His 1965 book, A Little Girl Is Dead, appeared fifty years after the events. Golden’s surviving research papers at the Charlotte Mecklenburg Library include files titled “Knights of Mary Phagan,” along with material on the Ku Klux Klan and New York Times coverage of the Frank case (Charlotte Mecklenburg Library, 1).

Golden also helped connect the Knights story to the rebirth of the Ku Klux Klan. Later scholarship repeated parts of this narrative. In a 1992 paper on the history of cross burning, Linda Lumsden cited page 300 of Golden’s book for a claim involving a large cross supposedly burned on Stone Mountain by the Knights of Mary Phagan on October 16, 1915. Lumsden then reported finding no mention of such a cross burning in the Atlanta Constitution for either October 16 or Thanksgiving (Lumsden, 5).

This is how a small paragraph in an anonymous 1915 newspaper article can grow into a much larger historical story. An unnamed graveyard organization becomes a vigilante society. Later writers identify it with the men who hanged Frank. Still later accounts connect the same supposed organization with the revival of the Ku Klux Klan.

Yet the June 26 article remains striking for what it does not provide. No named members. No officers. No eyewitness. No organizational records. No identified source. Its central phrases remain “are said to have met” and “is to be known.”

One final detail makes the article especially interesting. After reporting troops, rural crowds, secret meetings, hostility toward Slaton, and the supposed Knights in Georgia, the article abruptly shifts to New York City under the heading “Reception to Friends of Frank.” The Times reports a Woman’s Peace Society reception at Cosmopolitan Garden, 32 West Twenty-third Street, for people who signed the petition asking Slaton to commute Frank’s death sentence and for people who helped collect signatures (NYT, 3).

The same newspaper column therefore presents two very different scenes. In Georgia, readers encounter military preparations, anti-Slaton anger, secret meetings, and a mysterious oath-bound organization at Mary Phagan’s grave. In New York City, readers encounter a reception honoring people who worked for Frank’s commutation.

What can we actually prove from the June 26, 1915 article?

We can prove The New York Times printed the name “Knights of Mary Phagan.” We can prove the report supplied no names or organizational records. We can see its heavy reliance on qualified and anonymous language. We can also trace how later writers inherited the name and built a far larger story around it.

What the article cannot do by itself is turn an anonymous newspaper report into a documented organization.

THE NEW YORK TIMES

Saturday, June 26, 1915

Page 4

VIOLENCE FEARED IN ATLANTA TODAY

Militia Ready to Put Down Anti-Slaton Outbreaks as the Governor Retires.

LEAVES GEORGIA FOR REST

Great Crowds Expected at Inauguration—Many Mass Meetings Cause Apprehension.

Special to The New York Times.

ATLANTA, June 25 [1915].—Governor John M. Slaton will retire from office at noon tomorrow and a few hours thereafter will leave Georgia for some place not yet announced.

It is said that Governor Slaton will be out of the State for some time recuperating. He has worked hard during recent months, and this, together with the strain incident to the Frank case and the events that have followed the commutation, has caused the Governor to decide to take a long rest. He will be accompanied by Mrs. Slaton, and it is possible they will spend the next few months on the Great Lakes, in Canada, and in New York.

The hour at which Governor Slaton will leave has not been definitely stated. It is said that he will leave on Sunday afternoon, but there are rumors tonight that he plans to depart on Saturday afternoon, soon after he has turned over the Executive office to his successor, Judge Harris of Macon.

If the retirement of Governor Slaton and the inauguration of Judge Harris tomorrow pass without incident a bountiful crop of rumors will have come to naught.

Atlanta has been remarkably quiet since the attack on Governor Slaton’s home on last Monday night. The feeling has shown no signs of diminishing, although it has been restrained. It is generally believed that it has been the calm that precedes the storm and that preparations have been made for a great anti-Slaton demonstration at the capital tomorrow. Railroad men report that unusually large crowds are coming to the inauguration from the country towns and rural districts, and the prophets assert that the crowds will be here for the purpose of showing their disapproval of Governor Slaton’s action in saving Leo Frank from the gallows.

The authorities have taken unusual precautions to handle an outbreak should one occur. The entire Fifth Regiment of Atlanta has been mobilized and will be on duty during the inaugural exercises. There will also be a regiment here from Macon, the home of Judge Harris, and companies from other places. It is an open secret, however, that many of the troops do not approve of Governor Slaton’s action, and while they will do their duty as soldiers, they are not in love with it.

Governor Slaton was at the Capitol today winding up executive business. He seemed in better spirits and was apparently glad he was about to be rid of official duties. He was accompanied by an officer on the trip to and from the Capitol. A detachment of troops is still on duty at the Governor’s country home.

While the sentiment of Georgia at large undoubtedly strongly disapproves of Governor Slaton’s action, there is a minority which believes that he did right and that time will vindicate his action in commuting the death sentence of Frank.

It is certain that the pardoning and commuting power of Georgia Governors will be greatly curtailed for the future. Two measures for that purpose are already pending, and they will be merged into one and promptly passed.

One thing that makes the authorities apprehensive for tomorrow is the number of secret mass meetings that have been held nightly in Atlanta and the adjoining towns. These meetings have been held at Marietta, Hapeville, Jonesboro, and several other towns, and it is said that at these mass meetings plans were formed for a demonstration against Governor Slaton tomorrow. Atlanta newspapers have had reports of mass meetings all over the State.

One of the strangest of these meetings is reported to have been held at Marietta, where Mary Phagan is buried. One hundred and fifty citizens are said to have met at Mary Phagan’s grave and formed an oath-bound organization to avenge her death. This body is to be known as the “Knights of Mary Phagan,” and it is the purpose of the organizers to form lodges over Georgia, the members being pledged never to rest until the murder of the girl has been avenged. There seems to be little doubt that such a body has been formed.

Reception to Friends of Frank.

The Woman’s Peace Society will hold a reception in the Assembly Room of Cosmopolitan Garden, 32 West Twenty-third Street, this afternoon to those who signed the petition to Governor Slaton of Georgia, asking for a commutation of the death sentence of Leo Frank, and to those who worked to obtain the signatures.

Rachel Jacobs Frank’s explosive anti-Gentile outburst was not simply a story passed down through my family.

My grandfather, who attended the Mary Phagan murder trial, told me about the incident in person. Other members of my once-living family and ancestors were also present during the 29-day proceedings, held from July 28 through August 25, 1913, in Fulton County Superior Court in Atlanta, Georgia.

During Solicitor General Hugh Dorsey’s questioning of a witness, Rachel Jacobs Frank, Leo Frank’s mother, pushed her chair back abruptly, the legs screeching across the courtroom floor. She rose in anger and screamed, “Christian Gentile dog!” at Dorsey.

Defense counsel and court bailiffs escorted her from the courtroom. The judge later forgave her and allowed her to return after she promised there would be no more explosive outbursts.

This anti-Gentile incident was not based solely on family recollection. It was reported in a newspaper at the time. The New York Sun documented the outburst, independently confirming that it happened in open court and was witnessed by those present.

The Atlanta newspapers, however, softened the episode or censored the exact words Rachel Frank used.

The New York Sun,

Sunday, 12th October 1913,

Page 6.

Countrywide Appeal for Man Convicted of Killing Mary Phagan.

RACE HATRED CHARGED

Motion for New Trial in Georgia Halts the Hangman.

NEGRO'S STORY UNSHAKEN

Defence Hopes to Show That He Shelved Guilt on Frank.

ATLANTA, Ga., Oct. 11 [1913]. Although Leo M. Frank has been tried, convicted and sentenced to death for the murder of fourteen-year-old Mary Phagan, interest in the case continues as keen as when the condemned man was facing the jury. This is due to the fact that Frank's friends have denounced the verdict as a monstrous perversion of justice and have begun a campaign that is almost nationwide to get a reversal.

Frank was sentenced to be hanged on October 10, but a motion for a new trial prevented the sentence being carried into effect. This motion has not yet been argued but probably will be in two weeks. If Judge Roan, who presided at the trial of Frank, denies the motion, the case will be taken to the Georgia Supreme Court, and should that tribunal refuse to interfere Frank's attorneys say they will take the case to the United States Supreme Court, though it is difficult for a layman to see what Federal question is involved. In all the criminal history of Georgia no such determined fight has ever been made for a convicted man as is being made for Frank, and the vigor of the fight has much to do with keeping interest in the case keen.
Fight Against Verdict.

In their motion for a new trial Frank's attorneys give 115 reasons why the verdict against him should not be allowed to stand. Most of these reasons seem to be merely technical, but several of them, if true, seem to be substantial enough to warrant a new trial. Among other things, it is alleged that the feeling against Frank in Atlanta was so bitter that it was not possible for him to have a fair trial; that the "mob spirit" invaded the court room during the trial and intimidated the jury into returning a verdict of guilty, and that there were men on the jury who had said before being summoned for duty that Frank was guilty and that they wanted to get on the jury to "break his neck." To sustain these charges Frank's attorneys have introduced affidavits from a number of persons to show that one juror said that he intended to get on the jury and that he would "hang it until hell froze over" unless a verdict of guilty were returned. This juror is R. H. Henslee, and he was the first man of the twelve chosen to try Frank, neither the State nor the defence making objection. Solicitor-General Dorsey is now engaged in preparing an answer to these charges of the defence and as soon as he is ready the matter will be argued before Judge Roan. Just how the State will controvert the charges made against Juror Henslee remains to be seen, for the affidavits affecting him are sworn to by reputable citizens. If the defence can substantiate its charges against Henslee it is difficult to see how a new trial can be refused. This action, however, would only reflect on Juror Henslee and would not weaken the circumstantial and direct evidence which brought about the conviction of Frank.

An impression seems to prevail outside of Atlanta and Georgia and this impression has been sedulously cultivated by Frank's friends that he was convicted on purely circumstantial evidence.
Erroneous Impression.

This impression is entirely erroneous. There were powerful circumstances which pointed to Frank as the despoiler and murderer of little Mary Phagan and these circumstances would have made his acquittal difficult even if there had not been a shred of direct evidence to connect him with the crime. But the State had the evidence of an eye witness to support the circumstances which first caused the arrest of Frank. This witness was the negro James Conley, who swore that he came upon Frank bending over the body of Mary Phagan, that Frank confessed he had made improper advances to the girl, that she resisted and that he struck her and she fell unconscious. The negro also swore that Frank saw he had gone so far that he killed the girl to protect himself. Frank then, according to the negro's story to the jury, bribed the latter to take the girl's body to the basement and conceal it until opportunity offered to burn it in the furnace. It was this story, told by Conley to the jury, which clinched the circumstances against Frank and resulted in the verdict of guilty. And it is this story which Frank's attorneys will have to break down to free their client in the event that he gets a new trial and faces another jury.
Murdered in a Factory.

Mary Phagan was murdered on Saturday, April 26 Confederate Memorial Day in the National Pencil factory, of which Leo M. Frank was superintendent. The little girl had been employed in the factory for some months, but had been laid off a few days on account of a shortage of material. There was a small sum due her and she went to the factory on April 26 to get her money and then take part in the Memorial Day parade. The girl was to get her money from Frank, who paid off the employees. She left home about 11:30 in the morning, reached the factory about noon, entered Frank's office and was never seen alive again. It was a holiday and Frank was alone in the building with the exception of two workmen two floors above Frank's office. Frank admitted that the girl came to his office, but he says he paid her and that she left the building.

About 4 o'clock Sunday morning Newt Lee, the negro night watchman, in making his rounds came upon the girl's body in the basement. The negro at once telephoned the police, who came and moved the girl's body to the morgue. Examination showed that the girl had been stunned by a blow on the head and then strangled to death by a cord which was pulled so tightly as to cut into the flesh of her neck. Physicians also declared that she had been subjected to sexual violence.
Did Not Identify Her.

Frank, as superintendent of the factory, was notified of the finding of the body and the police went to his home Sunday morning and brought him to the morgue to identify the girl. Frank said he did not know who she was. Later on Sunday the body was identified as that of Mary Phagan by a girl friend. Meanwhile a search of the basement by the detectives resulted in the discovery of two badly written and badly spelled notes, purporting to have been written by Mary Phagan, saying that a negro "did this." The police arrested Lee, the negro night watchman, and also Arthur Mullinar, a young white man, who knew Mary Phagan. Later J. M. Gantt, former bookkeeper at the factory, was arrested as a result of a statement by Frank that Gantt had seemed to be fond of Mary Phagan. The Coroner's jury was in session several days and heard many witnesses. Gantt and Mullinar proved alibis and were released. Finally the Coroner's jury ordered that Frank and the negro, Lee, be held for the Grand Jury. While Frank was in jail awaiting the action of the Grand Jury the police arrested James Conley, the negro sweeper at the factory, on suspicion of knowing something about the crime. Conley was grilled by the detectives and finally told the story, which he afterward related on the stand, to the effect that Frank killed the girl after making improper advances to her and hired him (Conley) to help dispose of the body. Conley told several versions of the tragedy, but never varied from the main charge that he found Frank bending over the body of the girl and was hired by Frank to take the body to the basement.
Indictment of Frank.

On this evidence Frank was indicted and on July 28 he was put on trial for his life. The State first established the circumstances which incriminated Frank, the chief one being his own admission that Mary Phagan came to his office about noon on April 26. The State proved that the girl was never seen alive after she entered Frank's office and witnesses were introduced to swear that blood spots were found on the floor of a room just in the rear of Frank's office. The State also proved that Frank was alone in the factory nearby all of Saturday morning and all of the afternoon. It was also proved that when Lee, the night watchman, came on duty at 4 o'clock Saturday afternoon Frank sent him away and told him not to come back until 7 o'clock. The State also introduced an affidavit made by the negress who cooked for the Frank family to the effect that Frank was greatly disturbed on Saturday night and that she heard Mrs. Frank tell her mother that Frank tried to kill himself during the night. All of this was preliminary to the direct evidence against Frank of the negro Conley. Conley repeated at length the charge he made in his affidavit about Frank killing the girl and in addition told of acts of sexual perversion by Frank. Conley had been at the factory for two years and said that he had been employed as a lookout by Frank whenever the latter had girls in his office, which was almost weekly, according to Conley.
Acted as a Lookout.

The negro's story was one of the most remarkable and revolting ever told in a court room, and much of it was unprintable. He swore that he was acting as lookout for Frank the day Mary Phagan went to Frank's office and that half an hour after the girl entered he was summoned by Frank, who told him that the girl had resisted his advances, that he had struck her too hard, and had killed her to keep her from telling of his assault on her. In pantomime Conley reenacted before the jury how he and Frank took the girl's body to the basement, where it was later to be cremated in the furnace. Conley said Frank agreed to give him $200 to keep silent, and he said he had remained silent until Frank deserted him and seemed to be trying to fasten the crime on him. The negro was cross-examined for two days by Luther Z. Rosser, one of Frank's attorneys and one of the leaders of the Georgia bar, but the witness never varied from his story. Trap after trap was set by Rosser, but the negro refused to walk in.
Conley's Story Supported.

The State put on witnesses who corroborated Conley's story as to his presence at the factory on the Saturday of the crime. These witnesses swore they saw Conley at the street entrance of the factory. For Frank the defence first tried to establish an alibi. It was sought to account for every minute of his time on the day of the murder and to show that he was at home at luncheon when Conley swore that the body of Mary Phagan was being disposed of by himself and Frank. The theory of the defence was that Conley murdered the girl and that to save his own neck he told the story involving Frank. By many witnesses Frank's time was accounted for on Saturday, but over against this was Frank's own admission that he was practically alone in the factory nearly all of Saturday and that Mary Phagan came to his office. It was proved that she was never seen alive after entering the factory. The defence then put Frank's character in evidence. Many witnesses, most of them Jews, testified that his character was good. Rabbi Marx was one of these witnesses. He told how Frank was president of the local B'nai B'rith and what an interest he took in the synagogue. Many girls, employed at the pencil factory, were called who testified that Frank had always been respectful in his conduct toward them. In rebuttal, the State also called other pencil factory girls, who swore that Frank's character was bad in regard to women and who related specific instances of his conduct.
Frank's Statement.

Then Frank made a statement in his own behalf. It was a remarkable statement, covering every minute of the day of the crime. Frank, apparently, was able to remember everything that he did no matter how trivial. In fact, his memory for detail seemed uncanny. The summing up took several days. Luther Z. Rosser and Reuben Arnold, both leaders of the Georgia bar, spoke for two days in behalf of Frank. They charged that the negro Conley killed Mary Phagan and that his story involving Frank was told to save his own life. They also charged that the detectives, for reasons of their own, were bent on convicting Frank and that they had drilled Conley in his story. It was during Rosser's speech that the first reference was made to Frank's race. Rosser charged that Frank was being prosecuted because he was a Jew and asserted that the detectives were in a conspiracy to convict him.
Resented Racial Argument.

Solicitor-General Dorsey, summing up for the State, attacked Rosser for alluding to Frank's race. Dorsey showed how Mullinax, Gantt and Lee had all been arrested before Frank and said that action had been taken against the latter only because of the overwhelming evidence against him. Dorsey alluded to the fact that one of his own law partners was a Jew to show that he had no racial prejudice. Judge Roan's charge was brief and said to be absolutely impartial. The jury retired and in forty minutes returned a verdict of guilty without recommendation to mercy, which meant that Frank must be hanged. Two ballots were taken one as to Frank's guilt and the other as to whether he should be recommended to mercy, which would have meant life imprisonment. On the first ballot the jury was unanimous that Frank was guilty. On the question of recommending to mercy eleven jurors were for the death penalty and one for mercy, and he joined the majority.
Henslee Voted for Mercy.

Strange to say, the juror who voted for mercy was A. H. Henslee, who is now being charged by Frank's attorneys with having said before he was summoned for jury duty that Frank was guilty and ought to have his neck broken.

There was a great crowd about the court house, and when the verdict of guilty was announced a mighty cheer went up. As Solicitor-General Dorsey came out of the court house he was seized and carried on the shoulders of several men to his office across the street.

Since Frank's conviction much has been said to make it appear that he was the victim of race prejudice and that he was convicted because he was a Jew.

The facts hardly bear out this charge. It is generally conceded that if the circumstances and direct evidence had involved Mullinar and Giantt, the two young Gentiles first arrested, instead of Frank they probably would have been lynched.

At first there was absolutely no prejudice against Frank because of his race. Atlanta has probably been freer of the Juden-hetze spirit than any city in the South. Jews have been repeatedly elected to office and none was ever opposed because he was a Jew. Five Jews were on the grand jury that indicted Frank and they can hardly be accused of racial prejudice.
Prejudice Developed.

Prejudice did finally develop against Frank and also against the Jews, but Frank's friends were responsible for this anti-Semitic spirit. After Frank was indicted many Jews began to assert publicly that Frank was not guilty, that being a Jew he couldn't be guilty and that even if he were guilty the Jews would spend thousands to prevent his conviction.

Some Jews were credited with saying that even if Frank did kill Mary Phagan she was nothing but a factory girl. Such remarks as these soon caused a decided anti-Semitic feeling and it continued to grow during the trial of Frank. The feeling was increased when Frank's mother, who came here from Brooklyn to attend her son's trial, denounced Mr. Dorsey in the court room as "You Christian dog." The anti-Semitic feeling was the natural result of the belief that the Jews had banded to free Frank, innocent or guilty. The supposed solidarity of the Jews for Frank, even if he was guilty, caused a Gentile solidarity against him. That is the truth about Frank being the victim of Juden-hetze.
Feeling in Rural Districts.

No one, of course, can forecast the ultimate outcome of the case. Frank may get a new trial, but the general opinion is that he will be promptly convicted again if he is tried in Atlanta and if the State introduces the same evidence. If he should receive a change of venue and the case sent to a rural district, Frank would be in a worse position if possible, for the conviction that he is guilty is almost unanimous in the country counties. Circumstances, admitted by Frank and his attorneys, make the case dark against him, and when these circumstances are backed up by the direct evidence of Conley, the State's case becomes almost impregnable unless Conley's story be shattered. Conley may be lying but until he is proved a liar Frank will have little chance before a Georgia jury.

Rachel Jacobs Frank, Leo Frank’s mother, pushed her chair back so abruptly that its legs screeched across the courtroom floor. Rising during Solicitor General Hugh Dorsey’s questioning of a witness, she erupted in anger and shouted, “Christian Gentile dog!” at him.

Defense counsel and court bailiffs escorted her from the courtroom. The judge later permitted her to return after she promised there would be no more outbursts.

The 29-Day Trial

Members of my family who were alive at the time, as well as ancestors who died before I was born on June 5, 1954, attended the proceedings day after day. The trial ran from July 28 through August 25, 1913, in Fulton County Superior Court in Atlanta, Georgia.

My grandfather was present during Leo Frank’s trial for the murder of Mary Phagan. He spoke of it from time to time, but the memories were difficult for him because of the feelings they brought back. The case and the courtroom atmosphere remained deeply painful subjects.

The Antisemitism Claim

The historical record should be handled carefully, because it is often manipulated by Leo Frank activists. There is no reliable contemporary evidence that mobs at the trial were chanting, “Hang the Jew,” despite the claim’s frequent repetition in later accounts. That false claim of mob domination has been repeated so many times that some take it for granted. 

This does not mean antisemitism did not exist anywhere in Atlanta or in the larger public controversy surrounding Leo Frank in later years during 1914 and 1915 by Tom Watson making antisemitic comments in his Jeffersonian Weekly in 1914+ or Watson's Magazine of 1915. 

Nor does it erase the fact that Frank was lynched in 1915 because of his crime, not his religion. But it does mean that the specific story of a courtroom mob chanting “Hang the Jew” during the 1913 trial should not be presented as settled fact.

The available record does not substantiate the claim that jurors were threatened with words such as, “Hang the Jew or we’ll hang you.” Later narratives have often repeated the allegation without identifying a contemporary newspaper report, court transcript, or other primary source that proves it occurred.

Newspaper Coverage

Only one newspaper, the New York Sun, appears to have reported Rachel Frank’s outburst plainly. Atlanta newspapers softened the incident or omitted the exact words she used.

The wider coverage of the trial shows why claims must be separated from sources. Contemporary reporting and the official trial record should be the starting point, particularly when evaluating claims about what was said in the courtroom or among spectators outside it.
